Washington remained in constant contact with Ankara, Rubio said, pointing to Türkiye’s role in hosting talks between Russia and Ukraine.
He suggested that U.S. investment in its relationship with Türkiye could help diplomatic efforts.
On the proposed electricity interconnector between Greece and Greek Cyprus, Rubio said Washington would use private diplomacy to address obstacles to the project, which it considered important for diversifying energy supplies.
The United States and Greece also announced $4 billion in military sales following their strategic dialogue in Athens on Oct. 7.
The package includes upgrades to Greek F-16 fighter jets and purchases of missiles and precision-guided bombs, according to Greek officials.
Asked about Greece’s request for specific advanced weapons for its F-35s, including systems supplied to Israel, Rubio said the matter remained under review and that Trump would make the final decision.

articles.title: Zelenskyy blasts US over Russia ties as strikes kill 78 in Ukraine
articles.body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy accused the United States of being unwilling to help Ukraine after Russian strikes killed 78 people and wounded 215 across the country in two days, urging President Donald Trump to increase military support and sanctions against Moscow.
The attacks included a devastating strike on the eastern city of Kramatorsk, where at least 35 people were killed and 20 wounded, according to Ukrainian officials.
The bombardment followed a major Russian drone and missile assault a day earlier that killed dozens, including 22 people in a residential building in Pryluky, about 130 kilometers (80 miles) east of Kyiv.
Speaking to reporters Thursday in Pryluky, Zelenskyy criticized Washington for pursuing potential economic cooperation with Russia while attempting to mediate the war, now in its fifth year.
He also called on the United States to expand Ukraine's access to the Starlink satellite communications network, saying it could help Ukrainian forces identify and target Russian ballistic missile launchers.
"Open Starlink for Ukraine. You did open it when you were responding to Iran," Zelenskyy said. "Give it to us, help us defend our skies and dominate there. And then Putin will sit down at the negotiating table."
The Ukrainian leader questioned U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio's assessment earlier Thursday that the war had reached a stalemate and Washington would continue working toward a settlement.
Zelenskyy argued that Washington's pursuit of economic projects with Moscow contradicted claims that diplomatic progress had stalled.
"So where's the truth here, where's the honesty? Where's the stalemate? ... That's called unwillingness," he said.
"One cannot, on the one hand, negotiate with the Russians about future economic projects, whilst on the other hand say that we find ourselves in some sort of ... diplomatic stalemate," he added.
His remarks followed a Reuters report that senior Russian and U.S. officials, including U.S. Special Envoy Jared Kushner, had discussed bringing an American investor into the Nord Stream pipeline network, which transported Russian natural gas to Germany before Moscow's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
Zelenskyy urged Trump to increase sanctions pressure on Russia, arguing that stronger support for Ukraine could help bring Russian President Vladimir Putin to the negotiating table.
Ukrainian negotiators are scheduled to travel to the United States on Friday and Saturday for talks. Zelenskyy said he expected European partners to join the discussions, with air defense expected to be a key issue amid continued Russian attacks.
In Kramatorsk, a Russian guided aerial bomb struck the city Thursday, killing dozens and damaging two buses. A subsequent drone attack killed two more people, bringing the reported death toll to 35.
Regional Governor Vadym Filashkin accused Russian forces of deliberately targeting civilians.
"The Russians are deliberately targeting civilians. For them, a bus full of passengers is an attractive target precisely because a single strike can kill as many people as possible," he said on Telegram.
Images released by officials showed bodies scattered across a debris-covered street beside a charred bus. Some victims had not been identified, Zelenskyy said, warning that the attack would not go unanswered.
Elsewhere, a Russian guided aerial bomb killed two people in a village in southeastern Dnipropetrovsk region, while another person died in the western city of Ivano-Frankivsk, local authorities said.
The latest bombardment followed Wednesday's attacks, which killed dozens across Ukraine, including 22 people in Pryluky.
Russia also attacked Kyiv on Thursday morning, killing four people and wounding 19, Mayor Vitali Klitschko said.
The strikes disrupted water and electricity supplies in parts of the capital, with officials warning that restoring services would take time.
Moscow has intensified drone attacks on Kyiv in recent weeks, targeting warehouses, data centers and other infrastructure while renewing its campaign against Ukraine's power grid ahead of winter.
Russian technology company Yandex said it could not yet determine whether equipment at a data center hit by a Ukrainian drone attack could be restored.
Zelenskyy did not specifically address the strike on Yandex but said Ukraine was mirroring Russian attacks on data centers.
Ukraine has sought to regain the battlefield initiative as Russian territorial advances have slowed this year. However, Moscow's sustained air campaign continues to threaten civilians, critical infrastructure and the country's energy security.

articles.title: Wired for War: The German spymaster caught in Mossad’s web
articles.body:
Wired for War: The German spymaster caught in Mossad’s web
It took a bungled kidnapping for Germany’s former spymaster to be charged with espionage and treason, but August Hanning’s ties to Israeli spies and criminals should have set alarm bells ringing in Berlin long ago.
Hanning, who led Germany’s Bundesnachrichtendienst (BND) from 1998 to 2005, was arrested on Tuesday and charged with espionage, the disclosure of state secrets, and treason.
Prosecutors have alleged that Hanning bought state secrets from his former BND aide – identified as ‘Manfred D’, who remained in the agency after Hanning’s departure and served several of his successors. They claim Hanning acquired nearly 2,000 BND documents between 2010 and 2022, which he then leveraged in his work as a private security consultant at-large to the rich and powerful.
Hanning, part of the woodwork on the security conference circuit, used this material to prepare a report for an employee of a foreign intelligence service, and maintained “close contact with a representative of another foreign intelligence service,” to whom he passed information obtained by Manfred D “for several years.”
Prosecutors haven’t publicly identified which foreign services Hanning collaborated with, though media reporting suggests one is believed to be the Foreign Intelligence Service of Azerbaijan, a country Hanning has openly lobbied for since the mid-2010s. As for the other, Hanning’s involvement in a bizarre kidnapping plot suggests one obvious culprit.
The Israeli kidnapping plot
German investigators picked up Hanning’s trail last September, when Hamburg police searched his apartment as part of an investigation involving multi-millionaire Christina Block, whose father built Germany’s most popular steakhouse chain, as well as a burger franchise, boutique hotels and gastro-resorts.
Ms. Block has been in a custody dispute with her ex-husband, Danish banker Stefan Hansel, since 2021. She is currently on trial for ordering the kidnapping of her two youngest children from their father’s care in Denmark. According to prosecutors, Block hired Hanning’s consulting firm, System 360, to carry out the abduction in 2022, but Danish police intervened before the System 360 team could snatch the children.
Hanning apparently gave up on the direct approach and decided to outsource the job to his contacts from the world of intelligence. These contacts were Yaakov Perry, the former chief of Israel’s Shin Bet domestic intelligence agency, and Danny Yatom, the former head of Mossad.
Block’s trial is ongoing and details are murky, but the allegations are as follows: Hanning hired Perry and his private intelligence firm, CGI Group, to assemble an eight-man team to kidnap the children; the German spymaster requested that Yatom be involved; Perry brought in David Barkay, a former member of the IDF’s Unit 504 intelligence wing and alleged Mossad agent; Barkay led the team that carried out the kidnapping on New Year’s Eve, 2023.
Barkay’s team assaulted Hansel and dragged the children – a ten-year-old boy and 13-year-old girl – across the German border on foot, taping their mouths shut and threatening to kill them if they screamed for help.
Hanning denies any role in the kidnapping, as does Yaakov. Barkay has confessed to orchestrating and carrying out the operation, but has not implicated Hanning or Yaakov. Yatom has told Israeli media that he has “no connection to this case,” and furthermore, that his relationship with Hanning was a strictly professional one dating back to the late 1980s.
However, Yatom invited Hanning to join the board of his private cybersecurity company, World Health Energy Holdings (WHEN), in 2021. Speaking to the Jerusalem Post at the time, Hanning said that his “contacts with states, law enforcement and intelligence agencies” would be valuable to WHEN, a company that markets spyware to businesses seeking to monitor their employees.
Hanning added that he maintained “very close working relationships, even friendships” with Yatom and other Mossad officials long after he left the BND. Both men are still listed as board members on WHEN’s website.
The gray man
During his tenure at the BND, Hanning was the consummate ‘gray man’ of intelligence: a gaunt and bespectacled bureaucrat in the mould of John le Carre’s ‘George Smiley’. Le Carre met Hanning several times, and described the German spymaster as “courtesy itself.”
Yet his “career was clouded by speculation about his loyalties, with persistent whispers of too-close-for-comfort ties to Israel and Russia,” according to a recent Irish Times report. Prosecutors have ruled out any suspicion that Hanning colluded with Russian agents, according to German media, leaving only one possibility.
Hanning once remarked that “a good agent is one who doesn’t draw attention to himself.” In the murky world of Israel’s ‘private’ intelligence sector, however, Hanning could hardly have chosen a more conspicuous duo to work with than Yatom and Perry.
The Congo debacle
Perry’s private intelligence firm, CGI Group, is an outfit that will sound familiar to readers of our ‘Wired for War’ series. Founded by former Israeli spies and specializing in illegal or quasi-legal private spycraft, the company boasts that it hires “senior personnel from elite IDF units, the General Security Services and the Mossad.” Among them are:
- Yaakov Perry, president, Shin Bet Director from 1988 to 1995
- Zvika Nave, founder, described by CGI as serving “in many classified positions in the defense system”
- Oren Ziv, Italy manager, described by CGI as a “key figure in Israeli diplomacy and national security”
- Alon Pinkas, consultant, former foreign policy adviser to Israeli Prime Ministers Ehud Barak and Shimon Peres, former Israeli Consul General in New York
Before its alleged involvement in the Block kidnapping, CGI Group became infamous when it attempted to steal $60 million from the Bulgarian government in 2019. Some 30 years earlier, Israeli businessman Gad Zeevi attempted to buy a stake in Bulgaria’s national airline, but the deal fell apart and Zeevi claimed that he was owed $10 million in compensation from Sofia. International arbitrators agreed, but Bulgaria refused to comply with the judgment, and the Israeli government refused to chase the Bulgarians down for the money.
Zeevi reached out to Perry and Nave, who came up with a long-shot scheme to collect the debt. CGI Group would ask the government of the Congo to order $60 million worth of weapons from Bulgaria, with Yatom acting as a go-between. Once the Bulgarians had sent the arms and the Congolese government transferred the money to his account, Yatom would hand it to Zeevi, minus a generous cut for him and his co-conspirators in CGI Group.
It was never clear how CGI would convince the Congolese to order weapons that would never be paid for, and the plan never came to fruition. Zeevi and CGI Group threatened to sue each other for damages, but the case never made it to court.
Yatom and CGI Group refused to comment, giving similar answers as they did when questioned about the Block kidnapping. “I don’t want to talk about my business activities,” Yatom told Israel’s Globes news outlet in 2022. “We don’t talk to the media,” Nave said.
Red flags ignored
Despite the fact that Yatom and the CGI spies colluded to defraud a NATO and EU member state in 2019, German investigators didn’t ask questions when Hanning joined Yatom’s company two years later. No investigation was opened when he spoke to the Israeli media of his “close friendship” with the former Mossad chief behind the swindle. Hanning’s ties to the Israeli intelligence underworld, apparently the subject of “persistent whispers” in the corridors of the BND, were evidently brushed aside or ignored.
None of this is to say that Shin Bet or Mossad is, without a doubt, the “foreign intelligence service” that Hanning passed secrets to. However, his contacts with Perry and Yatom certainly point that way, as does his work to advance Israeli foreign policy goals.
Hanning aided Israeli efforts to push the US into war with Iraq in late 2002, when he told then-CIA Director George Tenet that the BND had “plausible and convincing” evidence that Saddam Hussein was developing chemical and biological weapons. Hanning’s source, an Iraqi defector codenamed ‘Curveball’, later admitted to fabricating the claims.
Hanning now sits on the board of ‘United Against Nuclear Iran’, a Washington-based think tank funded by pro-Israel megadonors Miriam Adelson and Thomas Kaplan, which has explicitly advocated for military strikes on Iran since 2008. Adelson and Kaplan supply around three quarters of the group’s funding, with the remainder coming from smaller Jewish organizations and individual donors.
Europe’s wilful ignorance
Anyone following our ‘Wired for War’ series will recognize the pattern here. Over and over again, the actions of private Israeli spy firms are ignored by European governments, even when the Israeli state itself is involved in the skulduggery. The British government has refused to investigate Israeli meddling in Scottish elections, in order to “avoid giving offense” to the perpetrators. The EU has stayed silent on Israeli interference in elections in Cyprus and Slovenia, and on the proliferation of Israeli spyware throughout the union.
Meanwhile, governments at the EU and national level continue to sound the alarm about Russia’s invisible and unprovable “hybrid war” against the West. Fires, false drone sightings, and even natural disasters are all presented as examples of this shadow war, while the most blatant malfeasance from other foreign powers is ignored.
One day before Hanning’s arrest, his successor at the helm of the BND, Martin Jaeger, warned German MPs that Russia is “waging a shadow war,” and that “no other country currently poses such a direct, comprehensive, and concrete threat to Germany.” Had he looked at the company August Hanning kept, he might have reassessed his position.

articles.title: Ukraine has returned to the club of ballistic missile-producing countries: what the first combat use of the FP-7 changed
articles.body:
Ukraine has returned to the club of ballistic missile-producing countries: what the first combat use of the FP-7 changed
Kyiv • UNN
Indigenous ballistic missiles give Ukraine new capabilities to strike targets at a considerable distance and reduce its dependence on partners’ long-range weapons.
The first combat use of Ukraine’s FP-7 ballistic missile marked an important milestone in restoring the country’s own missile capabilities. After decades during which ballistic missile production in the country had effectively been lost, Ukraine once again acquired the capability to create such systems. FP-7 may now become the foundation for the further development of Ukraine’s missile program, UNN writes.
On October 1, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy reported the first combat use of FP-7, developed by the Ukrainian defense company Fire Point. The launch site and target were not disclosed, but it is known that the missile has a range of about 250 km and a warhead weighing approximately 200 kg.
Returning to the ballistic missile producers’ club
Ukraine already had its own missile industry. During the Soviet era, enterprises operating in our country produced, among other things, intercontinental ballistic missiles. After the collapse of the USSR, a significant portion of these production lines was shut down, and the missile industry declined.
We have a very powerful missile school. Even 10–20 years ago, Ukrainian rockets were launching commercial satellites into space
Therefore, the emergence of FP-7 is significant not only as the creation of a separate weapons system. Following the first combat use of FP-7, The New York Times called it "Ukraine’s return to the small group of countries that produce ballistic missiles."
What Ukraine’s own ballistic missile capability provides
The emergence of its own ballistic missile is also directly important for conducting the war. Serial production of FP-7 could expand Ukraine’s ability to strike targets at a considerable distance from the front line. As experts point out, potential targets could include command posts, ammunition depots, logistics hubs, repair bases, air defense systems, and other military facilities that Russia is attempting to move farther away from the front.
Ukraine is indeed gaining new capabilities on the battlefield. This is a new trump card. The emergence of our own ballistic missile capability changes the balance of capabilities and is of strategic importance. We will no longer merely react—we are gaining the ability to respond
According to him, if Ukraine can scale up FP-7 production, it will have greater freedom in choosing targets and will be less dependent on partners’ supplies of long-range weapons.
FP-7 could become the foundation for the further development of an entire line of Ukrainian ballistic missiles. It may be not just one specific product, but a technological base on which subsequent systems can be created—with different characteristics, ranges, warheads, and operational capabilities. The company (Fire Point—Ed.) has every chance of becoming one of the foundations of Ukraine’s ballistic missile program. It has good specialists and the relevant expertise, and, most importantly, it already has practical experience
The next stage for Ukraine could be the development of missiles with a longer range. Fire Point is simultaneously working on FP-9, which will have a greater range and be capable of striking Moscow.
Therefore, the development of FP-7 and subsequent Ukrainian missile systems could become one of the important elements of a long-term system for deterring Russia. But the key word here is serial production. Individual successful launches demonstrate technological capability, while stable mass production creates a real military capability
Thus, the first combat use of FP-7 was not simply a test of a new missile in the war for Ukraine. It marked the country’s return to the narrow circle of states capable of independently creating ballistic weapons.

articles.title: Ukraine war briefing: Zelenskyy criticises US, calls for more Starlink access, amid deadly Russian assault
articles.body:
- President Volodymyr Zelenskyy accused the US of being unwilling to help Ukraine after a Russian bomb attack on Thursday killed at least 35 people in the east, sending the two-day death toll from Russian strikes to more than 70. Hours after the strike on the embattled city of Kramatorsk tore through two buses, Zelenskyy criticised Washington’s effort to pursue economic ties with Russia while also seeking to mediate the more than four-year war.
- Speaking to reporters in Pryluky, the Ukrainian leader urged the US to accede to his requests to expand Ukraine’s access to the Starlink satellite service to help it target Russian ballistic-missile launchers. “Open Starlink for Ukraine. You did open it when you were responding to Iran ... I’ve said quite openly – give it to us, help us defend our skies and dominate there. And then Putin will sit down at the negotiating table,” he said.
- UN rights chief Volker Turk said he was appalled by Thursday’s “horrifying strike”. “I am appalled by the wave of attacks killing civilians across Ukraine over the past four days, including today’s horrifying strike hitting two public buses,” he said in a statement. “The scale and manner of these attacks – killing and injuring people on buses, at their homes and work in different areas of the country – is reprehensible. In the last two days, 78 people were killed and 215 wounded by strikes across Ukraine, Zelenskyy said.
- Ukrainian negotiators will travel to the US on Friday and Saturday for talks, Zelenskyy said, urging US president Donald Trump to increase sanction pressure on Russia. Ukraine’s president told reporters that he expected Kyiv’s European partners to join the talks with the US. Zelenskyy said his chief of staff, Kyrylo Budanov, as well as Ukraine’s top officials: Rustem Umerov, Sergiy Kyslytsya and David Arakhamia will take part in the talks in Florida.
- The US-led peace efforts to end the Ukraine war have largely stalled, with Washington focused on its conflict with Iran. But US officials said they were making a fresh effort in an enlarged format, following visits to Moscow and Kyiv last month by Witkoff, Trump’s business friend-turned-roving envoy, and the president’s son-in-law Kushner. US officials said the envoys would discuss “security guarantees for Ukraine, a postwar prosperity plan, and other aspects of the conflict”. Witkoff and Kushner “will discuss new ideas and proposals that American negotiators began developing with the Russians and Ukrainians during their recent visit to the region,” a source familiar with the talks said.
- Nato said it would start its annual ‘nuclear deterrence’ exercises in Italy from Tuesday amid mounting concerns about Russia. The drills will run from 13-23 October and involve 17 nations. “The exercise is a long-planned, routine training activity that is part of Nato’s efforts to maintain readiness and test procedures that contribute to the alliance’s deterrence and defence,” said a Nato statement.
- South Korea will recall its ambassador to Ukraine, the foreign minister said on Thursday, following a dispute over Zelenskyy’s announcement that two North Korean prisoners of war were being transferred to Seoul. The two sides have been locked in a dispute after Seoul accused Kyiv of breaching a confidentiality agreement over the transfer of the captured soldiers.

articles.title: Why South Korea and Ukraine Are Fighting Over Two Prisoners of War
articles.body:
On Sept. 23, President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine spoke at the UN General Assembly about the military support Russia was getting from North Korea and the deaths of North Korean soldiers on the Ukrainian front. “Recently, we sent two North Korean prisoners of war to the Republic of Korea,” he revealed. He seemed to be trying to highlight the global reach of Russia’s war and also hoping that the revelation would increase popular and political support in Seoul for providing weapons and aid to Ukraine.
Zelensky ended up igniting a diplomatic dispute between Ukraine and South Korea. Seoul claimed that Ukraine had agreed to keep the transfer confidential; Kyiv denied that such an agreement existed and downplayed the episode as a misunderstanding. Now South Korea is recalling its ambassador to Ukraine.
The quarrel over diplomatic protocol highlights the human cost paid by two soldiers caught in a geopolitical conflict linking European and Northeast Asian security. Their story captures the complicated geopolitics of the two Koreas now playing out on a European battlefield. It also underscores South Korea’s push for inter-Korean peace, even as North Korea tests Seoul’s patience by launching hypersonic missiles and planting landmines.
The men from North Korea
The two soldiers at the center of the dispute were captured while fighting in the Kursk region of Russia in January 2025. They were part of a 10,000-strong North Korean contingent reinforcing Russian troops on the front line. Shortly after their capture, Ukraine’s military released video footage of the two soldiers. The images helped confirm North Korea’s direct involvement in the Russia-Ukraine war. Human Rights Watch raised concerns about Ukraine’s decision to release the video and expose the soldiers, given the potential repercussions for their families in North Korea, including torture, forced labor, imprisonment, or execution.
North Korean soldiers are instructed to take their own lives rather than risk capture. One of the captured soldiers reportedly attempted suicide before a Ukrainian medic stopped him. In North Korea’s eyes, a soldier who survives by surrendering, or worse by defecting to the South, is a traitor. Under the regime’s well-documented system of collective punishment, three generations of a defector’s family can face retribution through guilt by association.
By revealing the prisoner of war transfer to South Korea in New York, Zelensky offered Pyongyang an incentive to make an example of these soldiers’ families to demonstrate the consequences of defection. This stands in stark contrast to the regime’s response to the deaths of North Korean soldiers in Russia. Kim Jong Un, the leader of North Korea, promised their surviving families a “beautiful life” and granted them new luxury apartments.
The North Korean regime may have already tracked down the families of the prisoners of war after Ukraine confirmed their capture in January 2025. But Zelensky’s disclosure at the United Nations renewed the danger facing the two soldiers now resettled in South Korea, a point Seoul highlighted in its protest to Kyiv. A life in South Korea offers these soldiers personal safety, but one could imagine it might come at a crushing cost: abandoning their homes and living with the guilt that their families may suffer in their place.
Mending the rupture between Seoul and Kyiv
If this episode were only about the two North Korean soldiers, their resettlement might have passed unnoticed. The diplomatic kerfuffle between Kyiv and Seoul is rooted in the different geopolitical narratives that each nation seeks to project, or in Seoul’s case, downplay.
For Ukraine, publicizing the presence and resettlement of North Korean prisoners of war provides a valuable opportunity to solicit support from South Korea, a major arms exporter and a vital partner to NATO. Since 2022, Kyiv has been urging Seoul to supply it with lethal weapons, including Patriot interceptors and 155mm artillery shells. In light of Pyongyang’s direct military support for Moscow, Ukraine has intensified pressure on South Korea to move beyond non-lethal military, humanitarian, and economic assistance.
For South Korea, Ukraine’s public disclosure of the resettlement of these soldiers undermines its diplomatic outreach to North Korea. In his address to the UN General Assembly, President Lee Jae Myung of South Korea reiterated his vision of inclusive, peaceful coexistence built on “respect for each other’s systems” and the restoration of cross-border trust with North Korea. Accepting North Korean soldiers while publicly promoting dialogue weakens Lee’s reassurances to Pyongyang that Seoul desires “stable, peaceful coexistence.”
Pyongyang has maintained silence regarding these two soldiers. But North Korea considers South Korea’s reception of defectors as part of an effort to undermine its regime and eventually bring about unification on Seoul’s terms. While North Korea now defines the Koreas as two separate states, article four of South Korea’s constitution commits the nation to “peaceful unification based on the basic free and democratic order.”
As two nations dedicated to promoting freedom and democratic principles, South Korea and Ukraine must look beyond this diplomatic disagreement to protect their partnership. Seoul provided $400 million in aid to Ukraine in 2024 and announced $2.3 billion in long-term reconstruction aid through 2027. In return, Ukraine offers critical, real-world intelligence on North Korean military tactics and the weapons technology Pyongyang receives from Russia.
Given the complex legal situation of North Korean combatants captured by Ukrainian forces, Kyiv and Seoul must establish a protocol for handling North Korean prisoners of war and non-combatant defectors who seek asylum in South Korea. The need for such a policy will only grow. Similar episodes may unfold as the presence of North Korean troops and laborers in Russia grows, increasing the potential for future defections. Zelensky recently warned that another 10,000 troops from North Korea could soon be deployed in Russia.
With Kyiv’s cooperation, Seoul should affirm its commitment to accept future North Korean prisoners who voluntarily request resettlement, subject to standard security screening. That policy must fully comply with South Korean law and uphold international humanitarian principles and the values of a democratic society. To safeguard these individuals, both governments should protect prisoners’ identities, grant confidential access to impartial humanitarian representatives, and ensure that decisions are not made under coercion. Prisoners of war should not be forcibly repatriated, and public announcements of their transfer must be avoided without their explicit consent.
Crucially, not every captured North Korean soldier will want to go to South Korea. Their wishes must be determined through private, independent interviews conducted without pressure from governments, intelligence agencies, advocacy groups, or the media. Both governments may have followed such protocols. It remains unclear whether Ukraine eventually deviated from the agreed approach script or whether there was simply miscommunication.
Yet for the two soldiers already resettled, no policy can erase the personal toll. They must now rebuild their lives in a country they were raised to view as the enemy while carrying the lingering anguish about the fate of the families they left behind.

articles.title: Zelensky Visits Pryluky With UK’s Miliband, Thanks EU for €1.2B Tranche for Drones
articles.body:
President Volodymyr Zelensky traveled to Pryluky with UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband to honor the victims after a Russian barrage – coinciding with Russian President Vladimir Putin’s 74th birthday – left 22 civilians dead, including five children.
In a series of statements issued on Thursday, Oct. 8, Zelensky condemned Wednesday’s strikes and confirmed that the strike on the apartment building left 54 people injured. During the visit, the two leaders met with residents who survived the attack and were briefed on the scale of the destruction.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“We must support our people,” Zelensky said, pointing to a veteran who lived in the apartment building destroyed by Russia.
“When partners are literally standing alongside Ukrainians, it truly matters,” he continued, thanking Miliband for standing beside him in Pryluky and alluding to Western partners who continue supplying Kyiv with funding and air defense it needs to protect itself against Russia’s aggression.
A city left without homes and shelters
The damage extends far beyond the destroyed building. According to Zelensky, more than 100 residential buildings across Pryluky were damaged, along with schools, kindergartens, shops, businesses and other critical infrastructure the city depends on.
Residents who spoke with the president described a shortage of both shelters and housing. In response, Zelensky ordered the head of the Chernihiv Regional Military Administration to quickly help those who have nowhere to live, adding that temporary assistance should eventually be followed by permanent solutions.
Trump Envoys in Talks With Putin’s Money Man Over Russian Gas, Reports Say
“It is also important that the victims ultimately receive new housing,” he said.
Those whose homes were in the destroyed building should be allowed back into their apartments once the security situation permits, Zelensky said, placing the head of the State Emergency Service (SES) in charge of the process.
Human cost of Russia’s war
Ukrainian authorities consistently remind their partners that the war is not a distant fact on paper, but a reality measured in human lives and relentless terror.
This became particularly visible in the last few weeks, as Russia increased its strikes on civilians and civilian infrastructure following the departure of senior US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner from Moscow.
The two visited Moscow on Sept. 5 to hold talks with Russian diplomats and Putin himself, aiming to broker an end to the war. For the first time ever during their tenure, the envoys also visited Kyiv just a day after.
Despite all three sides describing the negotiations as positive and productive, Russian barrage amplified.
The latest attack on Pryluky left 17 civilians hospitalized, including a five-year-old girl. It also highlighted gaps in the city’s protection.
After the health minister briefed him on efforts to build shelters in medical facilities, Zelensky ordered officials to speed up the work and secure additional funding. The hospital’s own shelter must be repaired as a priority, he said, while a new, modern one is built in its place.
Together with city authorities, the health minister and the head of the Chernihiv Regional Military Administration will be responsible for the project, Zelensky said.
He also tasked the interior ministers with inspecting every shelter in the city.
Deadliest strike in a wave of attacks
The Pryluky attack was the deadliest in a broader Russian assault launched on Wednesday, Oct. 7.
A Kh-101 cruise missile was used to strike the five-story apartment block as Russia targeted cities across Ukraine with ballistic and cruise missiles, as well as Shahed drones, before continuing with aerial bombs during the day.
As rescuers continued recovering bodies, the toll from Russia’s latest attacks kept rising. By Thursday, Zelensky said strikes on Pryluky, Kramatorsk, Kyiv and other cities had killed 78 people and injured 215 in recent days alone.
He described the attacks as a severe escalation and “terror directed against people and life,” warning that world leaders must not ignore what is happening.
EU and US support to continue
The same concerns were raised during a telephone call with European Council President António Costa later on Thursday.
Zelensky also thanked Costa for the €1.2 billion (l $1.4 billion) tranche that arrived in Ukraine on Wednesday, saying the money would go toward defense, primarily drones.
“This will provide tremendous support,” Zelensky said.
Beyond immediate military needs, the two leaders discussed the timeline for opening the next clusters in Ukraine’s EU accession talks, a winter energy package and further financial assistance. The call came ahead of the EC summit in Brussels, scheduled for Oct. 15-16.
Between Zelensky and Costa, an agreement was reached to meet in a trilateral format with European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen.
Zelensky also briefed the EC President on meetings with US officials planned for the coming days, particularly Oct. 9-10, noting that a Ukrainian delegation is already on its way.

articles.title: Russia has a plan for Ukraine this winter, Ukraine says: intercepted document reportedly outlines up to 1,000 missiles, drones, and bombs targeting 60 critical infrastructure sites
articles.body:
Russia is planning a winter strike campaign involving up to 1,000 missiles, drones, and bombs targeting, among other facilities, electrical substations, hydroelectric and thermal power plants, and boiler houses. The information is contained in a document that, according to sources cited by The New York Times, Ukraine's Energy Minister Denys Shmyhal presented as an intercepted Russian plan to destroy energy infrastructure systematically. The newspaper reported on 2 October.
Russia has been striking critical infrastructure across Ukraine since the beginning of its full-scale invasion. Such attacks have become particularly frequent ahead of and during winter. Ukraine's recent battlefield gains may have prompted Putin to reconsider his strategy and attempt to force Ukraine to surrender through winter strikes, analysts at the Institute for the Study of War (ISW) suggest. Russia's reported plans to attack Ukraine's energy, water supply, and sewage systems could threaten the basic living conditions of millions of people. Such strikes could increase pressure on civilians and the Ukrainian economy while forcing the state to divert more resources to emergency infrastructure repairs instead of defense needs.
The New York Times was unable to verify the document's authenticity independently, but noted that it was written in Russian and dated August.
Warehouses, a home-improvement store, a farm: Russia’s strikes aimed past the grid at Ukraine’s civilian economy
A representative of Ukraine's defense-industrial sector who has reviewed the document believes it is more of a calculation than a finalized Russian military operations plan, according to Schemes, an investigative journalism project by Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty (RFE/RL), in a report published on 8 October.
60 targets: how Russia could attack Ukraine's critical infrastructure
The document outlines how many missiles, drones, and bombs Russia would need to deprive Kyiv, Kharkiv, and Odesa of electricity, heating, water, and sewage services, Radio Liberty reported on 9 October. The document's full list of priority cities also includes Dnipro, Zaporizhzhia, Mykolaiv, Kherson, Poltava, Chernihiv, Kryvyi Rih, Cherkasy, Kropyvnytskyi, Lviv, Vinnytsia, and Ivano-Frankivsk.
According to the document, Russia plans to begin by attacking substations near Ukraine's western border, through which the country receives electricity from Europe. Hydroelectric power plants could be targeted next, followed by facilities intended to shut down Ukraine's three operational nuclear power plants, Radio Liberty reports. The document lists a total of 60 key targets.
According to Schemes, the document states that Russia would need up to 770 Molniya and Geran drones, Dan-T/Banderol missile-drones, 170 FAB guided aerial bombs, and 75 Kinzhal and Iskander-M ballistic missiles to carry out the attacks.
Sewage systems could become Russia's next target
The document devotes particular attention to water supply and wastewater systems. These include pumping stations, treatment facilities, and other infrastructure essential for cities to provide residents with water and dispose of wastewater.
Russia has not previously attacked such facilities on a similar scale, The New York Times notes.
Preparing for possible attacks on water supply and sewage systems is significantly more difficult than protecting energy infrastructure, Oleh Popenko, head of the Ukrainian Union of Utility Services Consumers, told Current Time, RFE/RL's Russian-language network.
“Sewage is a very complex system. There are specific challenges: where to discharge wastewater, how to organize treatment facilities, and so on. Some work is also underway in this sector, but it will be much more difficult here than with district heating utilities,” Popenko says.
Creating alternative routes in case sewage pumping stations are destroyed is an expensive and technically challenging task, he adds. Such construction could cost billions of hryvnias.
14 dead in Pryluky, two each in Kyiv, Kremenchuk, and Oleksandriia: Russia’s night of 70 missiles
The priority is to equip water utilities with backup power sources so they can continue operating during power outages. However, if Russian strikes damage the sewage system itself, resolving the problem quickly will be much more difficult, Popenko believes. Specific solutions, including wastewater disposal and the operation of treatment facilities, will have to be determined according to the extent of the damage.
Sewage pumping stations play a particularly important role. They pump wastewater onward for disposal and treatment. If such a station is put out of operation by a strike, the city needs an alternative way to divert wastewater while the damaged facility is being repaired, Popenko says. Bypass pipes or channels could be installed for this purpose, but setting up such a system during wartime is far from easy.
Air defenses remain crucial to Ukraine's winter preparations
Preparations for winter are underway, but protection for energy infrastructure remains inadequate, Popenko believes. The main concern is large substations that transmit electricity from nuclear power plants and distribute electricity imported from Europe.
At the same time, some protective measures are already proving effective. Despite drone attacks over two days, one of Kyiv's substations withstood the strikes, and the city did not lose power, although scheduled outages were in effect, the expert says.
Popenko considers a repeat of last winter's scenario, when parts of Kyiv went without heating for weeks, entirely possible. Russian forces continue to attack energy facilities, and in his assessment, strengthening air defenses in Kyiv is the only way to protect its combined heat and power (CHP) plants from large-scale attacks.
“There are no other ways — for example, building some sarcophagi around CHPs or constructing shelters — because Russia can destroy these facilities again through massive strikes. And then the city risks being left 50–60% without heat,” Popenko believes.
Residents are also preparing for winter, but their options vary, he says. Some homeowners' associations participate in government programs to insulate apartment buildings and purchase backup power supplies for elevators and pumping stations. Owners of private houses are buying generators, among other measures. However, such equipment and preparations require substantial funds, meaning not everyone can afford them, he notes.
Ukraine has already experienced prolonged power outages during previous winters, particularly in 2022 and 2023. At the time, some regions went without electricity for 18–20 hours a day, the expert says. This experience may help people prepare for possible disruptions, but it does not eliminate the risk of further attacks and infrastructure damage.

articles.title: UK Announces $71M Winter Aid, New Sanctions on Russia
articles.body:
UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband pledged £54 million ($71 million) to Ukraine ahead of winter and unveiled fresh sanctions against Russia on Thursday, Oct. 8, during his first visit to the country since taking office.
Miliband announced the measures alongside President Volodymyr Zelensky and Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha, with whom he toured the site of a deadly Russian missile strike in Pryluky, in the Chernihiv region.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Five winters on, the people of Ukraine are still living under constant threat of Russian strikes, energy blackouts and death,” Miliband said, according to the UK governmental website.
“My message to [Russian President Vladimir] Putin is clear – You cannot wait us out,” he continued, reaffirming UK’s support for Ukraine despite ongoing hybrid warfare threats from Russia, which have significantly intensified in recent months.
The UK pledged another £6 million (approximately $8 million) to Ukraine specifically for the “pursuit of justice” for Russia’s war crimes. As of Oct. 2, Ukraine had opened nearly 244,000 criminal cases over crimes committed by Russian forces and their accomplices on the country’s territory, including almost 227,000 war-crime investigations.
Strike on Pryluky left 22 people dead
The strike on an apartment building in Pryluky coincided with Russian Putin’s 74th birthday, and it left at least 22 civilians dead, including five children.
Zelensky Visits Pryluky With UK’s Miliband, Thanks EU for €1.2B Tranche for Drones
According to Zelensky, 54 people were injured just in that strike alone, while the overall number of Russian attacks left 78 people dead and 215 injured nationwide in recent days. He described the attacks as a severe escalation and “terror directed against people and life,” warning that world leaders must not ignore what is happening.
During their visit earlier on Thursday, the three leaders spoke with survivors of the attack and with emergency workers who had taken part in the rescue effort.
“Russia could end this war tomorrow,” Miliband said. “Instead, we’ve seen escalating attacks, including on key infrastructure and Ukrainian cultural landmarks.”
According to him, the UK’s support for Ukraine is rooted not only in European and NATO security, but also in a wider global effort to defend justice and the rule of law.
How the funding will be allocated
The new funding comes as Ukraine continues to appeal to its Western allies for air defense and financial support ahead of the upcoming winter, when Russia is expected to intensify its campaign against critical infrastructure, including the power grid and water-supply systems.
Of the total pledged, £20 million (about $26 million) will go toward Ukraine’s energy security; to support crews carrying out emergency repairs to the power grid after Russian strikes, provide backup generators and solar power for use during blackouts, as well as to fund technologies to help Ukraine diversify its energy sources.
The remaining £34 million (roughly $45 million) will be allocated for heating and water systems. According to the UK’s government, the amount also includes direct cash assistance.
Aid will be delivered together with the Ukrainian government and partners including UNICEF, the UN Refugee Agency (UNHCR) and the Ukrainian Red Cross.
Fresh sanctions on Russia
Beyond financial support, Miliband announced fresh sanctions on around 40 individuals and entities in Russia’s financial, oil, and technology sectors.
With the latest package, more than 90% of Russia’s total oil production capacity is now covered by UK sanctions, according to the government.
So far, Britain has sanctioned more than 600 vessels and over 3,500 targets in total under its Russia sanctions regime.
On Oct.1, the UK has announced a new package of 31 sanctions, focusing on global disinformation networks and individuals responsible for the torture of Ukrainian civilians and the forced deportation of children.
Late September, when the EU compromised on the extension of the sanctions on about 3,000 individuals and entities in exchange for the delistment of two Russian oligarchs closely connected to Putin, the UK pledged to keep its own sanctions in place.
The measures are intended to send a message to Russian diplomats and those who support Russia’s war to step back from escalation and move toward a ceasefire.
According to Sybiha’s statement on X, the meeting coincided with the sixth anniversary of the Agreement on Political Cooperation, Free Trade and Strategic Partnership, which Ukraine and the UK signed in London.
Since then, he said, relations between the two countries have reached a new level, strengthened by the historic 100 Year Partnership Agreement that their leaders signed in Kyiv last year.
“We also launched the second meeting of the Political Pillar of the Ukraine-UK Strategic Partnership Dialogue and agreed to continue expert-level discussions in Kyiv,” Sybiha said, expressing gratitude to the UK for its “comprehensive support” – which currently equates to £25 billion (about $33 billion), including £16 billion (roughly $21 billion) in military support.

articles.title: How Real is the Threat of War in Europe?
articles.body:
A growing number of official bodies are warning of the possibility of Russia launching military operations against Europe. Germany’s Federal Intelligence Service said on Monday that there was an increased risk of hybrid attacks by Moscow, and Belgian Defence Minister Theo Francken has said the continent faces a “dark winter” and called for drone defence to become top priority. Denmark’s intelligence service has also warned of the growing risk of a limited military attack on a Nato country in the coming months.
Disinformation and panic-mongering
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Moscow is using intimidation tactics, warns Der Standard (Austria) :
“Russia is no longer merely pressing its most dangerous weapon against our foreheads – it has long since pulled the trigger. Its disinformation has been corroding European minds for years now, sowing doubts about Ukraine’s independence – as if it were up to Moscow to decide who governs there and whether or not the country joins Nato. Worse still, Moscow’s fifth column equates perpetrators with victims and stokes fears about an enraged Russia lashing out against Berlin and Vienna if it is further provoked. ... The reasoning behind this is simple: people who feel threatened will think twice before sending weapons to Ukraine.”
Putin targeting German trauma
Putin’s war threats land on particularly fertile soil in Germany, writes the Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung (Germany) :
Rubio Touts US Power, Calls on Europe to Emerge From ‘Slumber’
“Whereas the war is a political instrument for Putin, for the Germans it must be avoided at any price. The traumas inflicted by two world wars and the Nazi regime run deep, shaping public opinion and security policy decisions to this day. Germans are no more than moderately willing to take up arms to defend the nation. ... Putin is also stepping up his hybrid war as a way to get the political parties in Germany to demand an end to support for Ukraine. This, too, is meant to fuel the Germans’ fear of war and undermine their already limited spirit of resistance.”
Moscow holds the trump cards for now
Political analyst Kirill Rogov warns on Facebook about the Russian weapons that could potentially overwhelm Europe (Russia) :
“Moscow has expanded its arsenal of missile-type weapons. ... This development increases the threat not just for Ukraine, but also for Europe, which right now is virtually defenceless against such missile and drone attacks. With time, Europe will mobilise its resources and develop a response to the challenges from the air. But precisely this increases the incentive for the Kremlin to use this temporary ‘window of opportunity’ to test Europe’s mettle. In other words, it increases the likelihood of an imminent escalation by the Kremlin on the European stage.”
Perilous period ahead of mid-terms
ERR warns (Estonia) :
“Nuclear weapons are Russia’s last resort. Conventional weapons will never be enough to defeat Ukraine, let alone prevail in a conflict that pits it against the whole of Europe. But before that, it will test the effectiveness of hybrid means like sabotage, assassinations, electoral interference, etc. The aim is to intimidate Europeans enough to make them either end or at least reduce their support for Ukraine. A perilous period lies ahead. Russia might feel compelled to take some sort of action against Europe ahead of next month’s mid-term elections in the US. Because these elections could drastically change Washington’s attitude towards Russia, which until now has been very tolerant.”
Zero tolerance for border provocations
According to reports from Latvia, armed individuals attempted to smuggle a group of migrants from Belarus into the country on Wednesday. Shortly afterwards, masked men reportedly entered EU territory illegally, damaging electricity distribution boxes and stealing CCTV cameras in the process. Delfi calls for effective border protection measures for Latvia and Estonia (Estonia) :
“This kind of hybrid pressure fits the picture of the Putin camp and its determination to provoke problems in the West, which supports Ukraine. All it takes is for organised criminal groups to go about their business while the Belarusian authorities turn a blind eye. ... Latvia’s border must be reinforced to ensure that such provocations fail next time. At the same time it serves as a warning to Estonia – our eastern border must also hold firm. It must be rapidly upgraded into a military protection zone.”

articles.title: Long-Range Anti-Ship Missile Will Integrate onto B-52
articles.body:
The Air Force’s B-52 bomber may soon be able to carry up to 20 stealthy long-range anti-ship missiles to strike moving targets at sea, a key capability in a potential fight with China.
An Oct. 7 notice from Naval Air Systems Command states that the command plans to award a contract to Lockheed Martin to integrate its Long-Range Anti-Ship Missile on the B-52.
The anticipated award “is for efforts associated with LRASM integration on the B-52 aircraft platform, to include missile software updates, associated testing, test asset repair, and failure review boards,” the notice states.
The B-52 can already carry up to 20 Joint Air-to-Surface Standoff Missiles, on which the LRASM is based. The two missiles share similar dimensions.
Naval News first reported on the possibility of integrating the LRASM onto the B-52 in 2019, though the idea languished for several years. But the ability to put LRASMs on the B-52 would have massive implications in a large-scale conflict, retired Air Force Col. Mark Gunzinger, a former B-52 pilot, told Air & Space Forces Magazine.
“A handful of B-52s will be able to deliver more weapons on maritime targets and do so over much longer ranges than the Navy’s carrier-based aircraft per day,” said Gunzinger, now as the director of future concepts and capability assessments for the Mitchell Institute of Aerospace Studies.
Spokespeople for NAVAIR and Air Force Life Cycle Management Center did not immediately responded to a request for comment. Lockheed spokesperson Scott Swofford declined to provide any further details about the effort, deferring to the Pentagon, but did tout LRASM’s capabilities.
“As a precise, stealthy and survivable cruise missile, LRASM provides multiservice, multiplatform, and multimission capabilities for offensive anti-surface warfare,” Swofford said. “By leveraging Lockheed Martin’s expertise in successful cruise missile productions, LRASM brings low-risk and long-term, flexible capabilities to the warfighters’ anti-surface warfare environment that no other inventory weapon provides.”
A Necessary Tool
The Oct. 7 notice continues a push to integrate LRASM onto the bomber fleet—the Air Force revealed in June that a B-2A Spirit employed a LRASM to strike a decommissioned amphibious transport vessel during a Pacific exercise, the first time the U.S. military has acknowledged the B-2’s use of that missile.
Such a pairing is important, Gunzinger said.
“The Air Force’s bomber force will be our military’s predominant maritime strike force, considering the number of anti-ship cruise missiles they can carry per sortie and deliver over intercontinental ranges, if necessary,” Gunzinger said. “And LRASMs will give our bomber force the ability to strike moving targets at sea with unprecedented accuracy.”
The move will expand commanders’ options to strike maritime targets while launching from airbases in lower threat density areas, he said, without putting aircraft carriers at risk.
LRASM Development
- 2009: DARPA and the U.S. Navy initiate the program to develop advanced anti-ship strike capabilities.
- 2012: DARPA cancels the supersonic LRASM-B variant to focus exclusively on the subsonic, stealthy LRASM-A based on the JASSM-ER.
- 2013: Lockheed Martin completes the first successful air-launch flight test of the missile from a USAF B-1B bomber.
- 2015: The Pentagon officially designates the stealthy anti-ship missile as the AGM-158C.
- 2017: Lockheed Martin receives the first low-rate initial production contract
- 2018: The U.S. Air Force achieves Early Operational Capability with the AGM-158C on the B-1B Lancer.
- 2019: The U.S. Navy achieves Early Operational Capability integrating the missile onto F/A-18E/F Super Hornets.
- 2024: The U.S. Navy completes four-missile salvo testing and begins flight testing the round on the F-35C
- 2025: Initial flight testing expands to the F-35B short-takeoff/vertical-landing variant.
- 2026: Lockheed Martin expands factory capacity and contract modifications to boost annual production.
Sources: Lockheed Martin, Air & Space Forces Magazine, USNI
LRASM and JASSM
Lockheed produces both the the AGM-158 JASSM and the AGM-158C LRASM. There is also the AGM-158-JASSM Extended Range variant, which can hit targets out to 500 miles.
Currently, the B-1B Lancer, B-2A Spirit, B-52H Stratofortress, F-15 variants, F-16 variants, and C-130 Hercules can carry the JASSM.
The Air Force is also integrating the JASSM onto the F-35A Lightning II and the B-21 Raider.
The LRASM’s range hovers close to the baseline JASSM variant, just beyond 200 miles.
Air & Space Forces Magazine recently reported on JASSM and LRASM production progress based on Pentagon acquisition reports released in July.
The reports noted that, as of April, the Navy and Air Force were expanding their production plans for the shared munition. Lockheed had delivered a total of 5,348 JASSMs to both services. The company’s current production capacity is 600 JASSMs a year, with short-term plans to boost that to 860 missiles annually.
That’s key, as a recent Center for a New American Security report estimates that the Air Force has ripped through a quarter of its JASSM inventory during Operation Epic Fury.
Lockheed announced a new AGM-158 JASSM-FLEX variant in September at the AFA Air, Space & Cyber conference. The new variant lets users swap out the nose and launch options for various payloads and other configuration needs, which might include an LRASM option.
“The AGM-158 FLEX airframe concept was driven by a strategic need to keep pace with rapidly evolving threats, insert emerging technologies quickly, manage obsolescence, and provide, at scale, a cost-effective missile family that can be repurposed for a wide range of missions while delivering timely, relevant capability to the warfighter,” a Lockheed Martin spokesperson told Air & Space Forces Magazine via email.
The Air Force spent $200 million in fiscal 2025 for a second-source engine for the LRASM and JASSM-ER. Lockheed plans to spend between $8 and $9 million through 2030 to boost production on existing lines.

articles.title: Lithuania moves to lift constitutional ban on nuclear weapons: What it means
articles.body:
Lithuania’s parliament has taken the first step toward removing a constitutional ban on weapons of mass destruction being present on its territory, a move supporters say would allow the country to participate more fully in NATO’s nuclear deterrence arrangements.
The Seimas voted 106-18, with six abstentions, in favour of removing Article 137 of the Constitution. The provision prohibits weapons of mass destruction and foreign military bases on Lithuanian territory.
The change is not yet final. Under Lithuania’s constitutional amendment procedure, lawmakers must vote twice, with at least three months between votes. The proposal must receive at least 94 votes – two thirds of the total – in favour in each ballot.
Supporters stress that removing the provision would not automatically lead to nuclear weapons being stationed in Lithuania. Instead, they say, it would remove a legal obstacle to participation in NATO deterrence activities, including exercises involving allied aircraft or ships carrying nuclear weapons.
Why does Lithuania want to change the Constitution?
Conservative Homeland Union leader Laurynas Kasčiūnas, a former defence minister, said Lithuania’s current constitutional restrictions prevent it from participating fully in NATO’s nuclear deterrence plans.
He noted that Estonia, Latvia, Finland and Poland do not have the same constitutional prohibition.
Under the existing provision, nuclear weapons cannot be stationed in Lithuania, and even the flight of aircraft carrying such weapons over Lithuanian territory is prohibited, Kasčiūnas said. The restriction also prevents allied vessels carrying nuclear weapons from entering the country’s territorial waters.
“Given the current restriction, we cannot participate fully in NATO’s nuclear deterrence plans,” Kasčiūnas told parliament, describing nuclear deterrence as a central element of the alliance’s broader deterrence strategy.
Removing the ban would give Lithuania greater flexibility to participate in allied activities intended to deter potential adversaries, supporters argue.
Former Defence Minister Arvydas Anušauskas, also a conservative, said the amendment would enable more comprehensive participation in deterrence exercises, rather than necessarily leading to the deployment of nuclear weapons.
Social Democrat Remigijus Motuzas similarly argued that removing Article 137 would not turn Lithuania into a nuclear-armed state or mean that nuclear warheads would immediately appear in the country.
Would nuclear weapons be stationed in Lithuania?
Not automatically. Removing the constitutional prohibition would eliminate one legal barrier, but it would not itself authorize a decision to deploy nuclear weapons in Lithuania. Liberal Movement leader Viktorija Čmilytė-Nielsen said any future decisions on deploying such capabilities would require separate legislation.
“What specific measures will be needed for our security is something we will decide ourselves, of course together with our allies,” she said.
What about chemical and biological weapons?
Kasčiūnas rejected claims that removing Article 137 would open the door to the use of chemical or biological weapons.
He said Lithuania had ratified international conventions in 1997 and 1998 that have the force of law and prohibit the proliferation, production or use of those weapons.
Who opposes the change, and why?
Opposition to the amendment was concentrated among lawmakers from the opposition Nemunas Dawn party. Fourteen of its members voted against the proposal and two abstained.
Aidas Gedvilas of Nemunas Dawn questioned whether parliament should make such a consequential change without a public vote. He called for a referendum, arguing that alternative approaches were available.
Vitalijus Šeršniovas, a member of the Seimas’ mixed parliamentary group, proposed a narrower solution that would address the need to allow aircraft carrying nuclear weapons to fly over Lithuania without removing the entire constitutional provision.
He also argued that the issue should be decided by referendum.
Three other members of the mixed group and one lawmaker from the Lithuanian Farmers and Greens Union and Christian Families Alliance parliamentary group also voted against the amendment.
The existing Article 137 covers both weapons of mass destruction and foreign military bases. The proposal under consideration would remove the provision rather than replace it with a narrower rule.

articles.title: Lithuania puts up to 100 soldiers on Kaliningrad border as officials brace for possible Russian mobilization
articles.body:
Lithuania plans to deploy up to 100 soldiers to support border guards along its frontier with Russia's Kaliningrad Oblast, Defense Minister Robertas Kaunas said on 7 October.
Lithuanian Interior Minister Martynas Katelynas has described the deployment as a preventive measure linked to possible Russian mobilization and a recent incident on the Latvia-Belarus border, where masked, armed escorts tried to push a group of migrants into Latvia. Katelynas said Lithuania could face people trying to avoid mobilization and seeking asylum.
Kaunas said he had granted permission to use Lithuanian soldiers to strengthen border protection for the next several weeks.
“The order starts being implemented immediately,” he wrote on Facebook.
Russia denies a new mobilization
The Kremlin denies a new mobilization is coming. In early September, Russian President Vladimir Putin called reports of one "complete nonsense" and "an information attack on Russia." Ukraine's military and foreign intelligence services say Russia's General Staff has prepared a scenario to mobilize 600,000 people over 2026 and 2027. On 28 September, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that "in effect, the Russians have already begun additional mobilization."
Frontier-station patrols for a couple of weeks, possibly longer
On 8 October, the Lithuanian army said soldiers were being brought in to help the State Border Guard Service from that day. A company-sized unit was planned for the assignment, initially for two weeks, with the option to extend. Soldiers will patrol with border guards in frontier-station areas, while mobile patrols, mobile observation posts, and military police crews may be added as needed. The army described the deployment as preventive and a normal form of interagency cooperation.
Kaunas had told LRT TV the soldiers would stay until 16 October. On the morning of 8 October, he said the deployment "was supposed to start" overnight and that he would check with the army. On 8 October, the Lithuanian army said soldiers were being brought in to help the State Border Guard Service from that day. Kaunas also said that “on the Kaliningrad side” there were no physical barriers, unlike the border with Belarus.
Lithuania says its border guards are stretched
On 8 October, Katelynas said the border guard service’s capacity was insufficient, with shifts growing while officer numbers were not increasing. He said the threat level had not changed. In a Facebook post the previous day, he said the situation at Lithuania’s border was calm and there was no reason to panic. He said Russia was planning mobilization after the elections and that Lithuania may face people trying to avoid it and seeking asylum.
Lithuania's State Border Guard Service had turned back 1,693 people trying to cross illegally from Belarus this year and about 26,300 since the migration crisis began, as reported by ELTA on 8 October. Katelynas said 43 migrants tried to enter southern Lithuania last week and were turned back.

- Ukraine uses up Europe’s yearly supply of thermal sensors in about five months, so two Ukrainian firms will build their own plants in the West
- Russia has a plan for Ukraine this winter, Ukraine says: intercepted document reportedly outlines up to 1,000 missiles, drones, and bombs targeting 60 critical infrastructure sites

articles.title: Russian Refinery Seeks Air Defense Operators Amid Escalating Drone Strikes
articles.body:
Rosneft’s Kuibyshev Oil Refinery in Russia’s Samara region has begun advertising vacancies for personnel with experience operating combat vehicles to help defend against Ukrainian drones. The refinery, one of the largest oil refineries in the Volga region, has been repeatedly attacked by Ukrainian drones.
Postings for the positions appeared on the HeadHunter recruiting portal on Thursday, Oct. 8, according to a report by Verstka. The requirement is for individuals who have operated the ZSU-34-23-4 “Shilka” self-propelled anti-aircraft gun or the BMP-2 “Berezhok” armored vehicle.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
According to the report, successful candidates would need approval from the Russian defense ministry and would be required to sign a contract to join Russia’s mobilization reserve. The job advertisement states that recruits will undergo refresher training and take part in combat-readiness exercises as part of their duties.
Those selected would become part of duty crews and be accommodated in a “barrack-like setting.” Duties would include “protection of defense industry facilities” against aerial targets and the “maintenance needed to retain the operational condition” of the assigned combat vehicles. The work location was listed as 25 Groznenskaya Street – the location of the refinery.
According to the advertisement, the refinery would pay a monthly salary of up to 120,000 rubles ($1,400). That amount would be supplemented by an additional 100,000 rubles ($1,200) from the governor of Samara and 29,000 rubles ($340) from the Ministry of Defense, depending on the position filled (commander, driver, or operator). Along with barracks-style accommodation, those selected would receive three meals a day, along with mandatory health and life insurance.
Ukraine Strikes Russian Missile Fuel Plant, Oil Depot, Yandex Data Center as Moscow Claims 505 Drones Downed
As of publication, the postings have been removed from the recruitment website and replaced with a message that says, “the employer has likely already found the right candidate and is no longer accepting applications for this position.”
Since Kyiv intensified its campaign against Russia’s oil-refining infrastructure, facilities have employed a range of countermeasures, including anti-drone netting and protective fencing around processing equipment and storage tanks, as well as “barrage balloons” fitted with trailing steel cables. However, such efforts have been relatively unsuccessful. The potential use of military weapons indicates the increasing desperation of the Kremlin to protect these critical resources.
In May, Russia’s RBC media outlet reported that approval had been granted by Moscow for private companies to purchase weapons and equipment to defend against Ukrainian drone attacks. This could include anti-aircraft guns, turrets, vehicles, radar, and certain electronic warfare systems. The defense ministry was also developing a mechanism to transfer some of that equipment from military stockpiles, as per the publication.
