articles.title: US prepares options for intense three-day strikes on Iran
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
US military prepares options for three-day strike campaign against Iran
The US military is preparing options for a three-day campaign of intense strikes on Iran, The New York Times reported on Thursday, citing US officials.
At President Donald Trump’s direction, the Pentagon has drawn up plans to target Iran’s arsenal of drones and missiles, energy facilities and other military sites, the newspaper reported. The preparations come as three US aircraft carriers are expected to be in the Middle East soon in a major show of force.
The timing of any potential attacks remains unclear. Trump has said there have been "productive discussions" with Iran and claimed there would be no attack before the 3 November midterm elections.
But tensions between Washington and Tehran remain high.
Although the US has not struck targets in Iran for weeks, low-level hostilities continue in the Strait of Hormuz, which remains largely blockaded by Iranian forces. The US military has also imposed a counterblockade on Iranian ports, rattling global energy markets.
Iran has threatened to retaliate with full force if the US and Israel resume their war, which began on 28 February and quickly drew much of the region into a wider conflict.
US officials told the NYT that Trump’s national security team and the Pentagon had presented him with five proposals in recent months for major military operations targeting Iran or Yemen’s Houthi movement, which is engaged in a conflict with Saudi Arabia and Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces. Trump rejected each proposal but has now again ordered officials to prepare options for possible strikes.
The plans centre on a short, intense campaign lasting about three days, the newspaper reported. Potential targets include Iran’s missile and drone stockpiles, which the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps has reportedly replenished since the early stages of the war, as well as energy facilities, command centres and the IRGC’s main headquarters.
Senior national security officials discussed the plans at a meeting led by Vice President JD Vance at Camp David last Friday, according to people familiar with the discussions.
The preparations coincide with a significant US naval deployment. The USS Theodore Roosevelt left San Diego last week and is expected to join the USS George H.W. Bush and USS George Washington in the Middle East, potentially by the end of October.
The deployment would mark the first time since 2003 that three US aircraft carriers have been in the Middle East simultaneously. Each carrier strike group includes other warships, while the wider deployment is expected to put more than 20,000 sailors and Marines at sea alongside hundreds of aircraft by the end of October, according to the report.
The build-up is expected to be temporary. The USS George Washington is due to return to its home base in Japan shortly after the Theodore Roosevelt arrives next month to replace it.
Citing unnamed security sources, Israeli news site Walla recently reported that around 3,000 US troops are deployed across Israel. Their duties include operating air defence systems, serving as pilots and support crews, and handling logistics and headquarters operations, according to the report.
Despite the military build-up, there is no certainty that Trump will authorise further attacks, even after the midterm elections, the NYT reported.
Senior US officials are concerned that an expanded campaign could further deplete global stocks of defensive weapons needed to protect American bases in the Middle East. They are also worried about the US military’s ability to intercept Iranian attacks.

articles.title: More than 500 drones by Moscow’s count: Kh-101 fuel plant, second Yandex data center, and a far-north refinery hit
articles.body:
Drones struck a plant making fuel components for Russia's Kh-101 cruise missiles and a second Yandex data center overnight on 9 October, Russian officials and monitoring channels reported. The same night, fires were reported at a refinery in Russia's far north and an oil depot near Belgorod. Russia claimed it downed more than 500 drones, and Ukraine has not claimed any of the strikes.
Ukraine has spent months hitting refineries and arms suppliers deep inside Russia. Russia, meanwhile, keeps firing Kh-101 cruise missiles at Ukrainian cities, including the one that killed 22 people in Pryluky on 7 October.
The plant behind the Kh-101's fuel
The Redkino Experimental Plant in Tver Oblast came under attack overnight, Ukrainian monitoring channel Exilenova+ reported. It said the plant makes components of Decilin-M, a fuel for Kh-55 and Kh-101 cruise missiles, as well as additives for diesel and aviation kerosene.
Tver Oblast Governor Vitaly Korolev claimed a plant in Redkino caught fire as a drone attack was being repelled. He did not name the plant. No workers were hurt, he said.
The plant also makes ferrocene derivatives, which serve as burn catalysts in solid-fuel rocket motors, Militarnyi reported. The UK sanctioned it in September 2025. Drones attacked it in September 2023 and twice in one night in June 2024, the outlet said.
In February, drones of the Security Service of Ukraine's (SBU) Alpha unit struck the plant, sparking a large fire, SBU sources told Kyiv Post. The Kh-101 is the missile Russia used against Pryluky on 7 October, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said.
Yandex loses a second data center
Part of Yandex's data center in Kaluga was damaged in the drone attack, and several modules were completely knocked out, the company's press service told Interfax, Russian newspaper Kommersant reported. Some Yandex services may run with interruptions, no one was hurt, and the company is still assessing the damage, Yandex said.
Kaluga Oblast Governor Vladislav Shapsha claimed nine people were injured in the overnight attack on the region. A day earlier, a drone attack forced Yandex to fully shut its data center in Sasovo, Ryazan Oblast.
A refinery in the north, a depot near Belgorod
Locals reported an attack on the Ukhta refinery in the Komi Republic, followed by a fire, Exilenova+ said. The Lukoil-owned plant can process about 4.2 million metric tons of oil a year, making gasoline, diesel, fuel oil, and vacuum gasoil. The extent of the damage is unclear.
An oil depot north of Belgorod was also burning after the night's attack, the channel posted. Belgorod's regional headquarters claimed two people were killed and four injured, including a child, in the Belgorod district.
A large fire also broke out in Pushkino near Moscow, likely at a truck parking lot, Astra reported. The cause is unknown.
Repeated strikes on Redkino target a specialty fuel that Russia's cruise missiles depend on, while two Yandex data centers hit in two nights bring the war to services ordinary Russians use every day.
Read also
- “Killing Ukraine’s internet would take nuclear or chemical weapons”—MiroHost founder whose data center Russia just destroyed
- The tanks that fuel Moscow’s airliners are reported burning after Ukraine’s latest drone raid on the capital region
- Drones hit Russia’s Volgograd and Samara overnight—fires near a Lukoil refinery, a chemical plant, and likely Europe’s largest oil tank farm in Samara

articles.title: Syria weighs deploying thousands of troops to Yemen – Axios
articles.body:
Syria weighs deploying thousands of troops to Yemen – Axios
Syria could join a Saudi-backed military offensive against the Houthis in Yemen by deploying thousands of troops, Axios has reported, citing US officials.
Yemen’s internationally recognized government forces have launched a major counteroffensive to recapture territory seized by the Iranian-backed Houthis, also known as Ansar Allah, including areas around the strategic Bab el-Mandeb Strait. The Saudi-led coalition has backed the operation with extensive airstrikes against Houthi positions.
According to an Axios report, Riyadh and Damascus are discussing the deployment of up to 20,000 Syrian troops. Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa, who previously led the Islamist group Hayat Tahrir al-Sham (HTS), is reportedly considering the proposal but has yet to make a decision.
The issue came up during al-Sharaa’s meeting with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman in Riyadh on Tuesday, the sources said. Saudi Arabia is seeking to reinforce Yemeni government forces, which US officials described as less well-trained than the Houthis.
Washington does not oppose the proposal in principle and sees it as a way to bolster the offensive without deeper American involvement, according to Axios. US Central Command has also been consulted on how Syrian troops could be deployed.
The Syrian units under consideration reportedly include thousands of Islamist foreign fighters who fought against former President Bashar Assad under the HTS umbrella before his overthrow in December 2024. Their involvement could deepen sectarian divisions, as the fighters include Sunni Islamists, while the Houthis follow Zaydi Shiite Islam.
Reuters separately reported that Damascus was considering military assistance, including defensive support for Saudi Arabia or participation in operations inside Yemen. However, Syrian presidential adviser Ahmad Zaidan denied that Riyadh had requested troops, describing the reports as baseless.
Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa is in Riyadh for talks with MBS. https://t.co/LWZajNI04M
— Open Source Intel (@Osint613) October 6, 2026
The renewed fighting follows Houthi territorial gains along the Red Sea coast in September, threatening shipping through Bab el-Mandeb, a vital trade route connecting the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden. The waterway has gained particular importance following disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz caused by the US-Israeli war on Iran. The Houthis also claimed to have effectively encircled Taiz, a major city linking northern and southern Yemen with the Red Sea coast, after cutting a vital supply route to the southern port city of Aden.
The Saudi-led coalition said on Monday that 100 fighter jets had participated in the offensive and claimed to have destroyed 324 Houthi targets. The Houthis have retaliated with missile and drone attacks on Saudi territory, including strikes on airports in Riyadh and Abha that killed several people, according to the Saudi authorities.
Riyadh has also secured military support from Türkiye and Pakistan under a collective defense agreement dubbed the ‘Muslim NATO’ that was signed in August.
The Yemen conflict escalated after the Houthis seized Sanaa in 2014, prompting a Saudi-led military intervention the following year. Fighting largely subsided following a 2022 truce, before flaring up again this year.

articles.title: Ukraine takes aim at Russia’s AI data infrastructure
articles.body:
Ukraine takes aim at Russia’s AI data infrastructure
Drone attacks target Russian digital giant Yandex, as well as continuing strikes on missile plants and oil refineries, following a wave of Russian attacks on data hubs inside Ukraine.
Ukrainian drone strikes have partly disabled an AI data centre operated by Russian digital giant Yandex.
The strike on Friday followed an attack on another of the company’s data hubs the previous day, appearing to signal that Ukraine’s military campaign is widening its scope to target Russia’s technology infrastructure. Moscow has previously targeted data hubs inside Ukraine.
Yandex, which is heavily involved in Russia’s AI development efforts, said its data centre in the Kaluga region southwest of Moscow had been struck by Ukrainian drones and partly put out of action.
A day earlier, a Ukrainian attack shut down a major data hub in Sasovo in the Ryazan region, where two of the three supercomputers used to develop the company’s AI models are housed.
Yandex, which operates under close government observation, said the attacks had struck at the core of its operations and that it was trying to maintain its services.
“Our teams are working day and night to keep services running and help those affected by the incident. Right now this is our most important task, but unfortunately it is not an easy one,” it said in a statement.
The company operates numerous apps that many Russians consider essential, as well as social media networks.
Russia has struck several Ukrainian data centres and telecommunications infrastructure facilities over the past month, including targets in central Kyiv.
Damage from the attacks has forced some services to suspend operations. Roughly 100,000 households suffered temporary internet outages after an attack.
“We always respond in mirror-like fashion,” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Thursday, following the Ryazan strike. “You all know, they have been hitting and continue to hit our data centres. We are responding. I can’t share all the details.”
Missiles and energy
Kyiv also continues its campaign targeting Russia’s missile production and energy infrastructure, hoping to reduce the air strikes against which it has struggled to defend, as well as to hurt Moscow’s economic ability to wage war.
Ukraine’s military said it had hit three facilities involved in missile production across Russia overnight, including a factory in the Tver region making missile components and a centre for disassembling intercontinental ballistic missiles in the Nizhny Novgorod region.
In a statement on Telegram, the General Staff said the Russian facility for the “liquidation of intercontinental ballistic missiles” was hit to degrade Russia’s ability to source explosives and rocket fuel.
Nizhny Novgorod’s governor said that one serviceman was killed repelling the attack while drone debris caused “minimal” damage to infrastructure.
A drone attack sparked a fire at a plant in Redkino in the Tver region, but it was quickly extinguished, the local governor said.
The Ukhta oil refinery belonging to the state giant Lukoil, 1,900km (1,180 miles) from the Ukrainian border, was also struck, according to Zelenskyy.
Meanwhile, Russia’s air campaign has continued to hit civilians, despite the Kremlin’s insistence that it only attacks military targets.
Overnight strikes killed one and injured seven in the city of Zaporizhzhia, regional defence official Ivan Fedorov said on the Telegram messaging app.
Russia also struck a cargo vessel in Ukraine’s Black Sea port of Mykolaiv, the Ministry of Defence in Moscow said, according to state news agency RIA Novosti. The ministry said the vessel was being used to supply the Ukrainian military.

articles.title: ‘The smell of death is everywhere’: Inside the humanitarian catastrophe unfolding in Russian-occupied Oleshky, where hundreds are trapped without food, electricity, or medicine
articles.body:
‘The smell of death is everywhere’: Inside the humanitarian catastrophe unfolding in Russian-occupied Oleshky, where hundreds are trapped without food, electricity, or medicine
Since 2022, residents of Oleshky in Ukraine’s Kherson region have lived under occupation. In 2023, the city was flooded after the Kakhovka dam was blown up: the flooding destroyed dozens of residential blocks and all of its infrastructure. In the fall of 2026, Oleshky found itself cut off. There’s a humanitarian catastrophe there: the city has no electricity, food, or medicine. Every way out is mined and blocked by Russian troops. Meduza spoke to people who have miraculously managed to stay in touch with those who remain in Oleshky. Here’s what they told us.
‘The harvest was so plentiful there was nowhere to put it’
“Oh, it smells amazing here!”
Svitlana (not her real name), a former resident of Oleshky who fled the city in 2022 because of the war, smiles as she recalls her garden — and the compliments her friend Nina used to pay it. Before the full-scale war, Nina used to bring her homemade milk every Thursday.
“I had [about a third of an acre] of land, and I planted peony bushes all along the perimeter. The scent was intoxicating!” Svitlana says. “Nina asked why I didn’t take the flowers to market. But how could I sell something so beautiful?”
Svitlana’s yard brimmed with flowers until autumn, and hers wasn’t the only one. “It was as if the townspeople were competing over whose front garden was more lavish. Oleshky bloomed and smelled wonderful.”
Svitlana calls the land she lived on for three decades “rodiucha,” which translates from Ukrainian as “fertile”:
Stick a branch in the ground and it will sprout. Everyone had everything: tomatoes, cucumbers, orchards… I grew 14 varieties of grapes, three varieties each of apricots and peaches. There was so much of a harvest that there was nowhere to put it: I sold some and canned the rest. I shared preserves with people displaced from Donbas — I’d send volunteers whole crates of it.
On weekends, Svitlana liked to spend time along the Kinska River, a left tributary of the Dnipro. The Kinska had a beach and good fishing spots, and from its pier you could catch a pleasure boat or a passenger ferry to Kherson, about 9 kilometers (5.6 miles) away by water.
Russian cell service in Oleshky, which has been under occupation since the first days of Russia’s invasion, operates with severe disruptions. But because the city is close to Kherson, Ukrainian mobile networks can still be picked up at random spots around town. That is how Svitlana stays in touch with her neighbors Olha and Dmytro (not their real names), the people closest to her who remain in Oleshky.
These days, Svitlana hears little from her neighbors. She says the constant risk of a drone strike keeps them in the basement most of the time. In the spring, Olha wrote to her on Viber: “We just need to survive.”
‘Every day I hear explosions over the phone’
Mykyta (not his real name), another resident who also fled the city in 2022, keeps in touch with Oleshky through Ukrainian mobile networks. He calls his mother, Tamara (not her real name), every day, and to reach him, she has to go out into the yard, find a signal, and stay put wherever she finds it.
Sometimes the call cuts off mid-sentence. “My mother runs from drones. She hears a sound in the sky and rushes straight into the house, where the signal disappears,” Mykyta explains. “Every day I hear explosions over the phone.”
Mykyta spent six months living under occupation: he didn’t want to leave right away, thinking “it would all be over quickly.” “But then [representatives of the occupation authorities] came to search my place and beat my legs so badly that I couldn’t walk normally for two months. That’s when I realized nothing was going to end quickly, and I left.”
Tamara and her husband, Borys (not his real name), stayed in Oleshky. According to Mykyta, his father refused outright to leave the city — he didn’t want to abandon the household. “Dad used to say, ‘Let’s just sit tight, maybe things will get better.’ Nothing got better. He got seriously ill, and that’s when my mother said they were staying — Dad wouldn’t have survived the trip. She’s already buried him.”
After her husband’s death, Tamara kept putting off leaving because she didn’t want to abandon her two dogs. But both dogs died this year, Mykyta says:
My mother tried hard: she wouldn’t cook anything extra for herself, she’d give it to them instead. But she had to feed them whatever she could. A lot of people in Oleshky now eat purslane — it’s this fatty grass. My mother added it to the dogs’ food. They ate tomatoes, cucumbers, honey, pasta — whatever supplies were left. I think that’s what did them in.
The humanitarian crisis in Oleshky began in 2023. After the Kakhovka dam was blown up, the city was flooded by 90%, and its infrastructure was severely damaged. Since then, there has been no electricity or gas.
Only people with their own wells have drinking water. But pumping water from a well requires a pump, running the pump without electricity requires a generator, and the generator needs fuel. The last fuel delivery to the city coincided with the final food supplies, in late spring 2026.
Kseniia Arkhipova, a police officer in Oleshky before the invasion, tells Meduza this. In 2022, during the occupation, she began volunteering to help local residents, which angered the pro-Russian authorities. After they detained her, she left her hometown for Ukrainian-controlled territory.
Since getting out of Oleshky, Arkhipova has coordinated help for her fellow residents remotely, helping deliver food and medicine, taking part in organizing evacuations, and keeping a list of people who have died in the city during the war. By August 30, she had confirmed 136 deaths since the start of the invasion.
As far as the volunteer knows, no one has managed to bring food into Oleshky since spring 2026: vehicles that have tried have come under fire and been forced to turn back.
The Ukrainian news outlet Ukrainska Pravda has reported that by the end of summer it had become impossible to enter the city: Russian and Ukrainian drones clashed in the skies over Oleshky every day. The occupation administration itself accuses the Ukrainian military of blockading the city and claims that Ukrainian drones attack convoys carrying humanitarian aid.
Kseniia Arkhipova recalls:
In May and June, people in Oleshky still had supplies, then the harvest came in from their gardens: grapes, tomatoes, potatoes, zucchini. But the supplies ran out, and people started sounding the alarm — there’s no food. Mothers write to me: “Ksyusha, my child has nothing to eat, what do I do? He’s hungry all the time.” It’s like 1933 all over again, “wonderful Russian culture” in all its glory.
Kseniia is referring to the Holodomor, which killed nearly 4 million residents of the Ukrainian SSR. Ukraine’s official position, backed by 29 countries (Russia is not among them), holds that the Holodomor was a deliberate genocide of the Ukrainian people by the Soviet government.
Mykyta says that, just as in Soviet times, Ukrainians are dying of hunger because of Russia: “It doesn’t fit in my head that something like this could happen in this day and age. This is an actual Holodomor.”
In July, the occupation authorities in the Kherson region denied there was a humanitarian catastrophe. By August, however, they had acknowledged that Oleshky and nearby villages had no water or electricity, and that utility crews weren’t making repairs because of the shelling.
On September 21, Putin’s press secretary, Dmitry Peskov, called the situation in the Russian-occupied city “critical.” “The Kyiv regime is doing everything it can to hinder deliveries [of food and medicine]. Russian troops continue working to resolve the situation,” he said.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has also addressed the crisis in Oleshky. In one of his evening addresses in May, he said: “The situation specifically in this part of the occupied territory is extremely difficult, and it’s very hard to carry out evacuations. It’s important that international organizations — everyone able to help with this — are engaged and take decisive action.”
‘Oleshky is closed off on all sides’
Residents of Oleshky have very few ways to get food: Ukrainian authorities say the city is under a complete blockade.
Tetiana Hasanenko, who heads the Oleshky city military administration from Ukrainian-controlled territory, said in comments to Ukrainska Pravda that Russian troops have mined every route out of Oleshky:
People have two options: either die from starvation, or come under drone or artillery fire and be killed. There is no third option.
At the same time, Yevhen Voronetskyi, a serviceman with the 34th Independent Marine Brigade “Borysfen” of the Ukrainian armed forces, told Ukrainska Pravda that Ukrainian troops have mined some routes out of Oleshky to prevent Russian forces from bringing in weapons. Voronetskyi said Ukraine’s military keeps the main road out of the city clear so civilians can leave, even helping people make their way along it and sometimes guiding them with drones along a relatively safe route.
In 2023, Russian forces mined the fields around the city out of fear of a Ukrainian military landing on the left bank of the Dnipro. There is no confirmation that the Russian army has continued mining the main roads around Oleshky. Each side blames the other.
Petro Andryushchenko, a former adviser to the mayor of Mariupol who now heads the Center for Occupation Studies, said in an interview with the Ukrainian outlet NV that Russian forces are using the city’s residents as human shields: “This is a real humanitarian catastrophe, and one created entirely by the Russians as cover for military operations.”
The UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine reported on June 25 that “thousands of civilians trapped in frontline communities in southern Ukraine are facing a deepening humanitarian crisis.”
Oleshky became a front-line city in the fall of 2022, when the Russian army, under pressure from Ukrainian forces, retreated from the right bank of the Dnipro and left Kherson. Since then, the occupation authorities say, Ukrainian attacks have hindered their efforts to rebuild Oleshky — including after the 2023 flooding — and to deliver food and medicine to the city.
As FPV drones became more common on the battlefield, Oleshky, like Kherson on the opposite bank, grew increasingly dangerous. The front line runs right between the two cities, along the river, and it takes drones only a few minutes to cross the Dnipro and reach a target.
But drones aren’t the only threat in the city and its surrounding area. The area around the city has been mined so heavily that by early 2026, entering or leaving it had become very difficult. That, said Tetiana Hasanenko, who is trying to stay in touch with the city’s residents, is precisely what led to the sharp deterioration of the situation in Oleshky.
Vegetable gardens in Oleshky have turned into a deadly obstacle course. Neighbors told Mykyta that the plot around his house, which he abandoned in 2022, is “littered with mines,” including antitank mines and “petal” mines.
According to Mykyta, the areas around the city are unsafe too: “The riverbanks were mined, and after the flooding [from the destruction of the Kakhovka dam], the water scattered those mines who knows where.”
“Oleshky is closed off on all sides,” Kseniia Arkhipova sums up. “There are about 1,500 people caught in this trap.” Since the start of the Russian invasion, the city’s population has shrunk nearly 15-fold: according to figures from the Oleshky city military administration, 22,000 people lived in Oleshky before 2022.
Some residents risk their lives to walk to Radensk, a nearby village, in search of food. Like Oleshky, it’s under Russian control. The roughly 20-kilometer (12-mile) route is extremely dangerous: the road is mined, and the open terrain is exposed to drone fire.
Some still manage to get food, which is sold at an improvised market in Oleshky. Mykyta learned the prices there from his mother: “I’m in shock. A sack of potatoes costs 7,000 rubles! A can of sprats costs 1,000 rubles, compared to 60 in Radensk.”
Mykyta says a friend of his mother’s advised her to turn to “some religious people.” He doesn’t know who they are, but he’s heard from his mother that they have more food than many other residents. Through these people, his mother Tamara was able to get “a couple of kilograms of buckwheat, some pasta, canned meat, oil, flour — a little of everything.”
Mykyta has been trying to arrange food deliveries to his mother through charitable organizations in nearby cities, but so far without success.
The Ukrainian military sometimes sends humanitarian cargo into the blockaded city. Since March, Ukrainian forces have used drones capable of carrying up to 10 kilograms (22 pounds) of cargo, dropping boxes of canned meat, flour, crackers, oil, and grains directly onto Oleshky.
But this isn’t regular supply, and not every resident gets a package. “A ten-kilo package is enough for one family for a week. And then what?” Kseniia Arkhipova adds.
On September 27, the Ukrainian military dropped its largest shipment of food into Oleshky to date, delivering about four tons (4.4 tons) of food at roughly 100 pre-selected locations. Arkhipova afterward received many grateful messages from locals, and she shows Meduza one of them: “A huge, huge thank you to the guys. God bless them, a deep bow to them!”
Overnight on October 4, the Ukrainian military carried out another operation delivering four tons (4.4 tons) of humanitarian aid to Oleshky by drone.
‘There were more than 200 people on the lists. But no evacuation ever happened.’
According to figures from Ukrainska Pravda, no evacuation of Oleshky has ever been officially organized in four years of occupation. In the spring, the occupation authorities promised for the first time to move Oleshky residents to safer towns. Hoping that would happen, Arkhipova, the volunteer, began coordinating people in a Telegram chat.
Svitlana, the Oleshky resident who left her blooming garden behind in 2022, followed Arkhipova’s messages in the chat. On March 5, she wrote to a neighbor: “Olechka, the question of evacuating Oleshky residents is being decided at the highest level. They’re compiling lists of people so they know exactly how many buses are needed.”
Kseniia recalls how “everyone hoped the Red Cross would come and evacuate everyone”:
The Russians started urging people: “Come to the hospital, sign up, leave your contact numbers. We need to know how many buses to send you. We need to count you — who’s bedridden, who isn’t.” There were more than 200 people on the lists. But no evacuation ever happened.
Ukrainian Ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets said, without specifying dates, that Kyiv had agreed on “clear mechanisms” for evacuation with Russia, backed by the International Red Cross. But Russia, he said, has stalled the process: “For a long time now, after the talks that were held, the Russian side has not confirmed its readiness to carry out a humanitarian mission to evacuate people.”
Kseniia Arkhipova said that by believing the rumors about the Red Cross and an organized evacuation, people missed their last real chance to leave: “Most of those 200 people are still in Oleshky. In the end, only 67 risked leaving on foot.”
Volunteers coordinate on-foot evacuations from Oleshky remotely, Kseniia says. They put together a plan based on information residents share with them whenever they manage to get in touch.
The last “window of opportunity” for evacuating on foot opened on September 10 and lasted about two weeks, Arkhipova said. That was when Russian troops cleared mines from a stretch of one of the roads leading out of the city.
The first thing residents do is make their way to nearby Radensk (also occupied by Russia). After making the trip, some are “completely unable to move,” Kseniia continues:
They arrive dirty, emaciated, with nothing. Sometimes they weigh less than 50 kilograms (110 pounds), just skin and bones. No clothes, no shoes, no money — no home. Recently an 87-year-old woman was brought out on a cart. When she saw bread, she took out a handkerchief, wrapped a crust in it, pressed it to her chest and said, “I won’t give it up, this is my bread.”
In Radensk, refugees from Oleshky are housed with volunteers willing to take them in, and “they just rest for a few days,” Kseniia says. Some are put up in empty, nonresidential spaces, like stores. Then those who are able make their way to free Ukrainian territory — through Russia and Europe. About 30 Oleshky residents have left the occupation since the start of September.
The volunteer says that among those who left, everyone who initially didn’t want to evacuate “regrets, without exception, staying stuck for so long.” “I yell at them: ‘I told you to leave a year ago, two years ago, three years ago!’ And they answer: ‘Ksyusha, it’s hard to leave everything behind. You’re young — you just turned around and left. We can’t do that.’”
Among those Arkhipova has helped leave are also refugees who for a long time didn’t believe they were really in danger. She said they decided to evacuate only after someone close to them had been killed.
After being rescued from occupation, Oleshky residents can count on support that Ukraine provides to evacuees and internally displaced persons (IDPs). ”[But] while they fill out the paperwork and wait for that measly 2,000 hryvnias [about 40 euros or 3,800 rubles], what are they supposed to do in the meantime?” Kseniia says.
From time to time, she manages to persuade Ukrainian charitable foundations and Russian antiwar organizations to help refugees from Oleshky.
The “window of opportunity” for evacuation has now closed again, Arkhipova says.
‘These people are in a cage’
Dmytro Lubinets, Ukraine’s ombudsman, is convinced that an evacuation of Oleshky’s residents could realistically be carried out in a single day.
Kseniia agrees:
All that’s needed is to clear the road of mines and send in, roughly speaking, four big buses [into the city]. People will come out on their own, and those who can’t move will be wheeled out on carts. Loading everyone up and driving them out — the whole operation would take three hours! Why isn’t this being done? Because Russia can’t be negotiated with.
In late September, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha spoke about the crisis in Oleshky in an address to the UN and the International Red Cross. At Ukraine’s request, the OSCE called on Russia to give international organizations access to Oleshky, supply residents with food and medicine, and allow them to leave the city safely.
Vladimir Saldo, the Kremlin-appointed governor of the Russian-occupied part of the Kherson region, gave an interview to the television channel Vesti on September 28. Asked whether a full evacuation of Oleshky was possible and necessary, he said:
Of course such a possibility exists. But let’s try to understand the residents who are there. Taking them and forcibly removing them right now would probably be wrong and unfair. Those who wanted to leave have already left. There are no restrictions for anyone there.
Saldo then added: “We need to do everything so that they [the local residents] can get everything they need to live there: fuel, food, medicine, communications.”
Two days after Saldo’s interview aired, Kseniia Arkhipova learned that several Oleshky residents had again tried to walk to Radensk for food. She posted a notice in the city chat warning that four people had been injured by landmines along a certain route that day and urging anyone heading to Radensk to avoid that stretch of road:
Regardless of Saldo’s statements, many Oleshky residents genuinely don’t want to, or can’t, get out. For instance, Mykyta’s mother isn’t willing to abandon her home, he says: “She says if she leaves, everything will be looted. ‘And who needs us there [outside our hometown] anyway?’”
Kseniia Arkhipova also described the fear that residents still in Oleshky feel toward looters.
From her conversations with residents, she learned that Russian troops rotated through Oleshky around mid-September: “The ones who came in now are polite — they might come ask for food, [saying] ‘you leave us alone, and we’ll leave you alone,’” Kseniia recounts from her acquaintances’ stories. “But before that there were ones who took everything. Or they’d kick people out of their homes and onto the street because they had solar panels, which meant they had electricity.”
Among those who can’t leave the city are the people Arkhipova calls the “undocumented.” These are Oleshky residents whose Ukrainian passports and other documents were lost in the flooding after the Kakhovka dam was destroyed. They didn’t want to get Russian passports.
Now, to be evacuated from Oleshky, these people need at least some kind of passport: both the occupation authorities and border guards on the way to Ukrainian-controlled territory demand to see documents. Getting a Russian passport without other documents is very difficult: applicants first have to confirm their identity with the occupation authorities.
These bureaucratic hurdles come with additional checks, and the fighting makes moving between offices simply dangerous.
“I have acquaintances who have been trying to restore their documents for three years now,” Arkhipova says. “They have witnesses, they’re going through the courts, they’ve already gone around to every [office]. And they still won’t give them a passport.”
Without documents, Kseniia reasons, it’s impossible to cross any major checkpoint: “Not Novoazovsk, not Chonhar, not Armiansk will let them through. These people are in a cage.”
Kseniia calls other residents who remain in Oleshky the “low-mobility”: bedridden patients and elderly people who can’t be evacuated without special transport and an escort.
On top of that, Kseniia says, there are people in the city who are simply afraid of the filtration procedure at Russian checkpoints. According to Human Rights Watch’s observations, even civilians leaving occupied territory for areas under Ukrainian control often have to go through it — not just those entering Russia.
‘The smell of death is everywhere’
“Those who left after me say Oleshky is simply unrecognizable. The city is gone. There are no stores left, no post office,” Mykyta tells Meduza. “I look at photos myself, and I don’t recognize a lot of the places.”
Kseniia Arkhipova adds that in Oleshky, “people live in an isolated world”: “It’s worse than after the flooding [from the destruction of the Kakhovka dam]. There’s devastation and chaos in Oleshky. There’s no administration, no police. Cars don’t drive around — bicycles are the best you get.”
Arkhipova calls the hospital the “only intact island” in Oleshky. It used to give out food to those who were completely exhausted from malnutrition. But lately the facility “is operating on its last legs: there’s no medicine, no fuel — nothing.”
Mykyta also knows from his mother that there’s a medicine shortage in the city, and he recalls overhearing a Russian soldier say, back when he himself was still in Oleshky: “Why do you need medicine? Consider yourselves already dead.”
Still, Arkhipova says, the hospital can currently provide help: “There are doctors there who worked even before the war, even though they had chances to leave. They said, ‘I’m not going anywhere. What will people do without me?’ Recently an 11-year-old boy stepped on a ‘petal’ mine and lost his leg. If it weren’t for these surgeons, who would have performed the amputation? The child would have simply bled to death.”
The occupation authorities don’t allow burials for people killed in the fighting, the volunteer says. Novaya Gazeta reported that there is “no one to process” deaths in the city, but Arkhipova doubts that’s the real reason for the delay.
She says that people who die of natural causes are still being buried. “They [the occupation authorities] need a forensic medical examination so that a medical examiner will write: ‘These people were killed by the Ukrainian military,’” the volunteer explains. “And they need that so they can later pass that data on to the UN [and blame Ukraine]. That’s the scheme.”
The only way to bury those killed in the fighting, Kseniia says, is “quietly, in the garden.” But that’s dangerous: the occupation authorities consider these “spontaneous burials” illegal. “One girl buried a neighbor who was killed in a shelling attack in his own garden. They dragged her through the courts for two years afterward — had she killed him? They even came and dug up the body,” Arkhipova says. Meduza was unable to reach the Oleshky resident the volunteer describes.
Mykyta, whose father died under occupation, and Svitlana, whose husband, Ihor, also chose to stay in their hometown but then fell ill and died in the hospital, both confirm to Meduza that people who die of natural causes are allowed to be buried. Svitlana says that “by today’s standards” Ihor was buried “like a king.” She was able to send money to acquaintances in Oleshky, and they organized the ceremony.
“They reported everything to me: how they dug the grave, how a priest performed the burial service, how many wreaths they laid, what kind of cross they put up,” Svitlana recounts. “They buried my Ihor in not just one but two plastic bags, which was difficult because bags are in short supply there [at the hospital], and you have to sign for each one.”
Asked why her husband wasn’t buried in a coffin, Svitlana says: “There are no coffins left in Oleshky.” That’s what the acquaintance who organized the funeral told her. Svitlana believes it: there’s no way to bring new coffins into Oleshky, and getting wood from the forest is dangerous — it’s mined and exposed to drone fire.
Mykyta tells Meduza that his mother sometimes mentions acquaintances of hers who have been killed. “In March, a woman was killed — a strike hit a store while she was standing in line. Her husband hasn’t been able to retrieve the body since spring — they won’t give it to him,” Mykyta says, citing one example.
According to Kseniia Arkhipova, the morgue is “a small building not far from the hospital,” where bodies are “just stored.” “A body has been lying in a bag without refrigeration since January. What’s going to be left of it?” Arkhipova adds.
The Insider reported that the refrigerators in the morgue don’t work because there’s no fuel for the hospital generator. Tetiana Hasanenko, the head of the city military administration, said the morgue had effectively stopped functioning ever since the Kakhovka dam was destroyed. She said bodies have been stored in the hospital basement in recent months.
Sometimes, Meduza’s sources say, bodies are left lying right out in the street. “Russian [soldiers] lie on the roads for weeks, their own side doesn’t pick them up,” Mykyta says. “Dogs drag the bodies around. For my mother, these are just ordinary moments now — a dog tears off an arm or a leg and runs off.”
Kseniia Arkhipova also tells Meduza that stray dogs in Oleshky feed on human bodies. The Ukrainian news outlet Hromadske also reported that dogs dig up shallow graves in gardens and “drag off pieces of bodies,” while Ukrainska Pravda reported that bodies of not only Russian soldiers but also killed civilians lie in the city’s streets.
In the last days of September, Mykyta spoke with his mother again. Tamara told her son she had gone to see a doctor. “My mother says it’s hard to walk through the hospital,” Mykyta says. “The smell of death is everywhere.”
The Oleshky city military administration responded to Meduza’s request by referring to Tetiana Hasanenko’s previously published interviews. Meduza also sent a request to the occupation administration of the Kherson region but had not received a response at the time this story was published.
At Meduza, we are committed to transparency about our use of artificial intelligence in the newsroom. The story you’re reading was written by one of our living, breathing journalists and translated from Russian using an AI model configured to follow our strict editorial standards. This translation process is the result of extensive testing and refinements to ensure our English-language coverage is timely and accurate. A Meduza editor reviews every draft before publication.

articles.title: Houthis strike Saudi airports after ‘final warning’ (VIDEOS)
articles.body:
Three killed in Houthi-claimed strikes in Saudi Arabia (VIDEOS)
Saudi officials have confirmed three fatalities in missile strikes on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh and a Saudi aircraft, for which Yemen’s Houthi forces claimed responsibility.
Riyadh’s civil aviation authority GACA said three Saudi subjects were killed and multiple others were injured, including foreign nationals. Operations at the airport have been resumed, the statement issued on Friday morning said.
The Houthis hit the airport with two cruise missiles on Thursday evening, the group’s military spokesman, Yahya Saree, previously announced in a statement. Houthi forces also hit Abha Airport and King Khalid Air Base with ballistic missiles, Saree added.
“The strikes were precise and direct, resulting in the disruption of air traffic at the two airports and causing damage to them and the air base,” Saree said. The Saudi government has not acknowledged the strikes. The head of the Saudi military coalition against the Houthis in Yemen, Turki al-Maliki, has claimed that two missiles were intercepted before they reached Riyadh, and one was intercepted before it reached King Khalid Air Base.
Earlier on Thursday, Houthi forces hit King Khalid International Airport with a ballistic missile, which Saree said “struck its target with precision and caused the disruption of airport operations.”
Video footage shared by the Houthis showed a thick plume of smoke rising from the apron of the airport, while footage shared on social media suggested that the missile landed directly on a parked aircraft belonging to the Saudia airline.
After the first strike, Saree issued what he called a “final warning to all global airlines,” warning them to stay out of Saudi airspace, “which has become a theater for our military operations.”
Around 40% of flights in and out of Riyadh were canceled on Thursday. Almost two dozen carriers have canceled or suspended service to the Saudi capital amid the Kingdom’s escalating conflict with the Houthis. Air India and Lufthansa both announced on Thursday that they would not fly into Riyadh until next week.
Saudi Arabia has been waging war against the Houthis since 2015, although the fighting was paused by a ceasefire in 2022. Fighting resumed this July after Saudi-backed forces struck the runway at Sanaa airport to prevent an Iranian plane carrying a Houthi delegation from landing. The Houthis responded with strikes on Saudi targets, while Saudi jets resumed large-scale airstrikes on Yemen.
The conflict escalated further in September, when the Houthis made their largest territorial gains in years, taking Mocha and key positions along the Red Sea coast and around Bab el-Mandeb.

articles.title: 52-year-old Russian political prisoner Igor Yakovenko dies in Krasnodar detention center after being returned for “palliative care”
articles.body:
Igor Yakovenko, a 52-year-old political prisoner, died in Krasnodar’s Pretrial Detention Center No. 1, according to a report by Memorial’s Support for Political Prisoners project. Yakovenko is at least the ninth political prisoner to die in Russian custody since the start of 2026, according to a count by The Insider. Human rights advocates said he had been diagnosed with an inoperable brain tumor.
Several days before his death, Yakovenko underwent medical examinations and was then returned to the detention center “for palliative care.” Memorial also said Yakovenko had been beaten at the facility before he was sentenced.
On Oct. 3, 2025, the Southern District Military Court sentenced Yakovenko to five years in prison on charges of preparing to take part in the activities of a terrorist organization. Prosecutors alleged that on May 28, 2025, he began corresponding with a person involved in recruiting Russians for the Freedom of Russia Legion, which Russian authorities have designated a terrorist organization. Yakovenko allegedly planned to travel to Ukraine, sending the person a completed application form to join the Legion. FSB officers detained him two days later. Authorities did not disclose how they learned about the correspondence.
Memorial recognized Yakovenko as a political prisoner. The movement’s human rights advocates said they did not have access to the case files and therefore could not determine whether he genuinely intended to join the Legion or if had been the victim of an entrapment scheme. Memorial noted that only two days passed between Yakovenko sending the application and his arrest:
“Such a rapid sequence of events may indicate that from the outset he wrote to one of the Legion’s fake websites and sent his application there as well.”
In addition to Yakovenko, at least eight other political prisoners have died in Russian custody since the start of 2026:
- Roman Sidorkin died on Jan. 9 in the Saratov Region. The former employee of a defense company in the Kursk Region had been convicted of treason after investigators accused him and his former wife of passing technical documentation and samples of military products to Ukrainian intelligence. Sidorkin developed bronchitis-like symptoms in December 2025, and later pneumonia. He was hospitalized only four days before his death.
- Oleg Tyryshkin, a former miner and trade union activist from Kemerovo Region, died on Feb. 4 at age 64. He had been sentenced to two years in a penal colony over a comment posted on the social network VK about the 2004 death of Akhmat Kadyrov, the first president of Chechnya and the father of its current leader, Ramzan Kadyrov. Activists who corresponded with prisoners said heart problems were the cause of his death. Tyryshkin had previously complained about his health, including about a brain cyst.
- Alexander Dotsenko died on Feb. 19 after a massive heart attack. The jewelry artist had been sentenced to three years in a penal colony in a case involving anti-war postcards left in a Lenta supermarket in St. Petersburg. His wife, Anastasia Dyudyayeva, received a 3½-year sentence in the same case. After Dotsenko’s heart attack, prison officials failed to inform his relatives and lawyer about his condition for several days.
- Vladimir Osipov died in March at a pretrial detention center in Ukhta, where he had been transferred from the Moscow Region. The 56-year-old had been sentenced to 6½ years in a penal colony over posts made on Odnoklassniki about the Russian military and Vladimir Putin. Ambulances were called for Osipov several times during his trial, and at one hearing the judge refused to postpone his final statement despite complaints of high blood pressure.
- Andrei Akuzin, a 53-year-old artist from Komsomolsk-on-Amur, died by suicide on April 8 at a local pretrial detention center — six days after he was arrested. His friend said the criminal case stemmed from an online comment. Russia’s financial monitoring agency, Rosfinmonitoring, added Akuzin to its registry of “terrorists and extremists” only after his death.
- Vegan Khristolyub Bozhiy, formerly named Dmitry Kuznetsov, died on April 17 at Penal Colony No. 2 in Voronezh. The 43-year-old preacher and YouTube blogger, whose name can be loosely translated as “Vegan Christ-Lover of God,” had been sentenced to three years in prison over videos criticizing the invasion of Ukraine, the Soviet army, and Islam. It later emerged that he had been found hanged in a punishment cell and that, according to media reports, a negligence case was opened against the prison’s employees. His relatives did not believe the official account of suicide.
- Vladimir Yarotsky was found dead on the morning of May 7 at Penal Colony No. 9 in Khadyzhensk in Russia’s Krasnodar Region. The artist had been sentenced to five and a half years in prison on charges of spreading “false information” about the Russian armed forces and “desecrating symbols of military glory” over posts that included a caricature of Putin featuring a penis and a St. George ribbon. Authorities said Yarotsky died by suicide. Another prisoner said the artist had complained of pressure from the prison administration.
- Ibragim Kudzhanov, a 52-year-old resident of Ukraine’s Luhansk Region, died at Penal Colony No. 8 in the Omsk Region. His death became known in July. Kudzhanov had been sentenced to 5½ years in prison for serving as a driver in Ukraine’s Aidar Battalion in 2018 and 2019. His daughter said he had been tortured with electric shocks after his detention and that he died from a second heart attack accompanied by an aneurysm and kidney failure. His son, Artyom, is also imprisoned in Russia after being sentenced to 12 years in a penal colony on espionage charges in 2025.

articles.title: Drone Strike Hits Russian Plant Making Fuel Components for Kh-101 Cruise Missiles
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Drone Strike Hits Russian Plant Making Fuel Components for Kh-101 Cruise Missiles
Strike drones attacked the Redkinsky Experimental Plant in Russia’s Tver region, triggering explosions and a fire at a chemical facility linked to the country’s defense industry and production of components used in long-range cruise missiles, according to Ukrainian monitoring channel Exilenova+ on October 9.
Footage published after the attack showed drones flying over the area, followed by explosions and a fire near the industrial complex. Residents also reported hearing Russian air defenses operating during the raid.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Tver regional governor Vitaly Korolev later confirmed that a fire had broken out at the plant in the town of Redkino following a drone attack. He said employees had been evacuated to shelters in time, no one was injured, and emergency crews subsequently extinguished the blaze.
The Redkinsky Experimental Plant is one of the larger chemical manufacturing facilities in the Tver region and specializes in small-volume specialty chemicals. It produces more than 40 types of products used by Russia’s aviation, aerospace, and other industrial sectors.
Among its products are ferrocene derivatives used as combustion catalysts in solid-fuel rocket engines, as well as specialized materials, protective coatings, and fuel additives. These chemicals have applications across both civilian and military manufacturing.
According to Ukraine’s Security Service, the plant also produces components for Decilin-M, a specialized synthetic fuel used by Russian Kh-55 and Kh-101 cruise missiles. The facility is additionally linked to the production of additives for diesel fuel and aviation kerosene.
The Kh-101 is one of Russia’s principal air-launched long-range cruise missiles and has been used extensively in strikes against Ukrainian cities and infrastructure throughout the full-scale war.
The plant’s role in Russia’s defense and chemical sectors has already drawn international sanctions. The United Kingdom imposed restrictions on the enterprise in September 2025, citing its activities in sectors considered strategically important to the Russian government and its military-industrial base.
Previously, Russia’s far northern Yamalo-Nenets region started offering mobile fire groups $12,000 for every incoming drone they destroy, underscoring growing concern over Ukrainian long-range strikes reaching some of the country’s most remote oil and gas infrastructure.

articles.title: Ukraine Strikes Russian Missile Fuel Plant, Oil Depot and Yandex Data Center as Moscow Claims 505 Drones Downed
articles.body:
Ukrainian drones struck a chemical plant producing fuel for Russian cruise missiles, an oil depot near the border region of Belgorod and infrastructure in the Kaluga region southwest of Moscow overnight on Oct. 9, Russian officials and Ukrainian monitoring channels reported.
In the Tver region, which is situated between Moscow and St. Petersburg, drones hit the Redkino Experimental Plant and sparked a fire. The facility is the region’s largest chemical enterprise, according to Ukrainian monitoring channel Exilenova+.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The facility manufactures Decylin-M, a specialized rocket fuel component used in Kh-55 and Kh-101 cruise missiles, as well as fuel additives for diesel and aviation kerosene, Kyiv Post sources within Ukraine’s Security Service (SBU) said in February, after the first strike on the enterprise.
Both missile types are among Russia’s primary long-range weapons used in strikes on Ukrainian civilian and energy infrastructure.
Regional Governor Vitaly Korolev said the fire had been extinguished and plant employees had been evacuated to a shelter. No workers were injured, he added.
Oil depot fire reported near Belgorod
In the Belgorod region, two people were killed and four others, including a child, were injured when shells struck private homes in the Belgorod district, the regional operational headquarters said.
Following the attack, NASA’s FIRMS satellite monitoring system detected a fire at an oil depot north of Belgorod, Exilenova+ reported.

The depot supplies fuel to industrial and agricultural enterprises and gas stations across the region, according to its website.
Yandex data center damaged in Kaluga
A Yandex data center in Kaluga was damaged in a Ukrainian drone attack overnight, marking the second consecutive day that the Russian technology company’s data centers have come under attack, RBC-Russia reported, citing the company’s press service.
Several modules at the Kaluga facility were completely disabled, potentially disrupting some services, Yandex said.
On Oct. 8, Ukrainian drones struck another Yandex data center in Sasovo, Ryazan region, where servers host services used by the company and its clients. Operations at that facility were completely halted.
Kaluga Regional Governor Vladislav Shapsha said nine people were injured in the overnight attacks across the region, five of whom were hospitalized.
Drones targeted four municipal districts and the regional capital, Kaluga. Shapsha said the drones struck what he described as the city’s “infrastructure.” Private homes were also damaged in two municipal districts and in Kaluga.
Shapsha said Russian air defenses intercepted 26 drones over the region.
Moscow claims 505 drones downed
Russia’s defense ministry claimed its air defenses intercepted and destroyed 505 Ukrainian fixed-wing drones overnight over 19 Russian regions, occupied Crimea and the Black and Azov seas.
The ministry reported drone activity over Kaluga, Bryansk, Belgorod, Kursk, Tula, Tver, Smolensk and Moscow regions, as well as Krasnodar Krai and Tatarstan.

articles.title: Ukraine reportedly targets Russian cruise missile fuel plant in Tver Oblast
articles.body:
Editor's note: This is a developing story and is being updated.
Ukraine's military launched an attack on several Russian regions overnight on Oct. 9, striking three Russian facilities involved in missile launches and fuel production, including a factory that manufactures fuel components for Kh-55 and Kh-101 cruise missiles, Ukraine's General Staff confirmed.
The attacks targeted facilities in Tver and Nizhny Novgorod oblasts, while Russian and Ukrainian monitoring channels separately reported strikes on oil infrastructure in other regions.
In Nizhny Novgorod Oblast, Ukrainian forces struck a facility belonging to the V.P. Barmin Research Institute of Launch Complexes near Dalneye Konstantinovo-5, the General Staff said.
The institute is part of Russia's Center for Operation of Ground-Based Space Infrastructure (TsENKI), which develops, maintains, and operates rocket launch complexes, fueling equipment, and missile control systems.
Another strike targeted the Center for the Disposal of Intercontinental Ballistic Missiles near Surovatikha, also in Nizhny Novgorod Oblast. According to the General Staff, the attack was intended to weaken Russia's capacity to produce explosives and rocket fuel.
In Tver Oblast, the General Staff confirmed a strike on the Redkino Experimental Plant, where Telegram monitoring channel Exilenova+, citing resident accounts, had earlier reported flashes of explosions and smoke.
The plant, which produces components of Decilin-M rocket fuel, as well as fuel additives for diesel and aviation kerosene, was previously struck in a Ukrainian attack in February 2026. The attack destroyed around 6,000 FPV (first-person-view) drones and their components, the General Staff said.
The plant is under sanctions imposed by the U.S., the U.K., and several other countries.
Russia routinely uses Kh-55 and Kh-101 cruise missiles missiles to attack Ukrainian cities, including during recent mass missile strikes on Kyiv.
Elsewhere in Russia, a Ukrainian attack reportedly led to a fire at an oil depot located north of the city of Belgorod, according to NASA's Fire Information for Resource Management System (FIRMS) monitoring platform.
The extent of the damage caused was not immediately clear.
In Russia's Komi Republic, Ukrainian drones reportedly struck the Lukoil-owned Ukhta oil refinery on the morning of Oct. 9, with footage showing black smoke rising from the facility, independent Russian outlet The Moscow Times reported.
Independent Russian media outlet Astra geolocated eyewitness footage showing smoke rising from the refinery, while Ukrainian monitoring channel Supernova+ reported explosions and drone activity in Ukhta.
The refinery processed approximately 3 million metric tons of oil in 2025, accounting for around 1.1% of Russia's total oil refining output. It produces gasoline, diesel fuel, fuel oil, and vacuum gas oil.
Russian aviation authorities temporarily suspended flights at Ukhta airport amid the attack. Local authorities also declared a drone alert, while the city's mayor, Marina Meteleva, described the situation as under control.
The refinery, located approximately 1,700 kilometers (1,056 miles) from the Ukrainian border, was previously targeted by Ukrainian drones in February 2026 and August 2025.
The Kyiv Independent cannot immediately verify the reports. Ukraine's military has not yet commented on the reported attack.
While the weaponry used in the reported attack was not immediately clear, Ukraine has often used long-range drones to strike facilities and oil infrastructure that directly support Russia's war in Ukraine.

articles.title: Fought against Ukraine, now claimed to be victims: Kenya’s plea for five men held by Ukraine
articles.body:
Kenya wants five of its citizens captured fighting for Russia in Ukraine to be treated as victims of human trafficking rather than prisoners of war, Foreign Affairs Cabinet Secretary Musalia Mudavadi told Kenyan lawmakers on 8 October, Bloomberg reported. Botswana is also seeking a citizen's return.
In 2025, Ukrainian ambassador Ivan Kholostenko called Russia's role in Africa neocolonialism. As Africa Corps troops prop up friendly regimes, the Kremlin is carrying out "a typical colonial practice of resource extraction," taking gold, diamonds, bauxite, and uranium, according to Ukraine's Foreign Intelligence. Russia also uses the continent as a recruiting ground for its war: nearly 500 Africans have died fighting for Russia, Ukraine says.
Five Kenyans in a Ukrainian camp
Kenya is negotiating to bring the five men home, and President William Ruto has raised the matter with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Mudavadi told the Senate. One has been held since November 2025, the others since March and April. The youngest is 23, Bloomberg reported. Kenya's honorary consul found them held in humane conditions at the Zakhid-1 camp, with access to medical care, the government said. Ukraine also holds the remains of four Kenyans.
Victims or fighters for hire
African governments say some of their citizens went to Russia for promised work as drivers, security guards, or cooks and were then forced into military service. The Kenyans "report having been recruited under false promises of employment," Mudavadi said.
"The circumstances of their recruitment and conscription are consistent with trafficking in persons," he said.
Ukraine's POW authority sees most foreign recruits differently. "The main motive for most of these mercenaries is financial gain," Dmytro Usov, secretary of Ukraine's Coordination Headquarters for the Treatment of Prisoners of War, said in November 2025, while stressing that many had ended up in Russia's army through fraud or coercion.
Ghana negotiates Ukrainian drone deals as 1,780 Africans fight—and die—in Russia’s ranks
Ukraine holds that prisoners of war go home through exchanges, but Russia has never asked to trade for any foreign fighter except North Koreans, the headquarters said in May, adding it may consider other solutions if diplomats and lawyers find one.
Thousands of foreigners in Russia's ranks
Russia has recruited more than 28,000 foreigners from 135 countries, and more than 5,000 have been killed, a Ukrainian government website cited by Bloomberg says. Ukraine holds at least 213 foreign prisoners of war, not counting Russians and North Koreans, 37 of them African, according to documents Bloomberg saw. Russian dictator Vladimir Putin claimed on 3 September that people are "coming forward voluntarily and signing contracts."
Kenya's government counts 354 citizens linked to the war: 84 killed or missing, 34 hospitalized in Russia, and 62 repatriated. Petitioners told senators that 841 Kenyans remain unaccounted for. Mudavadi said his March visit to Moscow put Kenya on a Russian recruitment "stop list," with no new Kenyans enlisted since.
Some African governments take steps
In August, Botswana stopped eight citizens from joining the Russian military at airports in Botswana, South Africa, and Ethiopia, Bloomberg reported.
Ghana accused Russia of luring its citizens into the war the same month, after Kenya and South Africa. The European Parliament said in March that Russia strips African recruits of their documents. Ukraine, meanwhile, is drafting its first Africa strategy.

articles.title: Raytheon wins up to $6.3B to build more SM-3 interceptors
articles.body:
- Raytheon received a contract worth up to $6.3 billion over five years, plus two option years, to produce and sustain SM-3 Block IB interceptors.
- The interceptor was first used in combat in 2024, and production will take place mainly in Tucson, Arizona, and Huntsville, Alabama.
The U.S. Department of War and the Missile Defense Agency have awarded Raytheon a multiyear contract worth up to $6.3 billion to build and sustain Standard Missile-3 Block IB interceptors, the ship- and land-launched missiles the U.S. Navy uses to shoot down ballistic missiles in space.
The contract runs five years with two additional option years. It was issued as an undefinitized contract action, which lets Raytheon start work immediately while final terms and pricing are still being negotiated. Neither the Pentagon nor the company said how many interceptors the contract will buy or how quickly deliveries will begin. Production will take place mainly at Raytheon plants in Tucson, Arizona, and Huntsville, Alabama.
The SM-3 Block IB is built to destroy short- to intermediate-range ballistic missiles during the midcourse phase of flight, while they are outside the atmosphere, by hitting them directly rather than with an explosive warhead. It is launched from Aegis-equipped U.S. Navy destroyers and cruisers and from Aegis Ashore land sites, alongside the larger SM-3 Block IIA. The Block IB was first used in combat in April 2024, when U.S. Navy ships intercepted Iranian ballistic missiles fired at Israel, and it has been used again during this year’s war with Iran.
Raytheon said the award supports urgent replenishment of missile defense stocks that have been drawn down in combat.
“This award underscores Raytheon’s commitment to increasing production of critical munitions, ensuring our customers have the defensive capabilities they need, when they need them,” said Raytheon President Phil Jasper. “SM-3 Block IB has proven its relevance in combat and this contract helps ensure we can replenish inventories and keep pace with the evolving threats the U.S. Navy, MDA and their partners face around the world.”
The Pentagon said the multiyear deal is meant to give industry the production certainty to invest in assembly lines, solid rocket motor suppliers and smaller domestic subcontractors, where shortages have limited how fast interceptors can be built.
“Our warfighters must never face a fair fight, and the SM-3 Blk IB has proven its operational superiority to dominate any adversary across the globe,” said Michael P. Duffey, under secretary of war for acquisition and sustainment. “This contract provides production certainty to our defense industrial base, breaks sub-tier manufacturing bottlenecks, and ensures that our fleets and combatant commands have the interceptors required to dominate the battle space.”
The award is the latest under five framework agreements Raytheon signed with the Department of War in February, covering expanded production of Tomahawk cruise missiles, AMRAAM air-to-air missiles, SM-3 Block IB, SM-3 Block IIA and SM-6 under deals of up to seven years. Last week, Raytheon received a contract worth up to $24.4 billion for SM-6 production under the same framework.
The SM-3 Block IB line had slowed before the current buildup. In March, the Missile Defense Agency awarded Raytheon about $267 million for 23 more Block IB interceptors to restart production, bringing that order to 78 missiles, along with an $8.41 billion increase to the ceiling of a contract for SM-3 sustainment and engineering support.

articles.title: Zelensky Says Ukraine Is Aware of US-Russia Economic Discussions
articles.body:
Ukraine is aware of the content of various discussions between US and Russian authorities, but has no intentions of making the details public yet, President Volodymyr Zelensky said.
Zelensky made the remarks while speaking to reporters on Thursday, Oct. 8, in response to a question about which economic agreements Washington and Moscow are discussing.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“We know a lot… about various dialogues, but I am simply not ready to talk about them publicly and in detail,” Zelensky said, according to Ukrinform.
Although the President did not specify which discussions he was referring to, his comments came hours after Reuters reported – citing five anonymous sources familiar with the matter, including a White House official – that US and Russia had discussed bringing an American investor into the Nord Stream gas pipelines.
Nord Stream reportedly discussed
According to Reuters, the talks involved senior US special envoy Jared Kushner, President Donald Trump’s son-in-law and Kirill Dmitriev, a close adviser to Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Kushner reportedly sees business deals as key to securing a possible settlement.
Earlier in September, the two envoys visited both Moscow and Kyiv in an effort to broker an end to Russia’s war, which reached a deadlock over irreconcilable differences between Ukraine’s and Russia’s demands, including Moscow’s proposals that Kyiv cedes its sovereignty as part of a peace settlement.
Zelensky Visits Pryluky With UK’s Miliband, Thanks EU for €1.2B Tranche for Drones
Although all three sides – the US, Ukraine and Russia – described the negotiations as productive and positive, the Kremlin consistently rejects proposals for a ceasefire and has increased its strikes on civilians and civilian infrastructure since.
Dmitriev, Russia’s envoy who heads the Russian Direct Investment Fund and has long pushed for Russian gas exports to Germany to resume, has emerged as one of Moscow’s main points of contact with the Trump administration.
Late September, he headed to New York to meet with the Trump administration, with the agenda previously agreed upon with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Diplomacy remains stalled
Earlier on Thursday, during a visit to Pryluky, where a Russian missile strike killed 22 people the previous day, Zelensky questioned how Washington and Moscow could discuss future economic projects while efforts to end the war remain stalled.
He also announced that a Ukrainian delegation would travel to the US for talks on Friday and Saturday, Oct. 9-10, and called on Trump to increase pressure on Russia.
Ukrainian authorities have repeatedly argued that Moscow shows no real willingness towards ending the war, pointing to the repeated strikes on Ukrainian cities.
During the 81st United Nations General Assembly in New York held late September, 51 countries signed a joint statement urging Russia to accept an immediate, unconditional ceasefire.
However, the Kremlin has rejected and mocked every such proposal so far.
During the same summit in New York, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov reiterated that Moscow would not pause its “special military operation” – a term Russia uses to downplay the war in Ukraine, currently in its fifth year – even during negotiations.
He also claimed that Ukraine would have kept its 1991 borders if the European nations had not “engaged in their shenanigans.”
The comment came just a month after Ukraine marked its 35th Independence Day.
