articles.title: Zelensky ‘doesn’t give a damn’ about Ukrainians – Russian envoy
articles.body:
Zelensky ‘doesn’t give a damn’ about Ukrainians – Russian envoy
Vladimir Zelensky’s continued attempts to target Moscow despite harsh retaliation against Ukraine’s military-related infrastructure prove that he doesn’t care about the well-being of his country’s people, Russia’s ambassador to the Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE), Dmitry Polyansky, has said.
Moscow Region came under a major aerial attack on Tuesday night, with Ukraine firing 650 drones towards the Russian capital, Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin said. Despite most of the UAVs being shot down by air defenses, the raid resulted in the death of two people. Another civilian was killed in a Ukrainian drone attack in the region on Thursday, according to Governor Andrey Vorobyev.
During his speech at an OSCE session in the Austrian capital, Vienna, on Thursday, Polyansky said that Zelensky “still harbors hopes of inflicting at least some noticeable damage on Moscow” in order to present this to the West as “proof that Ukraine is still capable of carrying out military operations that are painful” for Russia.
“At the same time, the head of the Kiev regime never tires of threatening Russia with escalation – something he is incapable of actually delivering – only to then complain about large-scale strikes by Russia,” he said, as cited by TASS.
Zelensky should remember the proverb that “people who live in glass houses shouldn’t throw stones,” the envoy noted.
According to Polyansky, Russian retaliatory strikes on facilities supporting Kiev’s war machine are “many times more powerful” than those attempted by Ukrainian forces. Because of those attacks, Ukraine is “losing the last remnants of its industry and infrastructure,” while also teetering on the brink of a “total energy and transport collapse” ahead of winter, he added.
Zelensky, however, “doesn’t give a damn about his citizens. His only concern is siphoning more money out of the country into the corruption system of his creation,” Polyansky said.
Ukraine has been rocked by a series of high-profile corruption scandals since last year, with the largest centering on a $100 million kickback scheme at state nuclear operator Energoatom, which was reportedly led by Timur Mindich, a former business partner of Zelensky. Other recent graft probes have targeted former Ukrainian ministers, prosecutors, diplomats, and senior officials.
In an interview with Reuters last week, Zelensky said he had ordered the Ukrainian military to double the number of attacks deep inside Russia, particularly against the country’s oil refining facilities.
The Russian Defense Ministry responded by announcing that “following Zelensky’s statement, the strikes... on military and military-industrial facilities… in Kiev and other regions of Ukraine will be intensified.” The ministry maintains that it never targets civilians.

articles.title: Meet the Nobel Peace Prize Contenders Who Could Beat Trump This Year
articles.body:
President Donald Trump on Wednesday revisited his argument that he deserves to be awarded the Nobel Peace Prize this year, telling reporters in the Oval Office that he has done “far more” than any other U.S. President.
“I don't know what their decision is going to be. They have a reputation for maybe not giving it to people like me,” Trump said, insisting that it would be a “great discredit” to the Norwegian Nobel Committee if they do not announce him as the recipient Friday morning.
“I've stopped maybe the total obliteration of the world, because Iran will never have a nuclear weapon, and that's a positive thing,” he claimed, listing the reasons why he believes he is deserving of the prestigious prize.
Trump said he was “very honored to receive it indirectly last time by the recipient, who said nobody in history deserves it more” than him. The 2025 winner, Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado, notably gave her medal to Trump in January as she pressed the U.S. to support democracy in Venezuela, days after the U.S. capture of former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro and his wife Cilia Flores.
Following the regifting of the medal, the Norwegian Nobel Committee emphasized that “the prize itself—the honor and recognition—remains inseparably linked to the person or organization designated as the laureate by the Norwegian Nobel Committee.”
Trump has long said he is deserving of the prize. The leaders of Israel, Cambodia, and Pakistan have all previously said they nominated Trump. However, all nominations remain private and the Norwegian Nobel Institute doesn’t release a shortlist of contenders. Still, each year, names are circulated in public discourse and bets are made as to who might come out on top.
The Norwegian Nobel Institute has registered a total of 287 candidates for this year’s prize, of which 208 are individuals and 79 are organizations.
As Trump’s war with Iran stretches into its eighth month, polls have tipped him as an unlikely contender to walk away with this year’s award. Amid mounting speculation over who may be the chosen recipient, here’s a look at some of the contenders.
Sudan’s Emergency Response Rooms
The start of Sudan’s current civil war in April 2023 escalated an already desperate humanitarian crisis. Fighting between the army and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) in late 2025 pushed civilians further toward risk of famine, with even more people displaced and killed.
Sudan’s Emergency Response Rooms have provided desperately needed relief. The collapse of the state and increasingly difficult access for humanitarian groups over the past three years has led to a rise of 700 ERRs across all of Sudan’s 18 states, mobilizing over 26,000 volunteers, according to Alsanosi Adam, a journalist and ERR volunteer himself.
The community-led initiative provides healthcare, food assistance, education, civilian protection, and psychosocial support. According to Right Livelihood, volunteers have been detained and tortured while offering assistance.
The charity is a lead contender to win the Nobel Peace Prize, with Polymarket citing a 17% chance.
Mark Carney
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney arrived in Office last April amid an emerging trade rift with Trump and threats from Washington to annex Canada and make it the 51st state.
The tariff threats escalated and, following the collapse of negotiations in August, the U.S. and Canada are now engaged in a trade war.
Carney has opened up new trading and diplomatic relations with China and Europe in an effort to move away from U.S. reliance. He delivered a defiant speech at the World Economic Forum in Davos in January, denouncing “American hegemony” and insisting there has been a “rupture in the world order.”
Carney’s efforts to unite Canada in the face of Trump’s threats have seemingly helped his popularity at home, with his approval rating back up to 66%, according to new data from Liaison Strategies.
When it comes to the Nobel Peace Prize, he’s more an outsider, with a 1% chance of receiving the honor.
Pope Leo
Pope Leo XIV, the first American pope, has made strident global outreach efforts since his ascension to the head of the Catholic Church in April 2025.
His repeated calls for peace, including his spotlight on Gaza, have made an impact, and even earned him criticism from Trump.
“Today, sadly, war has returned, even to Europe: a new senseless slaughter, claiming countless civilian lives every day,” Leo told European leaders in September, referencing the Russia-Ukraine war. “We must ask whether we are truly making creative efforts to advance world peace, or whether we are simply seeking to stem the tide of war and better prepare ourselves for wars that we assume are still to come.”
In the aftermath of the first U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran in late February, Leo said “stability and peace are not achieved through mutual threats, nor through the use of weapons, which sow destruction, suffering, and death, but only through reasonable, sincere, and responsible dialogue.” 
Trump responded by falsely claiming that Leo would “be fine with Iran having a nuclear weapon”—Leo rejected the claim and urged critics to speak “truthfully.”
Pope Leo stands with a 1% chance of being awarded the prize.
Mykola Kuleba
Mykola Kuleba co-founded Save Ukraine in 2014 during the early days of the conflict in Eastern Ukraine. The organization’s work has become increasingly important since Russia’s full-scale invasion of its neighbor in 2022.
Missing Ukrainian children have become a focal point of humanitarian efforts amid the war, with Moscow contending that it relocated children in an effort to protect them. Save Ukraine has so far helped reunite 1,763 children with their parents, but the organization has said thousands more need to be brought home.
“[Kuleba’s] work combines direct humanitarian action with strong advocacy for children’s rights, making him a compelling candidate for international recognition,” said Haakon Gjerløw, acting director of the Peace Research Institute Oslo (PRIO), as he detailed his list of suggested candidates for the 2026 prize.
Kuleba is currently listed as having a 9% chance.
Yulia Navalnaya
Yulia Navalnaya, widow of Russian opposition leader Alexei Navalny, has become an activist in her own right, challenging President Vladimir Putin’s regime and fighting for democracy.
Alexei died in an Arctic penal colony in February 2024. A few weeks later, Yulia vowed to take up his cause in an interview with TIME, where she expressed hope that Russia might one day be a “normal, democratic country”—the future Alexei “dreamed about.”
Navalnaya is listed as having a 5% chance of winning the Nobel Peace Prize.

articles.title: Putin offers help to end Iran war while Russia continues its own in Ukraine
articles.body:
The Russian president met Pezeshkian in Turkmenistan and pledged to do “everything in our power” to end the ongoing war between the US and Iran, despite Russia not being among the official mediators.
Vladimir Putin pledged to do "everything in our power" to help end the war between Iran and the US on Thursday, positioning Russia as a would-be Middle East mediator while continuing his own full-scale invasion of Ukraine, now in its fifth year.
The Russian president made the remarks at a bilateral meeting with his Iranian counterpart Masoud Pezeshkian in Avazeh, on Turkmenistan's Caspian coast, praising Tehran for making what he called "genuine efforts" to resolve the war.
Pezeshkian said Iran and the US had exchanged proposals to end the war and reopen the Strait of Hormuz, and that Tehran was reviewing and amending them before consolidating them through mediators. Despite ongoing US attacks, he said Iran would not leave the negotiating table.
"We are talking, but every time we negotiate with the United States, they attack again," Pezeshkian said. "Nevertheless, we will not abandon the negotiating table and dialogue."
He said the revisions, once finalised, would be put to mediators. "We are supposed to sit down through the existing mediators and consolidate them," he said.
It was the seventh meeting between the two presidents since Pezeshkian took office, following a phone call on 7 October — Putin's birthday — in which the pair discussed regional developments and the Iran-US negotiations.
The two previously met in person on 1 September on the sidelines of the Shanghai Co-operation Organisation summit in Bishkek.
Russia is not a mediator in the US-Iran negotiations. So far, Qatar and Pakistan have led the talks.
Ties further deepen
Military, diplomatic and economic relations between Iran and Russia have strengthened since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in early 2022.
The Iran war, which began with joint US-Israeli strikes on 28 February, has sparked more frequent consultations between Moscow and Tehran on political and material support and financial co-operation.
Since 2022, Iran has supplied Russia with Shahed drone technology — which Moscow has since copied to create its own Geran-type variant, a key tool in its daily attacks on Ukrainian civilian and infrastructure targets — and short-range missiles.
Moscow also faces accusations of providing Tehran with targeting information for attacks on US interests in the Middle East.
Trade between the two countries rose by more than 21% in 2025 and continued on the same trajectory through the first seven months of 2026, Putin said, adding that relations were developing under a comprehensive strategic partnership agreement signed early last year.
Pezeshkian described the current situation as an opportunity to deepen co-operation and said Tehran and Moscow should coordinate "with greater speed and strength."
Billion-dollar loan delayed
Iranian state-run media reported in the days before the meeting that Russia was ready to extend a $1 billion loan to Tehran, described as the first tranche of a $20 billion package agreed at a meeting between Supreme National Security Council secretary Ali Larijani and Putin.
The semi-official IRGC-affiliated Fars news agency said arrangements to disburse the sum were complete, but disagreements among Iranian authorities over how to spend the money prevented Tehran from providing the account number needed to complete the transfer.
Iran's Planning and Budget Organisation wants to use the funds to import cars and collect customs duties, the Oil Ministry wants them for oil equipment, and the Agriculture Ministry is seeking to allocate them to basic commodity imports, according to the same report.
The bilateral meeting took place on the eve of the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) leaders' summit — a gathering of nine former Soviet republic heads focused on regional co-operation — and a separate Caspian Sea environmental conference, also held in Turkmenistan, bringing together the leaders of Iran, Russia, Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan and Turkmenistan.

articles.title: Ukraine’s Ground Robots Rescued 45 Soldiers Under Fire, Commander Says
articles.body:
Ukraine’s ground robots rescued 45 soldiers from under Russian fire and transported more than 41 tons of supplies to frontline positions during the summer of 2026, according to the Artan special unit under Ukraine’s Military Intelligence Directorate (HUR).
Artan commander Col. Viktor Torkotiuk, call sign Titan, said crews operating the unmanned ground vehicles (UGVs) worked continuously along the front, according to RBC-Ukraine.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
During the summer campaign, the platforms covered a combined distance of approximately 4,258 kilometers (2,646 miles), with tasks ranging from supporting frontline logistics to evacuating wounded Ukrainian troops and transporting captured Russian soldiers.
Robots enter areas too dangerous for vehicles
The ground platforms allowed Ukrainian forces to evacuate wounded troops from exposed positions without sending additional personnel or conventional vehicles into areas monitored by Russian drones.
Torkotiuk said the drones help free up valuable resources.
“Technology is transforming the combat capabilities of units on the front line,” Torkotiuk said. “Innovative logistics frees up capabilities and forces for active operations and offensive actions,” he added.
The unit did not specify how many vehicles took part in the missions, how many individual journeys they completed, or which ground-robot models they used.
Ground robotic systems vary in size and configuration. Some transport ammunition, food and other supplies, while others can carry wounded soldiers, conduct reconnaissance, clear mines or operate mounted weapons.
Russia Steps Up Production of Improved Su-34 ‘Fullback’ Bombers
Ukrainian troops have said such platforms are particularly useful inside the so-called kill zone, where ordinary evacuation vehicles can quickly be detected and targeted by surveillance and attack drones.
Frontline soldiers have previously told Kyiv Post that robots are not replacing troops but are increasingly performing the most dangerous logistical and medical evacuation missions.
Artan operates in Zaporizhzhia and near Lyman
Artan said its main area of operations is currently the Zaporizhzhia front in southern Ukraine, a region where over 70 percent is under Russian occupation, most of which since 2022.
The unit also participated in one stage of Ukraine’s Operation Vivaldi near Lyman in eastern Ukraine during the spring and summer campaign. The operation recovered at least 125 square kilometers (48 square miles) of territory and disrupted Russian attempts to advance toward Sloviansk and Kramatorsk.
Analysts suggest the operation has reversed Russian gains made in 2026 and thwarted Moscow’s goal to capture eastern Ukraine’s Donetsk region.
The HUR special operations unit was formed on June 1, 2022. Its personnel have fought in some of the war’s most contested areas and participated in land and Black Sea operations, including the 2023 campaign that helped open the road to Klishchiivka and create an escape route for Ukrainian forces encircled by the Russians in the Donetsk region’s Bakhmut.
Ukraine expands its robotic army
Ukraine is rapidly increasing its use of ground robots to reduce the number of soldiers exposed during supply runs and casualty evacuations.
President Volodymyr Zelensky set a target to provide the military with at least 50,000 ground robotic systems by 2026.
The systems are becoming a regular part of frontline operations as Ukraine seeks to compensate for personnel shortages and adapt to a battlefield where drones can detect and attack conventional vehicles several kilometers behind the contact line.

articles.title: Trump rules out Iran strikes as Pentagon draws up plans
articles.body:
(Getty Images)
The Pentagon has drawn up plans for an intensive three-day military campaign against Iran, the U.S. media reported on Oct. 8, even as President Donald Trump said Washington will not launch an attack before the Nov. 3 elections.
The U.S. military, acting on Trump’s orders, has developed options to strike Iran’s missile and drone arsenal, energy facilities and other military sites, The Times reported, citing U.S. officials.
Senior national security officials, led by Vice President JD Vance, discussed the plans at Camp David last week, with the options centering on a short, intensive campaign lasting about three days, according to people briefed on the proposal.
The strikes would focus on Iran’s missile and drone arsenal, much of which has been rebuilt by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) since the early phase of the war, the newspaper said.
Other potential targets include Iranian energy facilities as well as IRGC command posts and headquarters.
Axios separately reported that the Pentagon ordered the US Central Command (CENTCOM) several days ago to complete preparations for a possible resumption of major combat operations against Iran.
The directive did not set a date for strikes and Trump had not made a final decision, Axios said, adding that any renewed major combat operations were expected to include large-scale bombing of Iranian energy, infrastructure and nuclear targets.
The military preparations come as Trump said on Oct. 8 that the US would not attack Iran before the Nov. 3 midterm elections, while pointing to ongoing diplomatic efforts.
“I want to make it clear to everybody that, while Iran is in very bad condition, both Economically and Militarily, and while the Blockade will remain in full force and effect...we will not be attacking Iran at any time prior to the Midterm Elections,” he wrote.
In a post on his Truth Social platform, Trump said Washington and Tehran were having “productive discussions.”
Trump’s announcement on his Truth Social platform followed a surge in oil prices driven by media reports suggesting potential new US strikes prior to the elections.
The New York Times also reported that Trump has repeatedly declined proposals in recent months to resume major combat operations against Iran, despite ordering the Pentagon to prepare new options.
Three U.S. aircraft carriers are expected to be in the Middle East in the coming weeks as part of the major military buildup, according to the newspaper.

articles.title: It became known how many Russian military personnel and pieces of equipment the Armed Forces of Ukraine eliminated on the front over the course of the day
articles.body:
It became known how many Russian military personnel and pieces of equipment the Armed Forces of Ukraine eliminated on the front over the course of the day
Kyiv • UNN
Russia lost 1,710 military personnel, 1,757 drones, 67 artillery systems, and 617 vehicles over the course of the day. Total losses reached 1,549,490 personnel.
Over the past day, October 8, the Russian army lost another 1,710 military personnel killed and wounded. Russia’s total personnel losses since the beginning of the full-scale invasion have reached approximately 1,549,490. The General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reports this, UNN writes.
Details
According to the Ukrainian command, over the past day the Defense Forces destroyed 1,757 Russian operational-tactical unmanned aerial vehicles, 67 artillery systems, and 617 vehicles and fuel tankers.
In addition, the occupiers lost 3 tanks, 7 armored combat vehicles, 5 multiple rocket launchers, 1 air defense system, 18 ground robotic systems, and 4 pieces of special equipment.
Total losses of the Russian army as of October 9
Since the beginning of the full-scale war, the Russian army has lost 12,402 tanks, 25,509 armored combat vehicles, 50,950 artillery systems, 2,199 multiple rocket launchers, and 1,693 air defense systems.
Ukrainian forces have also destroyed 443 Russian aircraft, 356 helicopters, 2,908 ground robotic systems, 555,335 operational-tactical unmanned aerial vehicles, and 5,126 cruise missiles.
The General Staff emphasizes that data on the enemy’s losses is still being уточнено.

articles.title: Is Trump signalling a return to war with Iran after the midterms?
articles.body:
Is Trump signalling a return to war with Iran after the midterms?
US media reports suggest he may be weighing strikes before the vote but the president has ruled that out.
United States President Donald Trump has said that he does not intend to bomb Iran again until the November midterm elections, even though several US media outlets have reported that the Pentagon has drawn up plans to relaunch attacks before that vote.
Trump has been accused of misdirection on the issue in the past. The US launched its initial attacks on Iran on February 28, as talks with Iran were ongoing and despite Trump saying just the day before that he had not made any decision. One year previously, the US struck Iran towards the end of Israel’s June 2025 12-day war, despite Trump saying he would announce a decision about attacks “in two weeks”.
Still, striking Iran ahead of the midterm elections would be risky for the administration as the war remains deeply unpopular with Americans.
Resuming the war afterwards may have less of a negative impact on Trump, who is not eligible to run for another term as US president anyway.
Here’s what we know about Trump’s plans.
What has been reported by US media?
In the past two days, The New York Times, The Wall Street Journal and other publications have reported claims by unnamed officials that the Pentagon has drawn up plans to attack Iran before the midterms, if authorised to do so.
On Wednesday, US publication Axios cited US and Israeli officials saying the Pentagon has instructed US Central Command (CENTCOM) to prepare for imminent major combat operations. The Atlantic also reported along similar lines.
What has Trump said?
On Thursday, Trump posted on his Truth Social media platform that he will not order a resumption of strikes on Iran before November 3, when the US midterm elections will be held.
“I want to make it clear to everybody that, while Iran is in very bad condition…we will not be attacking Iran at any time prior to the Midterm Elections to be held in the United States on November 3rd,” he said.
The president added that the US is presently “having productive discussions” with the Iranian side. However, that was also the case on February 28, the day the US and Israel first struck Iran, triggering the war.
Trump did not make any reference to preparing for potential military operations, nor did he provide more details on the state of talks.
Why might Trump be hesitant about resuming bombing before the midterms?
Trump and Republicans are worried about a voter backlash against the war at the polls. The US war on Iran is intensely unpopular domestically as Americans have had to grapple with surging prices of gas, food and other basic commodities because of the crisis in the Middle East.
Since the start of the war, surveys have shown that large numbers of Americans did not approve of striking Iran.
Now, about 65 percent of Americans say they “disapprove” of the way in which Trump has handled the Iran war overall, according to a Pew Research Center poll released on Thursday. Trump stated at the start of the war that it would go on for just a few weeks, however, it is now into its eighth month.
According to Pew, most Americans now believe the war will continue for at least another year. Even Republican or more conservative-leaning voters are growing more negative about the war, its poll found.
The conflict has also severely affected Trump’s personal ratings and eroded support for Republicans. A Reuters/Ipsos poll on Thursday found that only 30 percent of his supporters were enthusiastic about voting in the midterms, compared with 48 percent of Democratic voters.
About 13 percent of those who voted for Trump in 2024 say they are not sure who to vote for in the congressional elections.
Delaying attacks until after the elections could potentially shield Republican candidates from voter backlash, analysts say.
While analysts say Trump will see a good performance at the polls as approval for renewed strikes, a Republican defeat at the polls could equally further incentivise him to hit Iran again as he will calculate that he has little to lose at that point.
While that could further affect Trump’s ratings, the president is not eligible to run in the next presidential election in any case.
Will the US restart the war after the midterms?
In recent weeks, the US president has threatened to “end” the war with force after the elections as talks with Iran have dragged on.
At a Republican convention in September, he accused Iran of trying to affect the outcome of the midterms and said that conflict “is going to end immediately after the elections”.
In an interview with Time magazine two weeks ago, he also said it would be “possible” to ramp up bombing in Iran after the elections, but declined to elaborate. Analysts say his comments were designed to calm voters, while at the same time warning Iran of potential aggression after the vote.
Last week, the US military dispatched about 7,000 sailors and 2,000 Marines aboard several ships now sailing to the Middle East amid threats of new attacks from Trump. The vessel formation included the USS Theodore Roosevelt carrier strike group.
The deployment increases the number of US troops in the region to 20,000, alongside hundreds of aircraft and at least three carrier strike groups.
In the past, US troop build-up in the Middle East and the Caribbean has subsequently resulted in military action.
In June, Washington and Iran signed a ceasefire agreement that quickly broke down over control of the Strait of Hormuz.
Trump has repeatedly said that the US has the upper hand in the strait, citing more oil exports and Iran’s weakened economy. He has also voiced aversion to a deal with Tehran over management of Hormuz, but said he might consider it because “they’re willing to offer us anything to stop”.
Washington rejected a recent proposal from Iran to reopen the strait based on certain conditions it wants the US to meet, including the lifting of sanctions, unfreezing Iranian assets and guaranteeing an end to attacks. Last week, Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Iran was considering a counterproposal from the US.

articles.title: From intelligence chief to trafficking secret information: August Hanning
articles.body:
August Hanning, currently in custody, led Germany’s foreign intelligence service (BND) for seven years and had access to the state’s most closely guarded secrets; the next chapter involved a private consultancy, corporate intelligence, and business activities spanning Europe (including Russia) and Asia, reports Politico.
Now, following his arrest by the German Federal Prosecutor's Office on the 6th of October on suspicion of espionage and treason, the 80-year-old Hanning finds himself at the center of an investigation. Prosecutors suspect he obtained classified intelligence from his former chief of staff and used it in his private business dealings. An EU intelligence official, speaking on condition of anonymity, described the situation as a disaster for both Germany and Western intelligence agencies. Everyone is reportedly in shock, and the scale of the incident is immense, particularly given the current climate. The official added that, since the alleged espionage came to light during the investigation of an entirely separate matter, a great deal more information is likely to emerge.
The case has arisen at an awkward time for the BND. In early October, German lawmakers began debating a new bill proposed by Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s government that would grant the intelligence service sweeping powers, aiming to restore Berlin to the ranks of the world’s top intelligence agencies. The timing is also significant for European intelligence services more broadly; with Russian hybrid attacks threatening Europe, governments across the bloc are rewriting long-standing security laws to empower their intelligence agencies and ensure they are taken more seriously.
Prosecutors stated that the former head of Hanning’s office—identified as Manfred D. in accordance with German privacy regulations—handed over approximately 2,000 BND documents to Hanning between 2010 and 2022. 
Many of these contained classified information intended solely for internal use by the intelligence service, including materials used to brief high-ranking German officials.
Speaking to the newspaper WELT, Hanning’s lawyer stated that while some of the charges brought against the former intelligence chief were true, he had not intended to cause harm to Germany. The lawyer pointed out that Hanning was indeed in possession of classified documents, but the accusation that he had passed on information capable of harming the state was false.
In one instance, charges were brought regarding the use of classified documents to prepare an analytical report for a foreign intelligence officer. Prosecutors also believe that Manning maintained a relationship with a representative of another intelligence service for several years and passed on political information that was partly based on documents supplied by Manfred D. Prosecutors have not identified the specific intelligence agencies with which Manning might have been linked, but German media have named Azerbaijan and Kazakhstan. Azerbaijan has denied involvement.
Another anonymous EU official stated that intelligence agencies log every action—specifically, who accesses information and when. If an analyst working on monitoring right-wing extremists suddenly begins viewing intelligence on China, it can raise suspicions. Conversely, high-ranking officials—such as a director's chief of staff—can access virtually anything without arousing suspicion. Moreover, chiefs of staff typically remain in their posts even when directors change; the only exceptions are cases involving disagreements with the incoming director. The official stated that 
each intelligence agency would now have to assess the information passed to the BND and the potential damage caused by this.
Hanning headed the BND from 1998 to 2005 and subsequently served as State Secretary at the German Interior Ministry until 2009. Upon leaving the government, Hanning turned to the private sector, founding Hanning Consult with his wife in July 2010. In the spring of that same year, Manfred D. agreed—in exchange for payment—to pass intelligence held by the BND to Hanning, who in turn utilized it for his private consulting activities.
Roderich Kiesewetter, a German Christian Democrat MP and representative on the Bundestag’s Foreign Affairs Committee, stated that there is a vast network of individuals in Germany who leverage information and influence gained during their time in public service to shape Berlin’s policy regarding countries such as China and Russia. Kiesewetter told Politico that the situation is not only lamentable but also damages Germany’s reputation; he noted that if someone wishes to engage with Russia, it suffices to enlist former government or intelligence officials.
Hanning is also linked to German businessman Samuel Danilowitsch, who headed the Swiss corporate intelligence consultancy Pluteos. Hanning became the chairman of the board at Pluteos and, in 2019, attended a meeting in Moscow with Danilowitsch focused on European-Russian relations. Russian politicians and businesspeople participated in the event, during which the annexation of Crimea was portrayed as a necessity rather than a choice made by Moscow.
Around 2014, Hanning joined the British consultancy G3 as a senior advisor. 
He later oversaw the firm's operations regarding Russia and former Soviet bloc countries.
In 2019, Hanning was invited as a guest of honor to an Arctic Council meeting organized by the Russian Security Council. It was chaired by the former Secretary of the Russian Security Council, Nikolai Patrushev, one of the most influential figures in Russian dictator Vladimir Putin's security circle.
Hanning has also spoken publicly about some of the politically explosive issues surrounding Russian aggression in Ukraine. In 2024, he told WELT TV that he considered it plausible that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy knew about the 2022 bombing of the Nord Stream pipelines. A few days later, Hanning went further, stating that a secret agreement between high-ranking Polish and Ukrainian officials lay behind the attack on the pipelines.
None of Hanning’s business dealings, contacts, or statements link him to espionage; however, they demonstrate that he continued to expand his influence even after leaving government service. Nor have any charges been brought regarding espionage on behalf of Russia.
Investigators discovered the classified documents in Hanning’s possession while probing an unusual guardianship case
 involving Christina Block, the heiress to a German restaurant empire. The Hamburg public prosecutor’s office charged Block with abducting her two youngest children from their father in Denmark. Block and two men allegedly hired an Israeli security team to snatch the children—then aged 10 and 13—from their father's custody. According to the charges, masked men beat the children's father and took the children across the Danish-German border to southern Germany. Four days later, the children were returned to their father by court order. Block denies having known about the abduction.
In September 2025, Hamburg investigators searched Hanning’s home and business premises in connection with the Block case. Prosecutors believed that Hanning and a retired police officer had accepted a deal worth 100,000 euros to intercept Block’s children on their way to school in November 2022. The plan failed because the children's father noticed suspicious individuals and called the police. Following the search, the German media outlet Taggeshau reported that investigators had found approximately 2,000 digital BND documents on Hanning’s properties, triggering an investigation that was taken over by the Federal Prosecutor's Office in May 2026.
Manfred D. was Hanning’s chief of staff and subsequently worked with the next BND directors as well, remaining in the position until March 2026. Both men are currently in custody.

articles.title: Polish man suspected of helping Russian plot to assassinate Zelensky sentenced to 5.5 years
articles.body:
Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!
Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.
A Polish man has been sentenced to five and a half years in prison for spying on behalf of Russia. The tasks assigned to him included reconnaissance of Rzeszów-Jasionka airport as part of a possible plan to assassinate Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky while he travelled through Poland.
The sentence was handed down by the court of appeal in Lublin on Thursday, increasing by two years a jail term issued by a lower court earlier this year. The ruling is now final and binding.
Sąd zaostrzył karę dla Pawła K. Chodzi o współpracę z rosyjskim wywiadem #lublin #szpieg #rosja #wywiad #wyrok https://t.co/Vg2zTx35l4
— Fakt (@Fakt_pl) October 8, 2026
The 51-year-old former Polish soldier, who has been named only as Paweł K. under privacy law, was detained by Poland’s Internal Security Agency (ABW) in April 2024.
Investigators found that the suspect had declared his willingness to collaborate with Russian intelligence and, between December 2022 and March 2024, had established contact via email and instant messaging with Russians involved in military operations against Ukraine, including army officers.
Prosecutors determined that Paweł K. had been assigned tasks including gathering and transmitting information regarding security at Rzeszów airport, which is the main hub for goods and people being transported in and out of Ukraine.
“These activities could have been used by Russian intelligence services, including in the context of planning a possible assassination attempt on the head of a foreign state, that is, President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelensky,” wrote Poland’s National Prosecutor’s Office earlier this year.
Poland and Ukraine have revealed further details of a foiled plan to assassinate @ZelenskyyUa at Poland's Rzeszów airport.
A Polish man was last month indicted in relation to the incident, which he is accused of seeking to carry out on behalf of Russia https://t.co/Lrp99vH4s2
— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 23, 2025
Last year, the head of the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) said that Paweł K. had been “recruited decades ago and firmly believed in the Soviet cause”. Polish prosecutors have not commented on that claim.
However, they did find that the suspect had declared his willingness to join Russian “sabotage structures”, including the Wagner mercenary group and Unit 29155 of the GRU, Russia’s military intelligence agency, which is tasked with carrying out destabilisation activities.
Paweł G. denied the accusations against him and claimed that he had actually been trying to help capture Russian war criminals by deceiving them into trusting him, reports the Polish Press Agency (PAP).
His defence attorney argued that the information Paweł G. had transmitted regarding Rzeszów airport was “trivial and publicly available”, according to news website Onet.
In January this year, Paweł K. was found guilty of espionage and illegal possession of ammunition by the district court in the city of Zamość, which sentenced him to three and a half years in prison.
However, prosecutors appealed against that ruling, arguing that the suspect deserved a longer jail term of seven and a half years. In a judgement issued on Thursday, the Lublin appeals court agreed that Paweł G’s initial sentence had been “grossly lenient” and increased it by two years, reports PAP.
“Submitting an offer to work for…the intelligence service of a country that is at war with a country directly neighboring Poland, a country that is making quite extensive unfriendly gestures towards Poland, cannot be treated leniently,” said judge Artur Achrymowicz.
Poland has charged three of its own citizens with working on behalf of Russian intelligence.
They are accused of spreading disinformation, conducting reconnaissance of NATO troops, and undergoing firearms training in preparation for acts of sabotage https://t.co/maYd0kb9HW
— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 20, 2026
Poland has become a primary target for acts of espionage, sabotage and disinformation conducted by operatives working on behalf of Russia.
In many cases, they are so-called “disposable agents”: individuals already on the ground, often amateurs hired and paid through messaging apps such as Telegram, rather than professional spies or soldiers.
The AWB last year launched 48 investigations related to espionage, more than twice as many as in 2024. Over those two years, there were more espionage investigations than over the previous three decades combined
A report published earlier this year by the International Centre for Counter-Terrorism found that Poland is the “primary focus” of Russia’s sabotage operations in Europe.
Poland is the "primary focus" of Russia's sabotage campaign in Europe, finds a new report by the International Centre for Counter-Terrorism.
Among 151 incidents identified since 2022, 31 of them took place in Poland – more than in any other country https://t.co/QXfSI00FD6
— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 3, 2026
In January, Polish prosecutors indicted five people – four Ukrainian citizens and one Russian – accused of carrying out a plot on behalf of Russia to plant explosives in packages that were then dispatched by courier services across Europe.
In April, prosecutors charged a soldier from Poland’s Territorial Defence Force with seeking to spy on behalf of Russia. The following month, three Polish citizens were charged with working on behalf of Russian intelligence to spread disinformation and conduct reconnaissance of NATO troops.
In July this year, a Russian married couple who had been studying in Poland were jailed for spying on behalf of Moscow and involvement in a plot to send a parcel bomb.

Daniel Tilles is editor-in-chief of Notes from Poland. He has written on Polish affairs for a wide range of publications, including Foreign Policy, POLITICO Europe, EUobserver and Dziennik Gazeta Prawna.

articles.title: Ukraine, Europe, US to meet in Miami for talks on ending war
articles.body:
Ukraine, Europe, US officials to meet for talks to end war
October 9, 2026
Ukrainian and European officials are set to meet US President Donald Trump's envoys in Miami on Friday to discuss "new ideas" to end Russia's war in Ukraine.
Ukraine's President Volodomyr Zelenskyy confirmed the meeting on Thursday evening, after a Russian attack on buses killed 30 civilians in the frontline city of Kramatorsk in eastern Ukraine.
Before the strikes in Kramatorsk, a Russian missile hit a five-storey apartment block in the northern Chernihiv region, killing 22 Ukrainians, including five children.
More than 70 people have been killed in Russian strikes on Ukraine in the past two days, Zelenskyy said.
What did Zelenskyy say about the Miami meeting?
"The Ukrainian negotiating team is due to meet Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff in the US tomorrow," Zelenskyy said. "The meeting is expected to last two days. We are also counting on a European team to join our negotiating group."
Zelenskyy's chief of staff, Kyrylo Budanov, and other top officials, including Rustem Umerov, Sergiy Kyslytsya and David Arakhamia, will also attend, the Ukrainian president said.
"They will discuss new ideas and proposals that American negotiators began developing with the Russians and Ukrainians during their recent visit to the region", one of the US sources familiar with the talks told AFP.
"They are all nervous about the winter. It will be a tough winter if the war does not stop," the US source said.
Zelenskyy blames US for inaction
Amid rising civilian casualties and fears of further escalation, Zelenskyy urged the US to accede to his request to expand Ukraine's access to Elon Musk's Starlink satellite service, which would help it target Russian ballistic-missile launchers.
"Open Starlink for Ukraine. You did open it when you were responding to Iran ... I've said quite openly — give it to us, help us defend our skies and dominate there. And then Putin will sit down at the negotiating table," he said.
Zelenskyy went on to accuse the US of being unwilling to pressure Russia into negotiations, adding that enabling Starlink would cost Washington nothing.
"So where's the truth here, where's the honesty? Where's the stalemate? ... That's called unwillingness," he said.
Ukraine president rejects Rubio claim that war is deadlocked
Zelenskyy was responding to remarks on Wednesday from US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who said the war in Ukraine was at a stalemate.
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said Thursday that he agreed with Rubio's assessment, adding that he saw no immediate prospect for a three-way summit between Russian President Vladimir Putin, Zelenskyy and Trump.
"One cannot, on the one hand, negotiate with the Russians about future economic projects, whilst on the other hand say that we find ourselves in some sort of ... diplomatic stalemate," Zelenskyy said, countering the US narrative. "We are not a diplomatic dead end," he said.
Zelenskyy also called for tougher sanctions to cripple the Russian economy, a point Ukrainian officials are expected to press US envoys on at the meeting.
Edited by: Karl Sexton

articles.title: Counter-Drone Task Force Taps Directed Energy Systems for December Shoot-Off
articles.body:
The Pentagon’s counter-drone task force recently selected four directed energy weapons it will test in a December shoot-off to identify lasers and microwave systems that could defend U.S. military installations from future aerial attacks.
The three laser weapons and one microwave system are the first to be selected for the Joint Interagency Task Force 401’s counter-unmanned aircraft systems directed energy pilot program, according to a Pentagon announcement. The pilot is a congressional requirement in the 2026 National Defense Authorization Act.
“High-energy lasers and high-powered microwave systems are tools that can be effectively used in a layered drone defense,” Army Brig. Gen. Matt Ross, director of JIATF 401, said in the announcement. “This pilot program will test these capabilities in an operational environment so we can understand how best to integrate and sustain them to defend the homeland.”
The four weapon systems selected to participate in the shoot-off at Dugway Proving Ground, Utah are:
- AeroVironment’s Palletized High-Energy Laser system
- Epirus’ Leonidas High-Powered Microwave system
- Kord Technologies’ Firefly High-Energy Laser system
- Boeing’s Compact Laser Weapon system
In May, JIATF 401 selected Grand Forks Air Force Base, N.D. and Whiteman Air Force Base, Mo.—along with Fort Huachuca, Ariz.; Fort Bliss, Texas; and Naval Base Kitsap, Wash.—to “support rigorous testing and operational assessments across diverse environments” for the pilot effort. U.S. Northern Command and the Federal Aviation Administration are also involved in the pilot, the announcement states.
The announcement of the four systems selected for the shoot-off comes seven months after an incident involving the firing of a military counter-drone laser on the southwest border that prompted the FAA to shut down all flight traffic over El Paso. The Pentagon and the FAA then quickly completed a “data-informed Safety Risk Assessment” of a high-energy laser counter-drone system which found that the counter-drone technology does “not pose undue risk to passenger aircraft.”
Epirus’ Leonidas system is the only high-powered microwave selected for the shoot-off so far. The Army awarded a $43.5 million contract to Epirus in July 2025, which included the delivery of two Integrated Fires Protection Capability High-Power Microwave, or IFPC-HPM Generation II systems, which rely on “weaponized electromagnetic interference” to down drones.
AeroVironment’s Palletized High-Energy Laser system features the firm’s LOCUST X3, a 30-kilowatt system the Army selected in September with a production contract valued at roughly $465 million.
Boeing’s Compact Laser Weapon is available in 2-kilowatt and 5-kilowatt versions. The 5-kilowatt system plugged into the Army’s Forward Area Air Defense Command and Control network to defeat Group 3 drones weighing up to 1,320 pounds during the September 2024 Red Sands Integrated Experimentation Center in Saudi Arabia, according to Boeing.
Kord’s Firefly High-Energy Laser is a palletized, mobile system that features scalable power from 5-kilowatts up to 30-kilowatts. It relies on advanced AI detection and tracking algorithms to “detect, track, intercept and defeat incoming drones at standoff ranges,” according to Kord, a subsidiary of KBR.
JIATF 401 plans to evaluate additional directed energy technologies that could be selected to participate in the shoot-off event, according to the announcement.
“Directed energy gives commanders another option within a layered defense, complementing existing counter-UAS capabilities with a scalable, safe, and effective way to respond to drone threats,” Ross said. “This pilot program will give us vital information in a real-world environment so we can employ these systems to protect the homeland.”
The Air Force is looking to up its counter-drone capabilities to defend bases, a mission it refers to as “point defense.” The service’s primary weapon system for doing so is the Small Unmanned Air Defense Systems, or SUADS. The system is capable of identifying and tracking enemy missiles or drones of multiple sizes, and downing incoming drones with an electronic warfare weapon, but officials have declined to identify what that system is. It can also interface with commercial counter-drone systems and other air defense systems, depending on the needs of a commander.
It’s unclear how much the service has spent or plans to spend on new counter-drone tech. The Air Force requested more than $1.5 billion for SUADS in the fiscal 2027 budget, most of it for missile defense components, according to budget documents. Additional counter-drone systems are being acquired with the assistance of JIATF 401, but those are not listed in the budget request and both Air Force and JIATF 401 officials have declined to provide funding details.
The Air Force Research Laboratory has experimented with high-powered microwave systems to down drones—in 2023, AFRL used the Tactical High-power Operational Responder, or THOR, to disable a drone swarm.

articles.title: Joy as USS Lincoln back home after troubled Gulf deployment
articles.body:
Families reunited as USS Lincoln returns from troubled 10-month deployment
The USS Lincoln docked in California on Thursday ending a record deployment of 265 days of uninterrupted time at sea marked by reports of deteriorating conditions onboard. Crew members were reunited with family they had not seen in nearly a year after their mission was prolonged by the war in Iran.
Thousands of emotional reunions unfolded Thursday as the USS Abraham Lincoln, whose lengthy deployment in the Gulf supporting President Donald Trump's war on Iran sparked fears for its crew's welfare, arrived back in its home port.
Families of servicemen and women had lined the quayside in San Diego, California, for hours, waiting to welcome loved ones they have not seen for almost a year.
There were tears of joy as more than 100 new dads met their babies for the first time, or fathers were reunited with children who are so much taller than last time they were together.
"Hi, baby girl, hi!" said one beaming sailor as he held his toddler daughter, planting a kiss on her forehead.
The nuclear-powered aircraft carrier left California in November 2025 for duty in the South China Sea and was rerouted to the Middle East before US-Israeli attacks on Iran that began in late February.
The vessel stayed at sea until a port call in Thailand in early September.
Ahead of the reunions, Alba Solano told AFP she had struggled to communicate with her partner during the mission.
"We heard from him through e-mails... we were able to text here and there. Phone calls were terrible. It never worked. He could hear us, but we couldn't hear him," she said.
"Video calls were very glitchy. So, it was ok. We got to hear from him when he was in Thailand. So, that was a good, clear phone call that we had in a long time."
Read moreUSS Lincoln crew hits the streets of Thailand's Pattaya after nine-month deployment
The lengthy deployment took a toll on US military personnel on the Lincoln and accompanying warships.
In August, military families and lawmakers sounded the alarm about issues including reported suicide attempts and food shortages aboard the carrier.
Last month, the Trump administration acknowledged in a letter to a lawmaker that there had been eight suicide attempts by US service members who were part of the Lincoln carrier strike group but said none of those people died.
The letter from Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao provided details on some of the suicide attempts.
It said a sailor assigned to an air wing "went overboard from the ship in early August" and was quickly recovered, while another sailor "attempted to go overboard in March and was stopped by his shipmates".

The letter also said that while food supplies on the carrier were "adequate", limited resupply options during combat led the "number of main entree options" to be reduced from "two to one for a short time".
'Land!'
Patricia Harmon, an Army veteran who was awaiting the return of her sailor son, said she imagined that life aboard the ship had been hard.
"I'm sure it had to be challenging, because there was no outlets," she told AFP.
"He was there longer than we expected, but that's life in the military."
But, she said, the hardships of the last few months were fading.
"Looking forward to seeing him, and he's excited. He's already texted me, and his first word: 'Land!' So, we're excited."
The arrival in port came the day after Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth boarded the Lincoln to congratulate the crew on their mission.
"What the USS Abraham Lincoln carrier strike group did, no other carrier strike group has ever done," Hegseth told sailors.
"Ten thousand sorties, 23,000 combat flight hours, almost 4,000 combat sorties," he said, later announcing the award of a presidential unit citation to the strike group for "extraordinary heroism against enemy forces".
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

articles.title: Defense Intel Chief: Russia targeting Ukraine's railways and Dnipro bridges in escalating strike campaign
articles.body:
Defense Intel Chief: Russia targeting Ukraine's railways and Dnipro bridges in escalating strike campaign
Moscow has introduced a new tactic and is attempting, through extensive long‑range strikes, to break Ukraine's infrastructure and the population's psychological resilience, says Col. Ants Kiviselg, head of the EDF Intelligence Center.
Kiviselg said at Estonian MoD briefing on Friday that in the battlespace, the downward trend in the number of combat contacts has continued, Russia continues to suffer heavy losses, and both sides continue long‑range strikes into each other's rear areas.
During this week, about 200 combat contacts per day have taken place, he noted.
"The most intense fighting has occurred in the same areas as in recent weeks: in Donetsk, the Pokrovsk and Konstantynivka directions; in Kharkiv oblast, the Southern Slobozhanske direction; in Zaporizhzhia, the Hulyaipole direction; and in Donetsk also the Lyman direction. Ukraine's counterattacks have continued in the Kupiansk direction in Kharkiv oblast, and in Donetsk in the Sloviansk, Lyman, and Kramatorsk directions," Kiviselg said.
"Losses of the Russian Federation have remained at an average of around 1,700 soldiers per day, which means the sixth consecutive week with more than 10,000 killed or wounded fighters per week. In response, Russia is slightly changing its behavior pattern: attempts are being made to break Ukraine's unity with intensive and very long‑lasting long‑range strikes," the military intel chief said.
Kiviselg pointed out that on 4 October Russia announced its intention to intensify long‑range strikes on Ukraine, and during the past 241st week such strikes hit various targets in 13 Ukrainian oblasts, followed in many places by power outages.
Ukraine setting up air defenses
Russia also repeatedly attacked bridges over the Dnipro River — both in Kyiv and Zaporizhzhia — attempting to intimidate civilians, hinder everyday life in Ukraine, and thereby affect the economy.
"In Kyiv, air‑defense systems operating with artificial intelligence have begun to be placed to protect the bridges, and alternative solutions are being sought in case traffic on the bridges is halted for a longer period; the possibility of installing pontoon bridges over the Dnipro river is also being examined," Kiviselg said.
Kiviselg noted that according to Ukrainian data, about 330 educational institutions in Kyiv have been damaged in airstrikes during the war — roughly one‑third of all educational institutions there — and in the first eight months of this year, 107 educational institutions have been hit.
"Ukraine's rail transport is also in a very difficult situation. More than 500 locomotives have been damaged during the war, and this year alone 60 percent of them have been hit. Attacks against railway infrastructure are 40 percent higher this year than during the entire year 2025. So we see that Russia has intensified attacks both against educational institutions and against railway and transport hubs," Kiviselg said.
"Ukraine, for its part, has carried out medium‑ and long‑range strikes against Russian fuel‑industry facilities in Volgograd, Nizhny Novgorod, Samara, and Moscow oblast. Military‑strategic targets have also been attacked in occupied areas in Krasnodar, and in Bryansk and Oryol oblasts, and in the Republic of Adygea," he said.
Russia's fuel exports diminished
According to Kiviselg, the impact of Ukraine's long‑range strikes has begun to clearly appear in Russia's fuel exports. If in 2025 Black Sea ports exported an average of 200,000 tons of fuel per week, then according to public data this transport fell to zero in the third week of September. "Russia's diesel and gas‑oil exports are currently taking place through the Baltic Sea port of Primorsk and amount to about 81,000 tons," Kiviselg said.
Kiviselg said that between 1 and 30 September, Ukraine liberated, according to public sources, 25 to 80 square kilometers of territory, compared with last September, when Russia occupied 258 square kilometers.
"The trend is changing significantly, and last September Russia did not suffer such extensive losses as this year. Speaking of Operation Vivaldi, which began by the Ukrainians in late spring, it is likely that much larger areas have been liberated there — we are talking about more than 100 square kilometers," Kiviselg said.
Kiviselg emphasized that the Russian Federation has not come any closer to its stated goal of occupying the entire Donetsk oblast.
"Large personnel losses reflect rather that unit leaders and commanders on the ground are trying to fight their way to lines that have already been reported to higher leadership as occupied areas. We will likely see similar intensity in the coming weeks — perhaps intensity will decrease, but personnel losses on the front will continue. From this we also see that Putin's statements, as if Russians had additionally occupied 1,300 square kilometers during September, are not true; these are rather doomed attempts by commanders to achieve previously advertised results," Kiviselg commented.
--
Editor: Aleksander Krjukov, Argo Ideon

articles.title: Pentagon prepares to resume military action against Iran — NYT
articles.body:
NEW YORK, October 9. /TASS/. The US military is examining the possibility of resuming the full-fledged military operation against Iran, despite President Donald Trump’s earlier remarks, The New York Times (NYT) wrote citing unnamed US administration officials.
The newspaper says that three aircraft carriers will soon be deployed in the Middle East. The Pentagon is also drafting plans of striking missile and drone storage facilities in Iran, as well as other military and energy industry targets in the country.
Over the past several months, the Pentagon and Trump’s national security team submitted to the president five proposals regarding a large-scale military operation against Iran or Yemen’s rebel Ansar Allah (Houthi) movement. Trump rejected all of them, the report says.
At the same time, many officials from Trump’s inner circle believe that a military operation against Iran will have no effect on Tehran’s plans. Some of them are convinced that the policy of economic pressure on Iran will eventually produce its result, but it will take slightly more time to pressure Tehran into making serious concessions.
Earlier on Thursday, Trump said the United States plans no strikes on Iran until the midterm elections to the US Congress, due on November 3.
The United States and Israel launched a war against Iran on February 28. In June, Washington and Tehran signed a memorandum of understanding envisaging an immediate ceasefire on all fronts, including in Lebanon. However, the United States resumed large-scale attacks on Iran overnight to July 8, having accused it of breaching the existing agreements in what concerned the Strait of Hormuz, a global chokepoint for approximately 25% of oil and some 20% of LNG supplies.
The Trump administration recently signaled an end to any large-scale use of force against Iran and a transition to putting economic pressure on the Islamic Republic through sanctions instead.

articles.title: NATO to hold major nuclear exercise amid escalating rhetoric with Russia
articles.body:
NATO to hold major nuclear exercise amid escalating rhetoric with Russia
NATO is seeking to reassure Russia that its upcoming nuclear exercise in Italy is nothing to fear, despite heightened tensions between the alliance and Moscow.
Source: European Pravda, citing Brussels-based politics and policy news organisation Politico
Details: NATO announced on 8 October that 17 member states would take part in its annual Steadfast Noon exercise, which will run from 13 to 23 October. This year's drills come amid a tense exchange of letters between Moscow and NATO after the allies held an exercise near Russia's Kaliningrad Oblast in August.
"We have been doing this every year and… this is also a clear message to nations like Russia that there is no need to worry. This is predictable and there is no reason to miscalculate," said Nassima Barrows, Deputy Director of Nuclear Policy at NATO.
"Its purpose is really essentially to train our allied forces so that we are ready and prepared, and we ensure the safety and security of our nuclear capability," she said.
Following a previous NATO exercise, Moscow sent the alliance a letter threatening to strike allied territory and referring to the possible use of its nuclear arsenal. NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte publicly condemned the move last week.
Tensions are mounting as European countries are accusing Russia of carrying out sabotage and intensifying so-called hybrid attacks across the continent.
"Our intention is to really keep things calm," a senior NATO official said. Russian officials "keep ratcheting up this mood of tension and we are going to keep trying to calm the mood", they added.
US Army Colonel David Bull, Chief of NATO's Nuclear Operations, said the exercise would involve a "similar" number of participants as in previous years. It would cover everything from "simulated alert to [a] live flight exercise", but "no live nuclear weapons".
Dual-capable aircraft and ground personnel will also take part to support the exercise and practise aircraft loading, refuelling and maintenance procedures, a senior NATO military official added.
Background:
- It was previously revealed that Russia had handed NATO a document stating the possibility of using its entire available arsenal, including nuclear weapons, in the event of an attempt by the Alliance to isolate Kaliningrad Oblast.
- NATO responded by emphasising the defensive nature of the Alliance and calling on Russia to stop its irresponsible nuclear rhetoric.
- NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte emphasised that Russian leader Vladimir Putin knows he will never be able to defeat NATO.
- Lithuania described the new Russian threats regarding Kaliningrad as psychological pressure.
