articles.title: UN says Pentagon plan to livestream execution of Fort Hood shooter would amount to torture – US politics live
articles.body:
UN says Pentagon plan to livestream execution of Fort Hood shooter would amount to torture – US politics live
Condemnation comes amid fierce backlash from US lawmakers who branded the move ‘grotesque’ and compared it to actions of some terror groups and oppressive governments
Livestreaming US execution would amount to torture, says UN
A decision by US officials to livestream the execution of convicted killer Nidal Hasan would amount to torture, the UN said.
US defence officials said US Army psychiatrist Hasan, who shot and killed 13 people at a military base in 2009, would face a firing squad and the execution would be broadcast live, adding that details would come later.
“The livestreaming of an execution is tantamount to a public execution and would breach the absolute prohibition of torture,” the Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights said in a message sent to AFP.
The UN body said it had made similar statements about public executions in Afghanistan and Iran, saying they “constitute a form of cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment”.
Mullin says Mamdani's comments after New York ICE shooting are 'dangerous and incite hostility'
At a press conference today, Markwayne Mullin – the Department of Homeland Security secretary – addressed the shooting by an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agent of a man in the Marble Hill neighborhood of the Bronx, New York during an enforcement operation on Thursday.
The man was conscious and hospitalized, authorities said, but the shooting quickly sparked angry protests from local residents and elected officials.
Officials on Friday identified the man as Oscar Belgal, who they said is the subject of an ongoing DHS investigation and was allegedly involved in the shooting of border patrol officer two years ago. On Thursday federal immigration agents attempted to arrest Belgal, officials said, but he allegedly refused orders to exit his vehicle, before accelerating toward the officers who fired shots that struck Belgal “superficially in the neck”. After he stopped his vehicle officers administered first aid and took him to the hospital, an Enforcement and Removal Operations (ERO) director.
Early reports indicated that there was a five-year-old child in Belgal’s car, in the residential area where agents fired multiple rounds, according to the city’s mayor, Zohran Mamdani. The child was physically unharmed, he said.
Later at a press conference, Mamdani demanded from the Trump administration that ICE stop its enforcement actions in New York City. “ICE is rotten to its core,” he said.
Today, however, Mullin said that agents weren’t aware there was a child in the car, but placed blame on Belgal. “He knew he had a child in his car,” Mullin said. “That outrage should be with him for endangering the five-year-old.”
He added that body cameras were worn by the ICE agents, and officials will release more information as the investigation moves forward.
Speaking today, Mullin also slammed the mayor’s comments, adding that his words are “dangerous and incite hostility”.
The homeland security secretary said that he spoke to the Mamdani several times on Thursday night, and said they mayor wanted official to release Belgal.
“President Trump actually got involved and said that we would release him to New York’s finest,” Mullin said. “If you abolish ICE, who’s going to take the criminals off the streets of your own town?”
Broadcasting an execution could cause post-traumatic stress disorder in the viewing public, mental health experts have said after Hegseth’s announcement that the firing squad execution of Nidal Hassan – the former US army psychiatrist who killed 13 people at Fort Hood – would be livestreamed.
Dr Simon Duff, a forensic psychologist at the University of Nottingham in the UK, said that while there was not a lot of research into the impact of watching an execution, studies examining journalists’ experiences of witnessing violence suggested evidence of trauma response.
“Certainly if people are not resilient they probably shouldn’t [watch], but if they have some underlying psychological driver towards viewing an execution they will likely do so regardless of the potential for harm,” Duff said.
“Recent events suggest that executions do not always go to plan,” he said, referring to the failed execution by lethal injection of Christa Pike in the US. “That possibility needs to be acknowledged, and the likelihood that this would increase the trauma for viewers.”
Neil Greenberg, a professor of defence mental health at the Institute of Psychiatry, Psychology and Neuroscience at King’s College London, said trigger warnings did not routinely lead to people avoiding media they may find distressing.
“Instead they are likely to suffer anticipatory anxiety before the ‘trauma’ is shown and some people will then become distressed,” he said.
“It is likely that people who have pre-existing mental health problems will be especially at risk of becoming distressed or experiencing a deterioration in their mental health.
“My advice would be not to watch the event at all and I would hope that mainstream media would not transmit highly traumatic images [or] sounds,” Greenberg said.
Public executions were once common around the world, including in the UK, but only two out of 17 countries that carried out executions last year did so publicly.
No ‘regulation or precedent’ for military execution to be live-streamed, says death penalty expert
In a statement to the Guardian, Robin M. Maher, the executive director of the Death Penalty Information Center, said that her group is “not aware of any regulation or precedent for a military execution to be live streamed on the internet or otherwise made widely available to the public”.
She added that “public executions are typically held in authoritarian countries to instil fear in the population, and to show the power and control of the government.”
Donald Trump has yet to weigh in publicly on the move from the defense secretary to livestream Nidal Hasan’s execution. We’ll bring you the latest as soon as we hear.
The preside will begin his day in Washington, and we’ll hear from him at a White House event to celebrate Columbus day at 11am ET. Trump will travel to Syracuse, New York later to rally with Bruce Blakeman, the Republican nominee for New York governor.
Democratic incumbent Kathy Hochul is leading Blakeman by double digits in the polls, but Trump will also be there to drum up support for down ballot GOP nominees in competitive House races in the state.
Hasan set to be the first service member executed in more than 60 years
Nidal Hasan’s execution marks the first time a member of the military will receive the death penalty in more than 60 years.
According to the Death Penalty Information Center, the last military execution, in 1961, occurred by hanging, which is no longer used by any American jurisdiction, and was imposed for rape, which is no longer subject to the death penalty, following precedent set by the supreme court.
The 3 December scheduled death would also be the first time in history the military has live-streamed an execution, and it would also be the first time since 1945 that a member of the military has been executed by firing squad, per the Death Penalty Information Center.
While there has been bipartisan backlash to Pete Hegseth’s announcement that the Department of Defense plans to livestream Nidal Hasan’s execution in December – some hard-right Republicans have welcomed the news.
“Public execution is what this terrorist deserves,” saidAndy Ogles, a GOP congressman from Tennessee. “We will be watching.”
While there’s limited research about support for public executions, according to a recent Pew survey, 66% of Americans favor the death penalty for those convicted of murder. Digging into the numbers, there is also a partisan split too – with 51% of Democrats supporting the death penalty compared to 84% of Republicans.
However, only 39% of Americans said that capital punishment actually deters people from committing crimes.
According to rights group Amnesty International, at least 17 public executions are known to have been carried out in 2025 – six in Afghanistan and 11 in Iran.
The Death Penalty Information Center says that 135 soldiers have been executed by the US military since 1916.
“Secretary Hegseth’s comments may be simply aspirational,” the center said in a statement.
“There is currently no regulation or precedent for an execution to be live streamed on the internet or otherwise made widely available to the public.”
Amnesty International Australia has urged the country’s prime minister Anthony Albanese to press the US to reverse its decision over the Pentagon’s livestreamed execution plan.
“The suggestion that an execution by firing squad should be livestreamed for public viewing is an appalling disregard for human dignity,” said Kyinzom Dhongdue, a campaign manager at the rights group.
“Turning a state-sanctioned killing into a public spectacle only compounds the cruelty of the death penalty.“
Livestreaming US execution would amount to torture, says UN
A decision by US officials to livestream the execution of convicted killer Nidal Hasan would amount to torture, the UN said.
US defence officials said US Army psychiatrist Hasan, who shot and killed 13 people at a military base in 2009, would face a firing squad and the execution would be broadcast live, adding that details would come later.
“The livestreaming of an execution is tantamount to a public execution and would breach the absolute prohibition of torture,” the Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights said in a message sent to AFP.
The UN body said it had made similar statements about public executions in Afghanistan and Iran, saying they “constitute a form of cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment”.
Pete Hegseth has said the execution of Nidal Hasan, the former army psychiatrist who killed 13 people at Fort Hood, will be a public event when the sentence is carried out later this year.
A defence department official later confirmed the execution would be livestreamed.
In an interview with the rightwing channel Real America’s Voice, the defence secretary said the firing squad would carry out the sentence at Fort Hood, Texas on 3 December. It would be the first US military execution in more than 60 years.
US voters are about to deliver their first national verdict on the second presidency of Donald Trump. On 3 November, millions of Americans will vote in midterm elections to decide control of the House of Representatives and Senate, as well as the governorships in 36 states. The results could have a huge impact on Trump’s final two years in office.
Today, the Guardian launches its 2026 midterm voter panel. Our reporters have interviewed nine voters across the country and the political spectrum about the issues that matter to them, from the cost of living, immigration and healthcare to the war in Iran and whether they trust their political leaders.
The answers – highlights of which are published below – offer insight into the national mood with less than a month to go until election day. The Guardian will return to its voter panel before the final votes are cast.
Pentagon's 'disgusting' livestreamed execution plan provokes fierce backlash across political divide
Hello and welcome to the US politics live blog.
The Pentagon’s plan to livestream the execution of Nidal Hasan, a former army psychiatrist who killed 13 people at Fort Hood, has received fierce criticism from across the political spectrum.
In an interview with Real America’s Voice, defense secretary Pete Hegseth said the firing squad will carry out the sentence at Fort Hood, Texas, at 1pm on Thursday, 3 December. This would be the first US military execution in more than 60 years.
A defense department official later confirmed the execution will be livestreamed, prompting condemnation across the political divide.
Speaking on CNN, Democratic senator Chris Murphy said:
I mean, that’s disgusting. What, is he mimicking ISIS executions? I mean, I understand that in this country we have the death penalty, but public execution is medieval. It’s frankly one of the things that we abhor about terrorist groups, and the fact that the United States is doing it - I just learned this.
That is just absolutely extraordinary, galling. No matter whether you support or oppose the death penalty, public hangings and executions? That’s what America has become? Um, that’s, that’s pretty extraordinary.
Republican senator Thom Tillis said public executions were what “oppressive dictators” did. In a social media post, he said:
Hasan should face the death penalty, but making his execution public and streaming it? Beyond disgusting. Public executions are what oppressive dictatorships like Iran and Afghanistan do. It should not be happening in America.
Meanwhile, Democratic senator Patty Murray commented:
We can seek justice in this country without glorifying violence and turning an execution into a grotesque public spectacle. What this criminal did was abhorrent and must be punished – but we as a country cannot condone livestreaming a man’s death for entertainment.
We are long past the days of public hangings in the town square. Kids watch what our leaders do and say, is this kind of bloodshed really what we want them seeing? The Pentagon must revoke this decision immediately.
And the Democratic representative Betty McCollum said:
Secretary Hegseth’s desire to conduct a public execution is disturbing and should be stopped. The Army has not conducted an execution by firing squad since World War II and the U.S. has not had a public execution since 1936. Nidal Hasan has been found guilty of his crimes and should be held accountable for them but turning a federal execution into a media spectacle is appalling and unbecoming of the U.S. military.
The Pentagon’s announcement also drew backlash from human rights groups, while New Zealand’s national censor said on Friday it would be unable to block the planned livestreamed execution.
Speaking about the prospect of the execution being livestreamed, Hegseth had said:
It was a radical Islamist attack in uniform inside the ranks, and so he’s going to get a firing squad of soldiers, as it should be, and we’ll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it’s public, because people need to understand there’s serious consequences for these types of things.
Hasan opened fire at a medical processing center on the Texas base on 5 November 2009, killing 13 people and wounding dozens more. A military jury sentenced him to death in 2013, and he has been held at Fort Leavenworth in Kansas ever since. He exhausted his appeals last year, which cleared the way for Donald Trump to approve the sentence this week on a recommendation from Hegseth.
In other developments:
In a televised Maine Senate debate Democrat Troy Jackson said that, in addition to Brett Kavanaugh, Republican Susan Collins has voted to confirm dozens of anti-abortion judges.
Republican Mike Rogers continually used Islamophobic attacks on Democrat Abdul El-Sayed in a Michigan Senate debate, accusing the Muslim candidate of being “bought off by Hamas, Hezbollah, al-Qaida”.
Donald Trump claimed that the US will not strike Iran “at any time prior” to the midterm elections on 3 November.

articles.title: Saudi nursery hit by debris as Houthis target Riyadh airport
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Saudi nursery hit by debris as Houthis target Riyadh airport
The Saudi civil defence agency said a kindergarten and a medical complex in Riyadh were damaged by debris from a missile interception on Thursday, as Yemen's Houthis announced attacks targeting the capital's airport.
Two witnesses said that a plane at the airport belonging to national flag carrier Saudia had cracks and holes in its fuselage. A source briefed on the matter said three planes suffered damage.
Saudi Arabia leads a pro-government coalition fighting the Houthis in Yemen's civil war. The Iran-backed group has repeatedly targeted Riyadh since the conflict roared back to life in July, vowing to hit critical infrastructure and disrupt Saudi airspace.
The scale and frequency of the attacks on the Saudi capital have been unprecedented in the eight months of wider war in the Middle East.
The Houthis announced three attacks on Thursday against Riyadh airport. Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said the group also launched missiles at an airport in Najran and an airbase in Khamis Mushait.
Recent attacks have also targeted oil infrastructure in the world's largest crude exporter.
The Houthis on Thursday warned workers to evacuate Saudi Arabia's oil facilities, having days before hit a major refinery south of the capital.
Earlier in the day, the Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis said it had intercepted two missiles fired towards Riyadh.
The kingdom's civil defence agency said "interception debris" had damaged a kindergarten and a medical complex in the city. It did not say if there were casualties or provide details of the damage.
Admissions by Saudi authorities of civilian targets being hit are relatively rare. There have been few statements on Houthi attacks in recent weeks.
Shelter in place
After resuming their fight against Yemen's internationally recognised government following a four-year lull, the Houthis last month seized all of the country's Red Sea coast in a lightning offensive.
The group, whose heartlands are among the Zaidi Shia Muslims in the northwest, had already controlled the capital Sanaa and most of Yemen's major population centres since the start of the war in 2014. Riyadh's military coalition intervened in 2015 to support the government.
Saudi Arabia and Yemeni government forces have struggled to roll back the Houthis' advance, despite an ambitious counter-offensive aimed at recapturing territory, including the area around a crucial sea route for global energy flows.
In Riyadh, diplomats were instructed to shelter at their respective embassies, some of them told AFP, after explosions echoed around the city on Thursday morning.
There were no text alerts warning residents, as there had been in the past.
An interior ministry campaign has repeatedly warned residents against sharing unauthorised information, images or footage of missiles, drones and their impacts, warning that violators of legal consequences.
Several residents told AFP that international schools were taking precautions, with at least one facility sending children into a basement for safety.
"My daughter called me," one parent told AFP on condition of anonymity, saying she was "completely distraught".
Two people working in Riyadh's business hub, the King Abdullah Financial District, told AFP that some companies were evacuating staff from the area.
'Heightened vigilance'
Numerous flights at Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport were delayed or cancelled, according to information posted for passengers.
The airport did not immediately acknowledge disruption, pointing only in a short statement to the "necessity" of contacting airlines before travelling.
The United States urged its citizens in Saudi Arabia to "exercise heightened vigilance" following the attacks at the airport, which US government employees now need "special authorisation" to use.
Previous attacks killed a Sudanese national at Riyadh airport, as well as an Egyptian and an Algerian national at Abha airport, civil aviation authorities said on Wednesday.
In Yemen, one of the world's poorest countries, civilians are paying the price for the renewed fighting, with more than 200,000 people displaced since July, according to UN data.
A humanitarian crisis caused by the war has left most of the nation's population dependent on aid.
After declaring its counter-offensive, Yemen's government claimed to have pushed Houthi fighters out of strategic areas on the Red Sea coast and the port city of Mocha.
But the Houthis insist they are holding their territory, and military sources from both sides have not reported any major changes on the ground.
The rival claims have been impossible to independently verify, with the situation moving fast and access for journalists difficult.
The Houthis recently seized areas south of Taiz, Yemen's third-largest city, cutting it off from the government's temporary capital in Aden and sparking shortages and soaring prices for food and energy.
(AFP)

articles.title: Armored assaults aren’t dead. Robots got the credit, but it was Ukrainian infantry in armored trucks that reversed a year of Russian gains near Lyman
articles.body:
- Defying the trend toward footborne infantry assaults, the Ukrainian 3rd Army Corps deployed armored vehicles for Operation Vivaldi
- The operation was a reminder that vehicles are still useful despite the ever-present danger from drones
- But vehicles need a lot of support to give them a fighting chance
Armored vehicles aren't dead in Ukraine—they just need a lot of help. That's one of the biggest lessons from the Ukrainian 3rd Army Corps' Operation Vivaldi, its recent successful counteroffensive just north of the town of Lyman in eastern Ukraine's Donetsk Oblast.
Russia spent 18 months building its salient toward Sloviansk; Ukraine took much of it back in three. By 30 September, three of four planned phases in, the operation had returned 176 sq km to Ukrainian control, taken 250 Russian prisoners, and cost Russia more than 5,000 killed and wounded, Ukraine's presidential office said. It also foiled a Russian plan to break into the rear of the Sloviansk-Kramatorsk urban area, the office said.
Defying critics who insisted vehicles couldn't possibly survive in the drone-patrolled gray zone, the 3rd Army Corps repeatedly deployed mechanized forces as it counterattacked across a roughly 100 sq km salient the Russian 20th and 25th Combined Arms Armies had extended toward Sloviansk, one of the last two big free cities in Donetsk Oblast.
Maneuvering for months under a veil of secrecy, the 3rd Army Corps found and exploited gaps along the flanks of the 20th and 25th CAAs, ultimately breaking into the Russian armies' rears and forcing them to pull back across the Zherebets River in order to avoid encirclement.
Armored vehicles were key to the Ukrainian effort. They sped assault troops into battle, dropped them off under fire, and then supported them as they clashed with the Russians. "Maneuver warfare isn't going anywhere," stated Ryan O'Leary, a US Army veteran who once commanded volunteers in Ukraine.
Ukraine is now sending its tanks into battle with drone escorts: they can drive into a Russian kill zone and come back alive
3rd Army Corps commanders knew they were taking a risk deploying armored vehicles in a Russian-controlled salient patrolled by first-person-view drones from Russia's elite Rubicon Center drone unit. But they clearly believed that, with adequate support, the vehicles could accomplish their missions—and survive.
They were right. A dramatic video shot by 3rd Army Corps troopers depicts the troopers disembarking from their armored trucks and rushing into the fight while small arms fire clatters all around them.
Given the intensity of the Russian fire, a mechanized assault "was the only real way to push positions in an effective manner to keep losses low as well as gain and hold momentum and aggression," O'Leary wrote. Walking into battle under the cover of trees might help the infantry avoid the attention of overhead drones, but it takes too long to sustain an aggressive assault, and it can be difficult to mass enough footborne infantry to overcome stiff enemy defenses.
"This is something that hasn't changed even with the advent of drone warfare coming of age," O'Leary added. "Suppression tactics and such have changed and now there is more than just indirect fires and counterassaults that you must be able to suppress and plan for."
But the concept of the infantry-carrying armored vehicle "isn't going anywhere," O'Leary stressed. "Especially when it takes a drone tens of minutes to get to target area, acquire target and hit the target. Right now, the front is extremely susceptible to maneuvering forces on assaults if it is planned right and executed properly."
The 3rd Army Corps' Operation Vivaldi is an excellent example of an operation that was planned right and executed properly—in ways that helped the corps' mechanized forces fight and survive.
Trending Now
Careful preparation
The corps explained that it deployed footborne scouts to find the best paths for follow-on vehicular assaults—and subsequent medical evacuations. Scouts "conducted recon of the front lines, ensured the breakthrough of equipment and led adjacent units along secret paths while evacuating the wounded," the 3rd Army Corps stated.
Before the armored vehicles rolled into action along the pre-scouted paths, the 3rd Army Corps deployed robotic engineering vehicles to clear Russian mines. After that, the corps sent in old BTR-60 wheeled armored vehicles modified for remote control and packed with anti-tank mines. These "robotic kamikaze complexes ... were used to demolish the enemy's strongest fortifications," the corps said.
Only after the assault routes were scouted and cleared of mines and Russian strongpoints did the manned vehicles and their precious infantry cargo roll out. We don't know how many losses the 3rd Army Corps' mechanized infantry suffered on the attack, but we do know they ultimately prevailed—when the battered Russian 20th and 25th CAAs retreated.
In Ukraine’s Vivaldi offensive, nobody rides in the BTR-60s. Bulgaria’s old troop carriers go into Russian bunkers packed with mines
"Recent Ukrainian operations demonstrate that maneuver is not dead," stressed Mick Ryan, a retired Australian army general. "Despite the difficulty in ground operations maneuver observed in eastern Ukraine over the past few years, offensive operations are still possible in modern war. But they need the intellectual effort to develop new techniques to make them viable and repeatable at scale."
In addition to the reconnaissance and robots-first engineering and suppression tactics the 3rd Army Corps employed, Ryan recommended commanders deploy more drone-grounding electronic warfare and use AI tools to help plan attacks.
But ages-old human elements are still essential, Ryan wrote. "Developing viable methods for offensive tactical and operational maneuver in the 21st century also demands the inclusion of older ideas about the employment of mass, logistic support and casualty evacuation [and the] maintenance of morale and leader's provision of purpose to their people."
Even when the assault route is clear, it's understandably terrifying to ride in an armored vehicle across drone-patrolled terrain. But a good leader can motivate their troops to try.

- Ukraine keeps finding ways to replace its MiG-29s. It’s running out of MiG-29s to find
- Ukraine is now sending its tanks into battle with drone escorts: they can drive into a Russian kill zone and come back alive

articles.title: Ukraine far from producing Storm Shadow/SCALP missiles on its own — UK defense official
articles.body:
PARIS, October 9. /TASS/. Ukraine is still a long way from independently producing Western Storm Shadow/SCALP cruise missiles due to the complexity of these weapons systems, UK Under-Secretary of State for the Armed Forces Louise Sandher-Jones told Le Figaro.
"I think we are still a long way from that due to the complexity of these weapons systems. We have already begun moving in this direction, but we are also considering other projects that could be implemented in the short term, including in the area of striking targets at operational depth," she said.
According to the defense official, Kiev’s needs are not limited to Storm Shadow and SCALP missiles. She noted that the UK military is working with Ukraine on the Brakestop project, which involves developing a low-cost, long-range cruise missile. Sandher-Jones noted that its development is focused on reducing production costs and ensuring the weapons can be manufactured in sufficient quantities.
In September, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham announced that his government had agreed to allow the MBDA defense company to transfer classified data on UK components for the SCALP long-range missile to Kiev. At that time, he also discussed the matter with French President Emmanuel Macron, who had announced back in July that an agreement had been reached with Kiev on the licensed production of various weapons, including AASM guided bombs, Aster 30 missiles for the SAMP-T air defense system, and SCALP missiles.
The SCALP (the French version of the UK’s Storm Shadow missile) is an air-launched cruise missile equipped with a subsonic turbojet engine, an infrared homing system, and an onboard processor with GPS. It can fly at extremely low altitudes (30-40 meters).

articles.title: NATO attempts to cool tensions with Russia ahead of key nuclear exercise
articles.body:
Crew members of aircraft carrier USS Harry S. Truman are pictured during a NATO vigilance activity in the Mediterranean on May 23, 2022. | Andreas Solaro/AFP via Getty Images
BRUSSELS — NATO is seeking to reassure Russia that an upcoming nuclear drill in Italy is nothing to fear, with tensions high between the alliance and Moscow.
NATO announced Thursday that 17 allies will participate in the annual Steadfast Noon exercise from Oct. 13-23. But this year, the exercise follows a tense exchange of letters between Moscow and NATO after allies conducted exercises near Russia’s Kaliningrad exclave in August.
“We have been doing this every year and … this is also a clear message to nations like Russia that there is no need to worry,” said Nassima Barrows, NATO’s nuclear policy director. “This is predictable and there is no reason to miscalculate.”
Advertisement
“Its purpose is really essentially to train our allied forces so that we are ready and prepared, and we ensure the safety and security of our nuclear capability,” she told reporters.
Following the previous NATO exercises, Moscow sent a letter to the alliance threatening to hit allied territory and mentioning the use of its nuclear arsenal — a move that NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte publicly rebuked last week.
Tensions are rising as European countries accuse Russia of sabotage and growing so-called hybrid attacks across the continent.
“Our intention is to really keep things calm,” said a senior NATO official, who was granted anonymity to speak freely. Russian officials “keep ratcheting up this mood of tension and we are going to keep trying to calm the mood.”
U.S. Col. David Bull, chief of NATO’s nuclear operations, said the exercise has garnered “similar” participation to previous years and involves everything from a “simulated alert to [a] live flight exercise” — but “no live nuclear weapons.”
It will also feature dual-capable aircraft and ground troops to support the exercise and train on loading, fueling, and maintaining planes, a senior NATO military official added.
Russia’s embassy to Belgium said that it took note of the NATO statement, but added: "these exercises — given that NATO considers our country as the main threat to security — do not contribute to reducing tensions on the continent and are part of the Alliance's nuclear policy, to which Moscow's negative attitude is well known."

articles.title: Ukraine Strikes Russian Missile Launch Institute and Intercontinental Ballistic Missile Disposal Facility
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine Strikes Russian Missile Launch Institute and Intercontinental Ballistic Missile Disposal Facility
Ukrainian forces struck two Russian missile-related facilities in the Nizhny Novgorod region overnight on October 9, targeting infrastructure involved in missile launch systems and the disposal of intercontinental ballistic missiles.
The General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine confirmed the strikes, identifying the targets as a branch of the Barmin Research Institute of Launch Complexes and a facility responsible for dismantling intercontinental ballistic missiles.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to the General Staff, Ukrainian forces hit a facility belonging to the Barmin Research Institute of Launch Complexes, a branch of the Center for Operation of Ground-Based Space Infrastructure, near the settlement of Dalneye Konstantinovo-5.
The institute specializes in the development, maintenance, and operation of missile launch positions, fueling equipment, and missile control systems, making it part of Russia's missile infrastructure.
In a separate operation, Ukrainian forces targeted the Center for the Disposal of Intercontinental Ballistic Missiles near the settlement of Surovatikha, also in the Nizhny Novgorod region.
The General Staff said the strike was intended to weaken Russia's military-industrial capacity to produce explosives and components used in rocket propellants.
In addition to the two facilities in the Nizhny Novgorod region, Ukraine's General Staff confirmed a strike on the Redkino Experimental Plant in Russia's Tver region.
The Redkino Experimental Plant is a major chemical production facility in Russia’s Tver region, specializing in small-batch manufacturing of specialty chemicals. The enterprise produces more than 40 types of chemical products supplied to Russia’s aviation, aerospace, and other industrial sectors.
Its product range includes ferrocene-based compounds used as combustion catalysts in solid-propellant rocket engines, alongside specialized materials, protective coatings, and fuel additives. These substances serve both civilian industrial purposes and military production needs.
Ukrainian forces also targeted the Lukoil-Ukhtaneftepererabotka oil refinery in Ukhta, Russia's Komi Republic, approximately 1,700 kilometers from the Ukrainian border, as Kyiv continues strikes against Russian energy facilities in response to Moscow's attacks on Ukrainian territory.

articles.title: OpenAI says it banned accounts linked to Russian, Iranian influence operations
articles.body:
Rabia Ali
09 October 2026•Update: 09 October 2026
OpenAI said Thursday it banned accounts linked to covert influence operations originating in Russia and Iran that used its artificial intelligence tools in attempts to shape public opinion abroad.
The company said in a blog post the operations combined AI with traditional influence techniques, using seemingly legitimate research platforms and fabricated journalist identities to spread geopolitical messages.
The Russian-linked campaign used a purported research platform focused on Latin America, while the Iran-linked operation used fake journalist profiles to pitch articles to online publications.
“What is most striking about these operations is that they closely resembled complex influence operations of the pre-AI age, but used AI to make some of the workflows easier,” OpenAI said.
The company said it had banned clusters of ChatGPT accounts associated with both operations and shared information about them with relevant authorities.
 
Fake journalists published articles online
OpenAI said the Iran-linked operation used seven fabricated journalist identities to pitch long-form articles to online publications.
The company identified almost 100 articles published under the fake journalists’ bylines across more than a dozen outlets.
The articles covered international affairs, geopolitics and the Middle East. Publication increased sharply after the outbreak of the US-Iran conflict, OpenAI said.
According to OpenAI, the operators used ChatGPT to edit articles, check drafts against individual outlets’ submission requirements and prepare emails pitching stories to editors.
The fake profiles presented themselves as Western journalists with expertise in international politics, the Middle East, human rights or conflict, the company said.
The operation also generated social media comments in English and Persian.
"The users asked for comments on topics such as missile strikes, ceasefires, and diplomatic maneuvering, specifying outputs that portrayed the US as the aggressor, Israel as an unreliable ally of the US, and Iran as a defiant but resilient victim," OpenAI said.
However, the company said the comments it identified publicly generally received little engagement. Some likes came from accounts linked to the operation itself, it added.
 
Russian-linked campaign targeted Ukraine, Latin America
OpenAI said the Russian-linked operation targeted audiences across Latin America, with much of its activity apparently aimed at "undermining Ukraine’s reputation." Other efforts focused on domestic politics in Argentina and Bolivia.
The operation allegedly used the Social Research Center, a self-described research platform covering Latin America. OpenAI said internal reports suggested Russian operators controlled the platform through a fabricated persona named “Mia Clark.”
The company said available evidence indicated that employees working for the platform in Latin America did not know they were working for a Russian group. They appeared to conduct interviews with regional experts and produce research papers in good faith.
The operators’ internal reports described efforts to spread fabricated stories, documents and audio recordings targeting Ukraine and political figures in the region.
OpenAI said its research found material matching some reported campaigns, including false claims that prompted fact-checks and official denials. It cautioned that some claims in the internal reports could not be corroborated.
OpenAI said both operations placed content in media outlets, potentially extending their reach beyond fake social media accounts.
“AI can give such false-front operations greater scale, efficiency, linguistic fluency, and editorial ability,” the company said.
OpenAI said it published the findings to help researchers and other organizations identify and disrupt similar campaigns.

articles.title: MEPs linked to Russia oppose European Parliament resolution declaring Russia’s new State Duma illegitimate
articles.body:
The European Parliament has adopted a resolution refusing to recognize Russia’s State Duma as a legitimate representative and legislative body. The measure passed on Oct. 8 with 482 votes in favor, 41 against, and 39 abstentions. “The ‘fake’ ballot was held in a climate of fear and against the backdrop of Moscow’s continued illegal war against Ukraine,” read a press release put out by the European Parliament on Oct. 9.
“[The European] Parliament notes that during the recent fake ballot, there were no genuine alternative candidates, no free media, no credible observers, and no political freedoms, with critics of the regime having been either imprisoned, murdered, or forced into exile. MEPs also condemn the fact that so-called “elections” were conducted in parts of the Russian-occupied Donetsk, Kherson, Luhansk, and Zaporizhzhia regions of Ukraine, as well as in Moldova’s Transnistrian region and in the Georgian regions of Abkhazia and Tskhinvali/South Ossetia,” it added.
According to the Parliament’s roll-call voting record, lawmakers who opposed parts of the resolution included German MEP Petr Bystron, who had been suspected of receiving money from an influence network linked to Viktor Medvedchuk; Slovak politician Luboš Blaha, who has met with Russian Foreign Intelligence Service chief Sergei Naryshkin; and Czech MEP Ondřej Dostál, who traveled to Moscow at the invitation of a Russian foundation linked to the GRU military intelligence agency.
Among those voting against the resolution were 23 members of the far-right Europe of Sovereign Nations (ESN) group, including Alternative for Germany (AfD) lawmakers Petr Bystron and Christine Anderson, Slovak MEPs Luboš Blaha and Milan Mazurek, Czech lawmakers Kateřina Konečná and Ondřej Dostál, and Luxembourg politician Fernand Kartheiser.
Also opposing the measure in the final vote were Polish far-right politician Grzegorz Braun and German MEPs Michael von der Schulenburg and Ruth Firmenich, who were elected on the Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW) ticket. Braun had previously been stripped of parliamentary immunity in connection with a Polish investigation into his alleged denial of Nazi crimes at Auschwitz (in July 2025, Braun publicly denied the existence of gas chambers at the Auschwitz-Birkenau concentration and extermination camp).
The Insider compared the roll-call vote with published information about lawmakers’ contacts with Russian representatives. It found that four of the politicians listed above — Blaha, Dostál, von der Schulenburg, and Firmenich — traveled together to Moscow in May 2025. The trip was timed to coincide with the 80th anniversary of the end of World War II. While in the Russian capital, the MEPs met with Russian politicians and public figures.
In an official declaration published by the European Parliament, Dostál listed the Russian Peace Foundation as a third party that covered part of the trip’s expenses. Dostál said he paid for his flight, accommodation, and meals himself, while the foundation provided bus transportation from the airport.
The Insider previously reported that the Russian Peace Foundation has links to Russian military intelligence. According to internal GRU correspondence, the organization has been involved in passing information about foreign visitors to the intelligence service for assessment and possible recruitment.
In the same investigation, The Insider reported that Luboš Blaha traveled to Moscow with David Lindtner, an adviser to Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico. During that trip, Blaha met with Sergei Naryshkin, director of Russia’s Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR). According to statements published by Blaha, they discussed the May 2024 assassination attempt against Fico, along with the activities of political opponents of the Slovak government.
Petr Bystron, another lawmaker on the list, had previously appeared in an investigation into the pro-Kremlin media platform Voice of Europe, which European intelligence services say was financed by a network linked to the aforementioned Medvedchuk. As The Insider previously reported, citing Der Spiegel and Deník N, Bystron and fellow party member Maximilian Krah were suspected of receiving money in exchange for cooperation with the platform. In 2025, the European Parliament lifted Bystron’s immunity in order to allow an investigation in a separate case to proceed.
A Transparency International database also contains records of meetings between some of the lawmakers and Russian representatives. According to the data, in May 2025 von der Schulenburg met in Moscow with Russian diplomats and State Duma representatives, and in July of that year with a representative of Russia’s mission to the European Union in Brussels. Dostál met at least twice with representatives of Russia’s permanent mission to the EU, while Fernand Kartheiser attended a forum in Sochi in November 2025 that included Russian politicians.

articles.title: Trump rules out new Iran attack before US midterm elections
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Trump rules out new Iran attack before US midterm elections
President Donald Trump on Thursday ruled out attacking Iran before the US midterm elections on 3 November, saying Washington was holding "productive discussions" with Tehran.
Trump's post on his Truth Social platform followed a surge in oil prices on Thursday driven by media reports suggesting potential new US strikes prior to those elections.
"I want to make it clear to everybody that, while Iran is in very bad condition, both Economically and Militarily, and while the Blockade will remain in full force and effect...we will not be attacking Iran at any time prior to the Midterm Elections," he wrote.
"We are having productive discussions with the Islamic Republic of Iran," he added, without providing additional details.
The Atlantic magazine reported on Wednesday that the White House had asked the Pentagon to develop options to strike Iranian targets that could be used before the midterms. The New York Times published a similar report on Thursday, saying the plans were being developed despite Trump's "ambivalence".
The rise in crude oil prices has also been fueled by persistent tensions in the Strait of Hormuz - a strategic chokepoint for the global oil trade - as well as hostilities between Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis and Saudi Arabia.
In a recent sign of those tensions, an oil tanker sailing off the north coast of Qatar reported being struck "by multiple projectiles," causing an unspecified number of casualties, the UKMTO maritime agency said Wednesday.
Polls suggest that US voters are strongly dissatisfied over rising fuel prices, linked to the conflict launched by the United States and Israel against Iran in February.
The US leader has repeatedly insisted in recent weeks that the United States has effectively won the Iran war, despite ongoing unrest and a recent security threat that forced the withdrawal of American bombers from a base in England.
But Trump's claims that prices will fall as soon as the Iran war is over have so far fallen on deaf ears with voters.
The midterm elections will shape the final two years of Trump's presidential term as his Republican Party risks losing its current grip on Congress.
Although Trump is not on the ballot, he is heavily involved in the campaign, holding numerous rallies in an attempt to limit the damage or even turn the political tide.
Trump has warned he faces a possible third impeachment if Democrats retake the House of Representatives, and the White House is preparing for a slew of investigations into corruption and abuse of power.
The US president also on Thursday sought to calm a furor over his comments at a rally earlier this week that Iran could "take out" the cities of Los Angeles and San Diego.
Trump, 80, blamed the "fake and artificial news" for misinterpreting the remarks, which Democrats pounced on.
"In actuality, what I was talking about was that a temporary increase in the price of Gasoline is a small price to pay for Iran not having a Nuclear Weapon and, if you want to see a big price, can you imagine what it would be like if they bombed San Diego and/or Los Angeles?" Trump said on Truth Social.
(AFP)

articles.title: Ukrainian strikes blast Russian frigates at Novorossiysk
articles.body:
A single Ukrainian drone attack on Novorossiysk has significantly degraded the land-attack cruise missile capability of Russia’s Black Sea Fleet, accounting for forty per cent of its Kalibr-capable surface ships, according to a Defence Intelligence update published by the UK Ministry of Defence.
In its update on Thursday, Defence Intelligence said: “Ukraine has launched two large scale uncrewed aerial system (UAS) attacks against the Russian Novorossiysk Naval Facility and Commercial Port within the last two months. The 08-09 September 2026 attack led to successful strikes against a GRIGOROVICH class frigate and a SVIYAZHSK light-frigate.”
It went on: “Both vessels have likely sustained sufficient damage to prevent them taking part in KALIBR Land-attack Cruise Missile (LACM) firings into Ukraine, likely for the short-medium term. This single attack has significantly degraded the LACM strike capabilities of the Black Sea Fleet, representing 40% of the KALIBR-capable surface fleet.”
Two ships out of action amounting to two fifths of the capability says as much about the size of the remaining fleet as it does about the damage. Russia has been firing Kalibr missiles at Ukrainian cities and infrastructure from Black Sea platforms since the opening days of the full-scale invasion, and the surface ships able to carry them have never been numerous.
The Admiral Grigorovich class are Project 11356R frigates, the newest conventional surface combatants the Black Sea Fleet has, each able to carry Kalibr in a vertical launch system. Defence Intelligence describes the second vessel as a Sviyazhsk light-frigate, a smaller Kalibr-armed surface combatant.
Ukrainian strikes drove Russian warships out of Sevastopol over the course of 2023 and 2024, and the Krasnodar Krai port became the main operating base for what remained. Pushing the fleet east was supposed to put it beyond easy reach.
Defence Intelligence uses a probability yardstick in which “likely” sits between 55 and 75 per cent, so the assessment that both ships cannot take part in Kalibr firings is a confident judgement without being a certainty. The phrase short to medium term carries no fixed definition, though repairs to a vertical launch system and the surrounding structure on a frigate are not quick work, particularly in a yard under periodic attack.
UK Defence Intelligence publishes its guidance on the use of probabilistic language at this link.

articles.title: Pentagon says execution of Fort Hood shooter will be livestreamed
articles.body:
Pete Hegseth has said the execution of Nidal Hasan, the former army psychiatrist who killed 13 people at Fort Hood, will be a public event when the sentence is carried out later this year. A defense department official later confirmed the execution will be livestreamed.
In an interview with Real America’s Voice, the Pentagon secretary said the firing squad will carry out the sentence at Fort Hood, Texas, at 1pm on Thursday, 3 December. This would be the first US military execution in more than 60 years.
“It was a radical Islamist attack in uniform inside the ranks, and so he’s going to get a firing squad of soldiers, as it should be, and we’ll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it’s public, because people need to understand there’s serious consequences for these types of things,” Hegseth said.
Hasan opened fire at a medical processing center on the Texas base on 5 November 2009, killing 13 people and wounding dozens more. A military jury sentenced him to death in 2013, and he has been held at Fort Leavenworth in Kansas ever since. He exhausted his appeals last year, which cleared the way for Donald Trump to approve the sentence this week on a recommendation from Hegseth.
Investigators had found that Hasan had exchanged 18 emails with Anwar al-Awlaki, a radical cleric who was subsequently killed in a US drone strike, in the months before the attack. At his court martial, Hasan said he had acted to stop American soldiers from deploying to Afghanistan to kill fellow Muslims, before his own impending deployment. A review led by William Webster, a former FBI director, concluded that the bureau should have investigated his correspondence more thoroughly.
In the interview, Hegseth said Barack Obama had called the attack “workplace violence”. The Pentagon initially treated the shooting as a workplace-violence incident rather than a terrorist attack, a classification that affected the victims’ eligibility for Purple Hearts and other combat-related benefits.
But there is no record of Obama himself using the phrase. At a memorial days after the attack, he instead described the victims as Americans who had been unable to escape “the horror of war”, while calling the shooting a tragedy and saying the killer would face justice.
The last known case of a military firing squad in the US was in November 1945, but the Trump administration has sought to bring it back in Trump’s second term to expedite capital punishment cases. Five US states allow for firing squads: Idaho, Mississippi, Oklahoma, South Carolina and Utah.
Abroad, Amnesty International’s most recent annual review lists Afghanistan, China, North Korea, Saudi Arabia, Somalia, Taiwan, the United Arab Emirates and Yemen among the countries that still use firing squads.
Asked whether Hasan had made a final request or reached out to Trump, Hegseth replied: “Don’t care. We’ll see him on December 3.”

articles.title: Iran taking concrete steps to resolve conflict with US – Putin
articles.body:
Iran taking concrete steps to resolve conflict with US – Putin
Tehran is striving to find a diplomatic solution to the war imposed on it by the US, Russian President Vladimir Putin said on Thursday at a meeting with his Iranian counterpart, Masoud Pezeshkian.
The Russian president noted that Tehran had recently put forward a proposal aimed at resolving the conflict peacefully, adding that Moscow is willing to play a constructive role in the process.
“Iran is making real efforts to end the conflict, which broke out in the region through no fault of its own, through no fault of Iran,” Putin said.
Putin also hailed the deepening cooperation between Russia and Iran, especially in trade and humanitarian affairs, during bilateral talks in Turkmenistan, where he is set to take part in a leaders’ summit of the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) and a Caspian Sea environmental summit.
Moscow has repeatedly condemned the US-Israeli military campaign against Iran and called for a diplomatic solution. During his visit to Tehran in July, former Russian president and current deputy chairman of Russia’s Security Council Dmitry Medvedev said that “there was no serious reason for the American attack” as Tehran “posed no threat” to Washington.
In late September, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi announced that Tehran had submitted a peace plan to the US. Under the roadmap, the Islamic Republic signaled its readiness to restore navigation through the Strait of Hormuz – a strategically important waterway for crude oil exports from the Middle East.
In exchange, Iran, which imposed a blockade on the crucial oil shipping route after the start of the conflict, expects the US to lift its own blockade of the Islamic Republic, ease restrictions on its oil exports, and release some of its frozen assets. Tehran is also seeking an end to hostilities on all fronts, including Israel’s military operation in Lebanon.
Addressing the UN General Assembly in New York last month, President Pezeshkian reiterated that his country was prepared for “dialogue and diplomacy” but would not negotiate under threats.
While there have been media reports of indirect negotiations between the two countries in recent weeks, President Trump has rejected the Iranian proposal outright. He told reporters that Tehran wants to “make a deal, but it is not the deal that I want to make.” The US president has also suggested that Washington is not ruling out resuming strikes on Iran in the coming weeks.

articles.title: ‘Not great, not terrible’: Why nobody trusts Russia to tell the truth about plague
articles.body:
A security worker looks out from the door of an infectious diseases hospital in the town of Shelekhov, where an employee of the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia and the Far East had died, on Oct. 7, 2026. | Tatyana Makeyeva/AFP via Getty Images
As whispers circulate of plague in faraway Siberia, it’s worth remembering that Russian obfuscation is so ingrained that it’s become a meme.
In HBO’s dramatized 2019 series about the nuclear disaster at Chernobyl, a Russian atomic scientist scoffs at a radiation reading that suggests a major calamity is taking place.
“Not great, not terrible,” says the fictionalized version of Anatoly Dyatlov, the real-life deputy chief engineer at Chernobyl in April 1986, as he looks at a dosimeter noting 3.6 roentgen per hour, just below a critical radiation level.
Advertisement
Except that reading was not accurate. Not even close. The nuclear reactor had already exploded and unleashed catastrophic levels of radiation that would go on to cause thousands of cancer-related deaths in the worst nuclear power plant disaster in history.
While dramatized, the scene is emblematic of a long-standing Soviet and Russian desire to downplay critical incidents — and even cover them up. That pattern has flared this week, with senior world health officials, the European Union and U.S. President Donald Trump demanding that Moscow be more transparent about a suspected outbreak of plague in far eastern Russia.
In dark comedic twist in the face of the potential plague, Dyatlov’s dismissive remark is now ubiquitous. Not great, not terrible.
Into the unknown
The death of a 28-year-old employee at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia and the Far East last week triggered unease across the globe due to her laboratory work — and a local Russian official linking her death to a case of plague.
Russia was quick to clamp down. Rospotrebnadzor, the country’s national public health agency, said that the employee died from “pneumonia of unknown etiology” and that no microorganisms associated with her work were identified in the patient sample.
Still, Russian health authorities placed nearly 200 people under supervision and local media reported that several hospitals were placed under quarantine. Rospotrebnadzor said Thursday these measures were taken due to “the patient's professional activities.”
Advertisement
The World Health Organization, which leads global response to international health threats, got in touch with Russian health authorities on Oct. 3. It requested more information using one of the tools laid out in the International Health Regulations, which Russia is signed up to. Under the IHR, countries have 24 hours to respond to the WHO — though Russia sent its response on Oct. 6.
Russian authorities said that “no case of plague had recently been registered in Irkutsk” and “no pathogens of dangerous infectious diseases were detected among any of the contacts.”
World Health Organization epidemic and pandemic management head Maria Van Kerkhove, who said "we still don't know exactly how this person died, at a press briefing in Geneva on Oct. 7, 2026. | Fabrice Coffrini/AFP via Getty Images
As of Thursday, Russian health authorities maintain that there is no “epidemic risk” in the region. Rospotrebnadzor said that it had concluded health inspections and found “no emergency situations involving pathogenic microorganisms.” It had also completed monitoring of 90% of the contacts, without identifying any infections, the agency added. Simultaneously, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov slammed media reports about the case as false and said Russia has been communicating with global health authorities.
Yet the WHO insists there’s still much left unknown about the events inside Russia.
“We don’t know exactly how this person died,” said Maria Van Kerkhove, director of epidemic and pandemic management, during a press briefing Wednesday. “We know that she had pneumonia. We know it was a fatal case. We understand that some laboratory tests have been done. They haven’t found the causative agent. This is why we need more information.”
The WHO said it requested further details on what laboratory tests were conducted, which pathogens were evaluated, which further analyses are being done to determine the patient’s cause of death — if not plague — along with more details on any potential lab incident and the 200 contacts.
Advertisement
Until those questions are answered, it’s impossible for the WHO to conduct a risk assessment.
“We don't yet have the full picture of this event, and we are not able to conduct a full risk assessment,” said Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, the organization’s director-general. “Timely, complete, and transparent information sharing under the international regulations is essential to clarify conflicting reports and enable an accurate assessment of potential public health risks.”
Omertà in Russian
It might be that the cause of death of the 28-year-old lab worker is not, in fact, plague.
But Russia’s incomplete, late and hazy communication about the case is fomenting fears and uncertainty from Geneva to Brussels to Washington. It would also not be the first time the Kremlin has downplayed or attempted to cover up public health threats.
That goes beyond the Soviet-era Chernobyl Nuclear Power Plant disaster, in what is now northern Ukraine, where the Kremlin was slow to take action and effectively denied the cause of the incident.
In 1979, according to an investigation by U.S. scientists, the Soviet Union covered up a deadly anthrax outbreak in the city of Sverdlovsk, now Yekaterinburg, which killed at least 66 people. Officials said the victims had fallen ill from eating contaminated meat, when in reality they had been exposed to anthrax because of an accident at a secret biological weapons lab.
Advertisement
Russia was also accused of covering up a mysterious 1988 alopecia outbreak in Chernivtsi region, in which more than 175 children lost their hair. Soviet authorities said the children suffered from thallium food poisoning, but later studies raised questions about that, with some suggesting the cause was hydrazine, or acid rain.
Over the years, the Kremlin has also dismissed, downplayed and underreported HIV cases, even while in the middle of a deadly epidemic. And, more recently, during the Covid-19 pandemic, Russia was accused of downplaying coronavirus deaths, particularly at the beginning.
An image taken from a helicopter in April 1986 shows a general view of the destroyed fourth power block of Chernobyl's nuclear plant a few days after the catastrophe, which was downplayed at the time by Soviet authorities. | Vladimir Repik/AFP via Getty Images
The tradition extends beyond public health. The 1999 apartment block bombings, the 2000 sinking of the Kursk submarine and the 2014 downing of Malaysia Airlines flight MH17 by Kremlin-backed separatists all raised questions over Russia's public messaging and commitment to transparency.
Talks with Putin
The EU and the U.S. are monitoring the Irkutsk situation closely, with both seemingly growing impatient with Russia’s communication.
“The whole world is waiting for the information from Russia,” said European Commission spokesperson Eva Hrncirova on Thursday.
“Russia should make information about the plague available as soon as possible,” she told reporters. “We need information from Russia. It’s linked to the Russian membership in the WHO Europe, sharing timely, precise, exact information so that the experts can assess the situation, because [it] can have cross-border implications.”
Advertisement
The European Commission’s directorate-general for health and food safety is planning to send a technical letter to Russia asking for more information, a Commission spokesperson confirmed.
In the meantime, Russia’s “patchy” communication is dangerous, said a Commission official, granted anonymity to speak candidly on the matter.
“This fuels speculation into all directions. It also renders preventive [and] precautionary action difficult, if not even meaningless,” the official said. These types of events happen all the time, but there is usually an exchange with the WHO and health authorities, the person added. “The lack of precise [and] reliable info is logically reducing adequate good preparedness.”
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Tuesday urged Russia to share more information, adding that it would be “irresponsible” to speculate until then. The Wall Street Journal reported Wednesday that the U.S. sent a formal diplomatic message to Russia requesting more information about the woman’s death and reminding the Kremlin that it has obligations under international law to share information about disease outbreaks in a timely manner.
U.S. President Donald Trump even said Tuesday he had a "call scheduled" with Russian President Vladimir Putin "very soon" to discuss the situation.
But, by Thursday, the two leaders were yet to talk, with Trump noting that Russia was “not saying much.”

articles.title: MEP blasts ‘Euro-Gestapo’ for lecturing Russia on democracy (VIDEO)
articles.body:
MEP blasts ‘Euro-Gestapo’ for lecturing Russia on democracy (VIDEO)
Brussels is steering Europe toward totalitarianism and a “Euro-Gestapo” while lecturing Russia on democracy, Slovak MEP Lubos Blaha has warned.
Blaha made the remarks during a European Parliament debate on Tuesday, responding to EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas, who denounced Russia’s recent parliamentary elections as undemocratic.
The politician questioned why Brussels was focusing on Russia while cracking down on dissent within the bloc.
He cited arrests of pro-Palestinian protesters in Germany and the imprisonment of Estonian opposition figures, who he claimed were jailed for opposing war with Russia.
“Are you going to set up the Euro-Gestapo here, Mrs. Kallas, and lock up everyone who wants peace?” he asked.
"Will you set up a Euro-Gestapo here, Ms Kallas, and lock up all of us who want peace?" Slovak MEP Blaha calls out warmongers von der Leyen and Kallas. "You criticize the Russians for holding elections, but you do not mind that Zelensky has been governing for a third year without any elections, without a mandate. You hypocrites."
— Chay Bowes (@BowesChay) October 7, 2026
The Slovak lawmaker also questioned why Brussels was debating Russia’s elections while Europe faced mounting unrest.
“You may not have noticed, but Spain is in the streets, France is in the streets, and you are here dealing with Russian elections. You must be joking,” he said.
Blaha went on to accuse Brussels of double standards over Ukraine’s suspended presidential elections.
“You blame the Russians for having elections, but you don’t mind that [Ukraine’s Vladimir] Zelensky has been governing for three years without any elections, without a mandate,” he said. “You are hypocrites!”
Zelensky’s presidential term expired in May 2024, but elections have remained suspended under martial law.
Blaha also cited the annulment of Romania’s 2024 presidential election, claiming the vote was canceled because “the wrong candidate won.” Romania’s Constitutional Court scrapped the result over alleged irregularities and accusations of Russian interference after EU- and NATO-skeptic Calin Georgescu won the first round. Pro-EU candidate Nicusor Dan won the rerun in May 2025.
The MEP argued that Russia had held elections despite the ongoing conflict and daily Ukrainian missile and drone attacks on its territory.
The September poll saw the ruling United Russia party win nearly 58% of the party-list vote.
Blaha also defended Russian President Vladimir Putin, contrasting his popularity with that of Western European leaders.
“You have nothing to criticize Putin for, Mrs. Kallas,” he declared. “Unlike you and your Merzes and Macrons, he has the support of his own population.”
Recent polls have put German Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s approval rating at a record low of 10% in October, while French President Emmanuel Macron’s support fell to 17% in September. Neither Kallas nor European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen was directly elected to her current position by voters, having assumed office through the EU’s institutional appointment process.
Blaha belongs to Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico’s Smer-SD party, which opposes EU sanctions on Russia and has criticized Western military assistance to Ukraine.

articles.title: NATO says 'Steadfast Noon' in Italy is a nuclear exercise
articles.body:
NATO on Thursday said its upcoming
'Steadfast Noon' exercise in Italy was a nuclear exercise,
obviously not featuring live weapons.
                                    
The exercise starting in Italy October 13 will be a "nuclear"
exercise, explained NATO's head of nuclear policy, Nassima
Barrows, during a meeting with media outlets, including ANSA.
                                    
While no live nuclear weapons are used in the exercise, training
to the high standards required for a mission of this type
remains crucial.
                                    
"It is therefore essential to ensure both discipline and the
ability to collaborate on collective defense—of which the
nuclear mission is a vital component," stated Colonel David
Bull, the Alliance's Head of Nuclear Operations.
