articles.title: China Wants to Sell The World on Xinjiang Farmed-Fish
articles.body:
When Chinese state television hailed inland salmon as a miracle in 2018, many viewers saw something more familiar: not a wonder, but a sales pitch.
The segment, aired by China Central Television that May, celebrated salmon farming in western China. Over images of sleek fish cutting through clear water, the narrator marveled that “a precious fish like salmon, which typically lives in the open ocean,” could now be raised inland, in the country’s barren western hinterland. The message was unmistakable. Technology had made the improbable possible. “The land is the same land, and the people are the same people,” the program declared, “but when technology is brought in, miracles are born.”
Online, viewers began poking at the claim almost immediately.
Was that salmon at all, many asked, or just rainbow trout dressed up as something fancier? On Chinese social media, the mood turned from curiosity to irritation. “People expect Atlantic salmon, but we’re getting freshwater rainbow trout that costs half as much,” one Beijing-based WeChat account complained. “How could you not be angry?” Science writer Fang Shimin dispensed with niceties: “This is cheap rainbow trout being passed off as expensive salmon. If you don’t want to deceive consumers, just call it rainbow trout.”
Such anxieties would only grow larger as China worked to sell an idea that, not long ago, might have sounded implausible: seafood from the desert. As China has rapidly expanded its fish farms as part of a state policy aimed at self-sufficiency, it has developed at least 1,000 fish farms in Xinjiang, a historically restive region located in the country’s mountainous and desert inland. The Outlaw Ocean Project, a news organization in Washington, D.C. that I founded and run, mapped these farms as part of a sweeping investigation showing how much seafood is reaching the U.S., including government facilities, in violation of the Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act (UFLPA).
The distrust was not irrational. The United Nations’ Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) said this year that while there is no official global estimate for seafood fraud, empirical studies suggest it may exist in up to 20% of the worldwide trade, sometimes appearing as species substitution and other kinds of misrepresentation.
For most people, seafood comes with an expected geography. Salmon belongs to Norway or Alaska. Cod evokes the cold North Atlantic. Shrimp suggests warm coasts and estuaries. Xinjiang, by contrast, calls up deserts, surveillance, cotton fields, and the Chinese government’s mass detention, forced-labor, and assimilation campaign against Uyghurs and other predominantly Muslim minorities, along with the long, hard distances of the country’s far west. The most landlocked patch on the planet, Xinjiang is among the last places many people would associate with premium fish.
And yet for years, Chinese officials, state media, and seafood companies have been trying to teach consumers to do exactly that. They have promoted “Xinjiang seafood” as one of the small wonders of a new China: fish raised in glacial meltwater, in cold mountain reservoirs, in alkaline lakes, and at farms built against the edge of the desert. The imagery is always some variation on the same promise. Geography is no longer destiny. Harsh landscapes can be made productive. A remote frontier, disciplined by engineering, can become a source of delicacy and pride.
In that sense, Xinjiang seafood is not merely an agricultural product. It is a narrative achievement. The state-led campaign to create that narrative matters because it offers a rare window into Beijing’s worries about food security and its methods for redirecting Western attention away from its human rights problems. It also showcases China’s larger ambitions of using industry to help settle a historically restive region. This campaign saw its zenith in 2023, when Xinhua News Agency reported that the “Xinjiang seafood” label had surged in prominence on Chinese social media. Government data from that year show Xinjiang as China’s second-largest producer of “salmon,” trailing only Qinghai Province on the Tibetan Plateau. Its success is also relevant to what Americans eat, as the Outlaw Ocean Project found that seafood from Xinjiang ends up in the U.S. in violation of federal law. One company, called Tianyun, now ships to 14 countries, including the U.S., and distributes to food companies that supply military bases, public schools, and U.S. congressional cafeterias, according to Bait to Plate, an online tool that tracks the fishing and seafood industries.
Xinjiang Tianyun said in a statement that claims of systemic forced labor “are completely factually unfounded” and described the UFLPA as an unreasonable and politically motivated framework that violates the principles of fair international trade. Xinjiang Tianyun insists that it strictly abides by China’s laws on labor and contracts and resolutely protects the legitimate rights and interests of every employee.
The 2018 salmon dispute exposed how fragile China's narrative of achievement in Xinjiang can be. To some consumers, the issue was simple: they feared they were paying salmon prices for a cheaper fish. But the outrage ran deeper because it also touched food safety. That same year, the Chinese food-safety expert Zhong Kai warned against serving trout raw, citing parasite risks common in freshwater fish. “I do not recommend eating it raw,” he said, advising thorough cooking. Online commenters accused state media of misleading the public. This was “not the salmon ordinary people think of,” they wrote. Masami Takeuchi, a food-safety officer at the FAO, noted that illnesses caused by eating raw freshwater fish can be serious, even when symptoms arrive late or are hard to trace.
The fear, then, was not simply that consumers were being overcharged. It was that they were being sold an aspirational image that obscured material differences in the fish itself.
That anxiety found ready soil in a country where food scandals have repeatedly taught the public to distrust official reassurance. China’s aquaculture industry has expanded at staggering speed, and with that expansion have come the familiar pressures of industrial animal farming: crowding, disease, waste, chemical intervention, and a recurring mismatch between the pastoral language used to market food and the industrial realities that produce it. A 2020 study in Nature found that aquaculture has the highest antibiotic-use intensity per kilogram of biomass among major animal-production sectors, exceeding use in both humans and land-based livestock.
Chinese researchers have warned for years about severe antibiotic abuse in the industry. Sedatives have posed another problem. Diazepam, sometimes used to calm fish during transport, has repeatedly shown up in official inspections despite being prohibited. In 2021, China’s Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Affairs began requiring routine diazepam testing, and a 2023 paper in China Food Hygiene Journal described diazepam residues as “widely detected” in water and seafood products. In 2025, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration issued an alert after detecting residues of prohibited substances—including malachite green, a carcinogenic veterinary drug—in seafood shipments from China, citing “significant public-health concerns.”
None of this proves that Xinjiang seafood as a whole is fraudulent or unsafe. But it helps explain why the category has struggled to inspire a durable sense of consumer trust. In a food system often shadowed by contamination scares and labeling disputes, grand claims end up feeling less like reassurance than marketing. The more insistently officials and companies promoted inland salmon, trout, whitefish, caviar, and other products from China’s far west as a new high-value frontier, the more some consumers wondered what, exactly, they were being asked to believe.
The answer, in part, was a story the state had been helping to write for years.
As early as 2011, Vice Minister of Agriculture Niu Dun was urging officials to “enhance brand building and awareness of the market expansion of Xinjiang’s seafood enterprises.” A 2017 government Action Plan for Fisheries Poverty Alleviation and Aid to Xinjiang and Tibet and Xinjiang went further, instructing local offices to “strengthen communication and coordination with mainstream media” and to “systematically publicize the progress of fishery poverty alleviation,” thereby creating what it called “an environment of positive public opinion.” The phrasing was telling. Fisheries in Xinjiang were to be built, yes. But they were also to be narrated.
That narration took many forms. Officials promoted fish-themed tourism. In Wenquan County, a local attraction described as “Xinjiang’s first cold-water fish theme park” invited visitors to tour a museum, sample whitefish sashimi and caviar, and even catch fish on site, weigh them, and bring them into town for processing. The scene was faintly surreal: a region associated abroad with coercion and repression recast domestically as a place of family outings, provincial pride, and specialty delicacies. The politics were never absent. They were simply plated more attractively.
Then, in late summer 2023, the campaign accelerated.
Posts about Xinjiang seafood surged across Chinese social-media platforms. Hashtags such as “Xinjiang welcomes everyone to come eat seafood” and “No joke—Xinjiang really does produce seafood” climbed Weibo’s Hot Search List. On Douyin, the Chinese version of TikTok, interactions tied to Xinjiang seafood jumped spectacularly. A seafood industry report later said that videos associated with “Xinjiang seafood” and “Xinjiang salmon” amassed more than 150 million views in 2023. One widely circulated Douyin clip, “Xinjiang Salmon ‘Leaps’ onto the World Table,” drew more than 2.7 million views and helped touch off the frenzy. Like many of the videos that followed, it lingered on crystalline mountain water, gleaming facilities, and the visual incongruity of prized fish emerging from the country’s interior.
Soon, the theme leapt beyond China’s own internet. YouTube, which is banned in China, saw a sharp rise in Xinjiang seafood videos that fall. The message was no longer meant only for domestic audiences. Xinjiang seafood was being staged for foreign consumption, too—not just as food, but as an emblem of innovation, abundance, and purity.
The timing was hard to miss. On August 24, 2023, Japan began releasing into the Pacific Ocean treated wastewater that had accumulated since the Fukushima nuclear disaster. Beijing denounced the move as “selfish and irresponsible” and imposed a blanket ban on Japanese aquatic products. In the tense weeks that followed, content promoting Xinjiang seafood leaned heavily on purity: glacial melt from the Tian Shan, cold inland reservoirs, waters safely removed from allegedly contaminated seas. Xinjiang seafood was being sold not only as novel or upscale, but as patriotic, safe, and strategically desirable.
To some analysts, the speed and scale of the online surge suggested something more coordinated than ordinary virality. Fergus Ryan, a senior analyst at the Australian Strategic Policy Institute, said the pattern bore the hallmarks of top-down and algorithmic amplification rather than grassroots enthusiasm alone. In his view, the campaign may also have served another purpose: redirecting attention from mounting scrutiny of China’s seafood sector after an October 2023 investigation by the Outlaw Ocean Project reported that seafood plants in Shandong had used thousands of Uyghur labor transfers to process fish destined for major Western markets. Against that backdrop, Ryan argued, the flood of upbeat Xinjiang seafood content functioned as a kind of information flooding, crowding search and recommendation systems with stories of “fishery miracles” rather than forced labor.
Whether every post was centrally directed matters less than the political usefulness of the category itself. Xinjiang seafood offered the state an unusually supple symbol. It could suggest scientific prowess, dietary upgrading, regional development, ecological management, and ethnic harmony all at once. It could showcase “clean” water, advanced facilities, and smiling workers. Most of all, it could recast one of the world’s most scrutinized frontiers as a landscape of abundance.
That ambition extends beyond domestic image-making. Beijing plainly hopes to export not just Xinjiang seafood but the idea of Xinjiang seafood. Yet that effort faces an obvious obstacle: In the United States, the UFLPA presumes that goods made wholly or partly in Xinjiang are produced with forced labor unless importers can prove otherwise, while in Europe, a 2024 forced-labor regulation will bar products made with forced labor from the E.U. market once it begins applying in December 2027.
This is where the events depart from a conventional tale of food fraud. In many countries, misleading labels thrive because supply chains are opaque and enforcement is weak. In Xinjiang, opacity was part of the business model. The product itself was being woven into a larger political narrative about what the region was and what it was becoming. Fish farms were not merely farms. They were exhibits.
Part of the effort to promote Xinjiang seafood involved government-orchestrated media tours for foreign journalists and vloggers, often called “frontier influencers” or “global stringers,” to visit Xinjiang, including its fish farms. After being shepherded to government-run facilities and through regions like Tibet or Xinjiang that are typically off limits to most other journalists, these influencers tend to create seeing-is-believing style videos that offer “happy life” testimonials from locals, while showcasing the region as a high-tech and indispensable hub for global development and “green” innovation.
By 2025, Xinjiang seafood had become a recurring stop on that circuit. A state-funded outlet released a video featuring an American vlogger identified as Jack exploring what it called the “agricultural miracle” of a fish farm on the edge of China’s largest desert, the Taklamakan. That same month, a British creator toured a reservoir in Alar City and praised its role in both flood control and local fish production. A Russian student, one of the better-known foreign influencers working this terrain, filmed herself at a salmon farm in Nilka, announcing cheerfully that she had come to be “an employee for a day” and see the industry for herself. Some of the footage circulating during this push featured Tianyun, one of the companies caught up in the earlier inland salmon labeling dispute.
Even some of the industry figures tied to those disputes were later recast as patriotic exemplars of frontier development. In 2025, one prominent executive from Xinjiang’s salmon business was honored in Beijing by the Communist Party as a “National Model Worker,” then pledged to help expand China’s salmon industry and improve the skills of workers from all ethnic groups. The symbolism was familiar by then. Commercial actors were being folded into a larger state story about modernization, unity, and progress in the far west.
All of which points to the larger feat behind Xinjiang seafood’s rise. China did not simply have to learn how to raise cold-water fish in unlikely places. It had to construct a category and teach consumers how to feel about it. It had to make fish from a landlocked, desert-heavy, politically burdened region seem not only possible but desirable: clean rather than contaminated, premium rather than ersatz, modern rather than improvised, harmonious rather than coercive. That required hatcheries, reservoirs, feed, transport networks, and technical expertise. But it also required softer definitions, confident reassurances, staged tourism, influencer testimony, and a steady current of triumphal images.
In the end, Xinjiang seafood is best understood not simply as a product of ponds, pipes, hatcheries, and feed, but as a product of narrative force. Fish flash through cold inland water; cameras glide across reservoirs; influencers smile into the desert light; officials speak of innovation and harmony. The image holds. Until, somewhere behind it, the old questions return: What is this fish, really? Where did it come from? What story is being wrapped around it? In Xinjiang, those questions do not fade when the meal arrives. They sit there at the table.
(The reporting for this story was part of a larger investigation conducted by an international team of journalists based at The Outlaw Ocean Project. Ian Urbina is the founder and executive editor of The Outlaw Ocean Project.)

articles.title: Russia attacked Ukraine with 136 drones: 114 neutralized, including more than 80% of the jet-powered ones
articles.body:
Russia attacked Ukraine with 136 drones: 114 neutralized, including more than 80% of the jet-powered ones
Kyiv • UNN
Overnight, Russia launched 136 drones at Ukraine, including 93 jet-powered ones. Air defense shot down or suppressed 114 unmanned aerial vehicles; the attack continued.
Russia attacked Ukraine with 136 drones during the night of October 9, 93 of them jet-powered. A total of 114 were shot down or suppressed, including 77 jet-powered drones, or 82.8%. UNN reports this, citing data from the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine.
From which directions and with what did Russia attack?
According to the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, during the night of October 9 (from 18:00 on October 8), the enemy attacked with 136 Shahed-type attack UAVs (93 of them jet-powered), Gerbera drones, and Parody-type decoy drones from the following directions: Orel, Primorsko-Akhtarsk — Russia, the temporarily occupied territory of Donetsk, and the temporarily occupied territory of the Autonomous Republic of Crimea — Hvardiiske.
How many were destroyed?
The air attack was repelled by aviation, anti-aircraft missile forces, electronic warfare and unmanned systems units, and mobile fire groups of the Defense Forces of Ukraine.
According to preliminary data, as of 08:00, air defense forces had shot down/suppressed 114 enemy Shahed-type UAVs (77 of them jet-powered), Gerbera drones, and drones of other types
Hits by the enemy's air-attack weapons were recorded at 8 locations, as well as the crashes of downed targets (debris) at 7 locations.
The attack is ongoing; several enemy UAVs remain in the airspace.

articles.title: Patriot missile launcher displayed at Pingtung high school
articles.body:
TAIPEI (Taiwan News) – A military instructor arranged an exhibition featuring a Patriot missile launcher at National Pingtung Senior High School on Thursday, CNA reported.
The school displayed the third-generation Patriot launcher and other military hardware to promote all-out defense education among students and faculty. Past exhibits have included Clouded Leopard armored personnel carriers, Humvee-mounted missile launchers, and Navy underwater operations equipment.
Developed by US defense contractor Raytheon, the Patriot is a surface-to-air missile system designed to intercept aircraft, cruise missiles, drones, and tactical ballistic missiles. Its components include radar for detecting and tracking targets, an engagement control station, launchers, and interceptor missiles.
Military instructor Chen Kuan-ming (陳冠名) said he had to apply for approval several times. He added that the exhibition was finally approved ahead of the National Day long weekend.
Chen is the school’s last military instructor and is scheduled to leave the military in November 2027. He aims to promote defense education using real-world examples.
Pingtung High School Principal Wang Yu-hui (王玉輝) said students previously learned about national defense through videos or pictures. He said the event allowed them to observe the equipment firsthand.

articles.title: 80% of Moldovans say country is unprepared for attack as Russian drones flow into its airspace, but few back NATO membership
articles.body:
More than 80% of Moldovans believe the country is not prepared to withstand external aggression, according to a CBS AXA poll presented ahead of the Moldova Security Forum 2026, NewsMaker reports.
The findings come as Moldova has faced a sharp increase in Russian drone incursions linked to Russia’s war against Ukraine. Moldova recorded 44 airspace-violation incidents in the first nine months of 2026, compared with 17 in all of 2025. Authorities have reported Russian drones crossing Moldovan airspace, while drone and missile debris has also fallen on Moldovan territory.
According to NewsMaker, more than 60% of those surveyed said Moldova is completely unprepared for a possible armed attack, while nearly 24% described its preparedness as weak.
Moldovans see country as unprepared for attack
The survey found that 82% of respondents also do not feel sufficiently informed or prepared to know what to do in a major crisis. According to CBS AXA Deputy Director Vasile Cantarji, respondents tend to trust specialized emergency institutions more than Moldova’s main state institutions.
More than half said they trust Moldova’s General Inspectorate for Emergency Situations, while 35% expressed trust in the church. Trust in the government, parliament, and courts was much lower, at roughly 4–6%.
The findings come as Moldova faces a security environment shaped by Russia’s war against Ukraine, hybrid threats, energy dependence, and disinformation. Moldova’s government has supported Ukraine and strengthened security cooperation with European partners, while repeatedly condemning Russia’s war and its spillover effects.
The repeated drone incursions are now increasingly exposing Moldova to risks from the war next door.
Three Russian missiles and two drones strike Moldovan territory in morning attacks on neighboring Ukraine. Moldova is increasingly exposed to the risks of Russia’s war next door
Most favor neutrality over NATO membership
Despite the widespread perception that Moldova is poorly prepared for external aggression, only about 4% of respondents said joining NATO would be the right way to make the country safer.
Around 45% instead favored maintaining Moldova’s neutrality. At the same time, six in 10 respondents said Moldova needs continued external support to strengthen its security and defense.
Nearly two-thirds considered cooperation with the European Union and Romania important for Moldova’s development.
Moldova’s constitution establishes permanent neutrality, while the country has been deepening security and defense cooperation with European partners.
EU seen as preferred source of emergency assistance
The poll also asked whom Moldova should turn to for help during a major disaster such as an earthquake or flood.
About 33% selected EU countries, followed by Russia at roughly 16% and Romania at 15%. The CIS, NATO, UN, and Ukraine each received support from 4% or fewer respondents.
War in Ukraine is one of several security concerns
Respondents identified a range of threats to Moldova’s security, with internal problems ranking alongside external risks.
Corruption was cited by more than 15% of respondents, while poverty was named by 13.5%. Just over 13.5% identified the war in Ukraine as a security risk. Energy dependence and disinformation were each cited by nearly 10%.
Other concerns included economic instability, crime, and external aggression.
CBS AXA conducted the survey from August 25 to September 9 among 2,009 Moldovans aged 18 and older. The reported margin of error is 2.2%. NewsMaker published the findings on October 7.
Moldova strengthens protection at Ukrainian border
Moldovan authorities are now responding to the Russian drone threat by creating protected areas at border crossings with Ukraine where border guards, officials, and civilians can shelter during potential drone attacks, Interior Minister Daniela Misail-Nikitin said on October 7, according to NewsMaker.
Authorities are also moving Moldovan personnel from joint checkpoints located on Ukrainian territory back to Moldova. The measures follow an incident at the Palanca–Maiaki–Udobne crossing in which a Moldovan border guard was injured by a falling projectile.
Transnistria adds another security challenge
Moldova also faces a longstanding security problem in Transnistria, a breakaway region along the country’s eastern border with Ukraine. The region declared independence from Moldova in 1990 and has remained outside Chisinau’s control since a brief war in 1992.
Transnistria is not internationally recognized as an independent state. Russia maintains a significant troop presence there and has long supported the separatist authorities, making the region a persistent source of tension between Chisinau and Moscow.

articles.title: Switzerland condemns deadly Russian attack on Ukrainian buses
articles.body:
Switzerland condemns deadly Russian attack on Ukrainian buses
Switzerland has condemns Thursday’s Russian attack on two Ukrainian civilian buses, which left at least 30 people dead and 18 injured.
The Russian air strike took place near Kramatorsk in the Donetsk region, which has not yet been fully captured by Russia.
“Our thoughts are with the victims, their families and those who have been injured,” wrote the Swiss Federal Department of Foreign Affairs (FDFA) on the social media online platform X.
Switzerland is calling for de-escalation and reiterates that all parties must comply with international humanitarian law at all times, in particular with regard to the protection of the civilian population, the statement added.
More
Cassis: Swiss want to get Ukraine peace talks back on track
On February 24, 2022, Russian President Vladimir Putin gave the order for a military invasion of Ukraine. Since then, massacres of the Ukrainian civilian population have taken place, and according to the UN, Ukrainian prisoners are being tortured and raped.
Putin himself has been wanted by the International Criminal Court in The Hague on a war crimes arrest warrant since March 2023.
Meanwhile, Russian troops occupy just under 20% of Ukrainian territory, but despite their clear numerical superiority in terms of troops and equipment, they are making no headway and have instead recently been subjecting the Ukrainian civilian population to rocket and drone attacks.

articles.title: Zelenskyy revealed which drones the Defense Forces used to strike Russian oil refineries: modified FP-1s and An-196 RS
articles.body:
Zelenskyy revealed which drones the Defense Forces used to strike Russian oil refineries: modified FP-1s and An-196 RS
Kyiv • UNN
President Zelenskyy reported that Russia’s Omsk Oil Refinery was hit by FP-6 drones (modified FP-1s), while the Ukhta Oil Refinery was struck by An-196 RS unmanned aerial vehicles.
President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy said exactly what weapons the Defense Forces used to strike Russian oil refineries. According to him, the Omsk Refinery was attacked by FP-6 drones (modified FP-1 drones). An-196 RS unmanned aerial vehicles (part of the family of Ukrainian long-range "Liutyi" drones) were used to strike the Ukhta Refinery, UNN reports.
Omsk Refinery is Russia's largest oil refinery, with a capacity of about 22 million tonnes of oil per year. It is located approximately 2,500 km from the Ukrainian border in Russia's Omsk region. The facility is owned by the Russian company "Gazprom Neft." It produces gasoline, diesel and aviation fuel, lubricants, and other petroleum products.
Another target of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, the Ukhta Refinery, is located 1,900 km from the Ukrainian border in the Komi Republic. The facility is owned by the Russian company "Lukoil" and processes about 4.2 million tonnes of oil per year. The refinery produces gasoline, diesel fuel, fuel oil, and other petroleum products.
According to the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, both facilities are involved in supplying the Russian army.
The president also confirmed the strike on another Russian data center, calling it a mirror response to Russia's strikes on Ukraine. The defense company Fire Point, whose drones were used by the Defense Forces to hit the target, said that it was the largest data center of the Russian company "Yandex" — "Yandex DC Kaluga." It is located in the Grabtsevo industrial park in Russia's Kaluga region.
Photo source: @firepointofficial
The facility's designed capacity is 63 MW. According to the Ukrainian defense company, several modules of the data center were completely disabled as a result of the strikes.
As of 2026, "Yandex" has five large data centers, two of which have been attacked by the Defense Forces of Ukraine over the past two days. On October 8, Ukrainian drones struck the company's data center in Sasovo, Ryazan region. Following the strike, disruptions to the operation of a number of online services were recorded in Russia.
Recall
On October 8, the Defense Forces struck the "Gazprom Neftekhim Salavat" oil refinery complex in Bashkortostan with FP-1 drones. The drones traveled more than 1,300 km to carry out the attack.
The capacity of the Salavat complex is up to 10 million tonnes of hydrocarbon feedstock per year. According to the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, the facility is involved in meeting the needs of the Russian army.

articles.title: Trump promises not to attack Iran before November’s US midterms
articles.body:
Donald Trump has promised not to attack Iran before November’s US midterm elections, outlining a pause on the protracted war he has struggled to end after almost eight months.
In a Truth Social post on Thursday, the US president said Washington was “having productive discussions with the Islamic Republic of Iran”, which he claimed was “in very bad condition, both Economically and Militarily”.
The strait of Hormuz, through which roughly a fifth of the world’s oil and liquefied natural gas passed through before the war, was all but closed after the US and Israel struck Iran in late February.
On Thursday, however, Trump suggested that oil was moving through the strait in record volumes: “22 Million Barrels, last night alone”, he claimed, “with not one barrel coming from, or going to, Iran”. The figure could not be independently verified.
“We will not be attacking Iran at any time prior to the Midterm Elections to be held in the United States on November 3rd,” Trump wrote. “IRAN WILL NOT HAVE A NUCLEAR WEAPON!”
The US first imposed a blockade on the strait of Hormuz in April after talks in Islamabad collapsed, and reinstated it in July after a short-lived June deal to end the fighting. Fighting flared again in early September, when US forces struck rocket launchers on Iran’s Larak Island and Tehran responded with missiles aimed at American military bases in Jordan and the United Arab Emirates.
Trump’s public position on the elections has shifted over the past month. On 2 September, as the US exchanged fire with Iran for the first time in weeks, he told reporters he was “not affected by the election”, adding that he was not on the ballot himself but intended to help his party.
A week later, before heading to the Republican “midterm convention” in Dallas, he said he expected the war to end almost as soon as the voting was over, and accused Tehran of holding out in the hope that a change of power in Congress would leave it free to pursue a nuclear weapon. He also conceded that US oil prices were unlikely to fall before polling day.
A Reuters/Ipsos survey from late September found that only about a third of Americans approved of the strikes on Iran, while more than four in five expected the conflict to last for an extended period, and that approval for Trump among Republicans had fallen from 82% to 73% in a week.
Polling averages now show Democrats leading Republicans by roughly nine points on the generic congressional ballot, according to forecaster Nate Silver, the widest margin of this election cycle.
The Wall Street Journal reported in September that JD Vance, the US vice-president, and secretary of state Marco Rubio had privately warned Trump the conflict could extend through the remainder of his presidency.
Trump’s post did not say what the US would do after 3 November.

articles.title: Warehouses, a home-improvement store, a farm: Russia’s strikes aimed past the grid at Ukraine’s civilian economy
articles.body:
Russian drones hit Ukraine's power grid, warehouses, a food warehouse, a home-improvement store, and a farm overnight on 9 October, Ukrainian officials and emergency services reported. The strikes triggered emergency power cuts in Kyiv and other regions and killed at least three people across the country.
As Russia continues its daily terror attacks, it has likely begun its winter strike campaign early, aiming to make civilian life in Ukraine unbearable, ISW assessed. Those strikes now reach beyond the grid to the businesses that store and sell goods, adding to damage Ukraine's Economy Ministry expects to reach up to $10 billion this year.
Power cut in Kyiv and other regions
Russia launched 136 drones overnight, 93 of them jet-powered, Ukraine's Air Force said. Air defenses downed or suppressed 114. Drones hit eight locations, and debris fell at seven more.
DTEK, Ukraine's largest private energy company, introduced emergency power cuts on Kyiv's right bank and in the Bucha and Vyshhorod districts on the grid operator's orders. Ukrenergo, the national grid operator, imposed emergency outages in some regions, citing the strain Russian attacks put on the system. Planned schedules were suspended there. Hourly cuts across parts of Ukraine had already been set for the whole day.
The cuts came a day after a Russian strike knocked out several grid elements supplying Kyiv, leaving many consumers without power. Russia has sharply stepped up attacks on Ukraine's energy system in recent weeks, deliberately targeting power lines and transformers, Ukraine's Energy Ministry said.
Ukraine’s war leadership sets new electronic warfare tasks as Russia’s jet-powered drones slip past nearly half of its air defenses
Warehouses and a store
In the Bucha district of Kyiv Oblast, Russia hit warehouses and injured three people, Ukraine's State Emergency Service said. One was hospitalized. Rescuers were searching for a woman who may be under the rubble.
In Odesa, a strike damaged the roof of a warehouse storing food and started a fire, the region's emergency service reported. In the south of the oblast, Russia damaged buildings at holiday resorts and destroyed a café.
Near Chernihiv, Russia hit a site just outside the city after 03:00, the city council said. A Suspilne correspondent at the scene reported that a drone hit the Epicenter store, part of a large Ukrainian home-improvement chain. Russian forces also struck a farm in the Kulykivka community. No one was hurt in Chernihiv Oblast.
Russia has already destroyed more than two-fifths of Ukraine's modern warehouse space.
Three killed overnight
In Zaporizhzhia, Russia struck near an apartment building, killing a man, the Zaporizhzhia Oblast administration said. The number of injured rose to nine, including a 14-year-old girl, regional prosecutors said. One strike landed near an after-school education center.
In Ivano-Frankivsk, falling drone debris started a fire, and a man born in 1959 was killed, Ivano-Frankivsk Oblast head Svitlana Onyshchuk said.
In Shyroka Balka, Kherson Oblast, a Russian drone dropped explosives on a house at about 06:20, killing a 74-year-old woman and injuring a 68-year-old man, regional prosecutors reported.
Russia injured three women in a Kharkiv suburb, Kharkiv Oblast head Oleh Syniehubov said. In the Nikopol district, a 24-year-old woman was injured, Dnipropetrovsk Oblast head Oleksandr Hanzha said.
Poland scrambled military aircraft as Russia struck targets in western Ukraine, its Operational Command said.
The past day's toll
Over the past 24 hours, Russia killed two people and injured 18 in Zaporizhzhia and the Zaporizhzhia district, regional council head Ivan Fedorov said. In Sumy Oblast, one man was killed and 14 people were injured, including two 12-year-old boys, the regional administration reported.
In Kherson Oblast, four people were injured, including a child, Kherson Oblast head Oleksandr Prokudin said. In Mykolaiv Oblast, a Russian drone injured two children aged three months and one year, acting oblast head Heorhii Reshetilov said. Three people were injured in Kharkiv Oblast, Syniehubov reported.
In Donetsk Oblast, Russia killed 35 people and injured 25 on 8 October, Donetsk Oblast head Vadym Filashkin said. Thirty-two of them died in Kramatorsk, most in a Russian bomb strike on two passenger buses.

articles.title: Trump says Witkoff 'doing very well' in Iran talks
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Trump says Witkoff 'doing very well' in Iran talks
US President Donald Trump said US envoy Steve Witkoff is "doing very well" in talks with Iran, as the president once again predicted that the months-long war will end "very soon".
Speaking at a campaign rally in San Antonio, Texas, on Wednesday, Trump said Witkoff was making progress in negotiations with Iran but suggested that reaching a deal was not his preferred outcome.
"He's working on the Iran deal and doing very well. I think the deal isn't really something that I want to do, but they're willing to offer us anything to stop," Trump said.
"They will never have a nuclear weapon," he added.
The US president also said he expects the war with Iran to end soon.
"That war ends - it's going to be very soon. It's got to be very soon," Trump said, describing Iran as "a failed nation."
Despite expressing initial reluctance to strike a deal with Tehran, Trump said in a Thursday post on Truth Social that the US is continually engaged in productive discussions with Iran.
"We are having productive discussions with the Islamic Republic of Iran," Trump wrote.
He added that the US blockade of Iranian ports remained in place and that oil was continuing to flow through the Strait of Hormuz, amid discussions on reopening the vital global energy shipping route.
"We will not be attacking Iran at any time prior to the Midterm Elections to be held in the United States on November 3rd," Trump said.
The statement comes amid GOP concerns that any escalation in the US-Iran conflict ahead of the November midterm elections could put Trump's Republican Party at risk of losing control of both houses of Congress.
However, recent reports said the White House had asked the Pentagon to develop military options for potential strikes on Iranian targets before 3 November.
Trump officials were also debating the possible scale and targets of any strikes, as well as whether the president would ultimately authorise military action, according to The Atlantic.
Several of Trump's advisers reportedly believed the timing would be more appropriate after the elections, the publication reported.
Axios also reported that the Pentagon had instructed US Central Command (CENTCOM) to prepare for a possible resumption of major combat operations in Iran.
Citing US officials, the report said the directive did not specify a date for any potential military action.
The latest developments come as diplomatic efforts to end the conflict remain uncertain.
Washington has emphasised restrictions on Iran's nuclear activities as a key condition for a lasting agreement.

articles.title: US imposes fresh sanctions on Iran's shadow fleet
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
US imposes fresh sanctions on Iran's shadow fleet
The US imposed fresh sanctions on Iran on Thursday, targeting individuals, networks and 17 vessels for transporting Iranian crude, oil products and petrochemicals, the Treasury Department said, as Washington stepped up economic pressure on Tehran.
The sanctions are part of the department's "Operation Economic Outcast," which aims to cut Iran's funding for the war with the US, missile construction, cyberattacks and the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, or IRGC.
"Today's action represents the most significant blow yet to Iran's remaining illicit maritime infrastructure by neutralizing the vast majority of the shadow fleet," a Treasury official told reporters on a call. "Treasury is cutting off the regime's last major source of illicit revenue and strengthening international pressure to hold Tehran accountable."
The move tightens the squeeze on Iranian oil sales after the US reimposed its blockade of Iranian ports on 14 July following the breakdown of a memorandum of understanding between Tehran and Washington to end the war.
Iran has only about 20 million barrels of crude oil left on vessels outside the blockade, off Singapore, Malaysia and China, the Treasury official said. The world uses about 100 million barrels of oil per day.
A second Treasury official said Iran has stopped loading and offloading crude oil vessels due to the blockade and sanctions.
President Donald Trump said on social media on Thursday that the US is having "productive discussions" with Iran over the war that began on February 28. Trump said the US will not attack Iran before the midterm elections on November 3.
An analyst said the fact that the US is sanctioning vessels after Iran has delivered virtually all of its oil at sea means the impact will be muted.
"This is economic warfare conducted in the rearview mirror, designed to generate headlines rather than results," said Brett Erickson, a managing principal at Obsidian Risk Advisors.
Vessels targeted by the US sanctions include the Comoros-flagged Paritosh, the Panama-flagged Bitu and the Bahamas-flagged Gas Lucky.
(Reuters)

articles.title: Blackouts return to Kyiv as Russia prepares to freeze civilians over the winter
articles.body:
Power outages have returned to Kyiv after Russian attacks damaged the energy infrastructure supplying the capital, with authorities warning that the situation could worsen as Russia intensifies its campaign against Ukraine’s energy system ahead of winter.
Russia has repeatedly targeted Ukraine’s power, heating, and other critical infrastructure to disrupt the systems civilians depend on and create a humanitarian crisis during winter. Ukrainian officials have repeatedly warned that this winter will be especially severe, as Russia has expanded its strike capabilities since the summer and Ukraine continues to face shortages of air-defense systems needed to protect its energy infrastructure.
Ukrenergo said on 8 October that emergency outages were being imposed in parts of Kyiv and Kyiv Oblast because of falling voltage in the high-voltage network. Previously announced hourly schedules were suspended, with predictable schedules to resume once the system stabilizes.
In the evening, further disruption came after a Russian attack on an energy facility important to Kyiv. Energy Minister Denys Shmyhal said that energy workers were working to restore power.
Kyiv has been under Russian attack throughout the day, with four people killed and 19 injured.
The attack continues into the evening of 8 October, with air raid alerts active across most of the country.
Kyiv loses power, water, and public transport
The damage throughout the day quickly spread beyond electricity.
The Kyiv City Military Administration said power disruptions temporarily halted metro trains and escalators. Part of the capital’s public transport system was also suspended because of the lack of electricity.
Reduced power to water infrastructure caused lower pressure on the right bank of the Dnipro, particularly in the Holosiivskyi, Sviatoshynskyi, Solomianskyi, and Shevchenkivskyi districts. Some buildings could temporarily lose water, the administration warned.
Russia is hitting the energy system as winter approaches
The outages come as Russia has stepped up attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure ahead of the heating season.
Ukrenergo said Russian attacks had caused new power outages in Donetsk, Kharkiv, Sumy, and Zaporizhzhia oblasts. The company said damaged equipment was already limiting the grid’s ability to supply consumers and warned that further Russian strikes could rapidly change the situation.
For 9 October, Ukrenergo announced all-day power restrictions in affected regions, including hourly outages for some consumers. Industrial and business consumers will also face restrictions. The company urged Ukrainians to conserve electricity, particularly during the evening peak from 5 p.m. to 10 p.m.
Ukraine’s energy authorities have been warning about the consequences of repeated Russian attacks for months. In late September, Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said attacks on energy facilities had been occurring almost daily since the summer, with the September 29–30 attack marking the first massive combined strike on the energy system since the previous heating season.
The renewed strikes mark the beginning of Russia’s winter campaign against the energy system, with Russian missiles and drones increasingly targeting power-generation and transmission infrastructure in Kyiv and surrounding regions.
Russia has openly threatened another winter of blackouts
The campaign follows years of Russian attacks aimed at disrupting the infrastructure that keeps Ukrainian homes heated and supplied with electricity and water during the winter.
In August, Russia’s Defense Ministry openly taunted Ukrainians over its attacks on energy-related infrastructure, posting images of attack drones with the message that Ukrainians would “get a freeze” in winter.
Russia’s strategy has repeatedly linked attacks on electricity infrastructure to disruptions in heating and water supplies. This makes damage to the power grid particularly consequential as temperatures fall: a strike on an electrical facility can leave not only homes without lights, but also affect water pumps, heating systems, transportation, and other essential services.
The return of blackouts to Kyiv before the heating season is fully underway is an early indication of the pressure Russia’s renewed energy campaign is putting on Ukraine’s civilian infrastructure.

articles.title: Callous Kallas: The bitter diplomat dragging the EU down the warpath with Russia
articles.body:
Callous Kallas: The bitter diplomat dragging the EU down the warpath with Russia
Kaja Kallas, the Estonian diplomat and former prime minister currently serving as the vice-president of the European Commission, has shown a deeply confrontational attitude towards Russia and the Russians.
It is perhaps worth pausing here to note that this is particularly personal, given her family history. Her mother, Kristi Kallas, was only six months old when she, together with her mother and grandmother, was deported to Siberia during the Soviet mass deportations of March 1949. She remained there until she was ten, and later studied medicine and worked as a pediatrician.
Her father, Siim Kallas, had a very different experience with the Soviet system. He was a member of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union from 1972 to 1990 and held senior positions in the financial system of Soviet Estonia, including heading the Estonian branch of the USSR Savings Bank. He later became President of the Bank of Estonia, Prime Minister of Estonia and a Vice-President of the European Commission.
These two sides of her family history – one marked by deportation and the other by a successful career within the Soviet system – form a striking background to Kaja Kallas’s present-day political position.
Last month, Kallas described the German people as being blind to the Russian threat because of their resistance to providing further financial support to Ukraine. Now, I suppose Russian people are also considered blind because of the convincing victory of President Vladimir Putin’s party in September’s legislative election. I am definitely not blind.
Kaja Kallas is not alone in her hostility towards Russia. Other senior EU officials, including European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, have supported substantial financial and military assistance to Ukraine. The EU has committed up to €90 billion in support for Ukraine for 2026 and 2027, including funding for both defense and general budgetary needs.
The question Europeans should be allowed to ask is how these decisions affect their own societies. Public money is limited, and European citizens also need investment in healthcare, education, transport, housing and infrastructure.
Since 2022, Europeans have been paying a heavy price for the transformation of their energy system. The decision to move away from Russian pipeline gas was made in the name of security, and the EU has succeeded in diversifying its supplies. But security has come at a considerable economic cost. The European Commission reports that although wholesale energy prices have fallen substantially from the extraordinary peaks of 2022, industrial gas and electricity prices remain two to four times higher than in the EU’s main trading partners. The Commission warns that this continues to threaten the long-term competitiveness of European industry.
The EU’s energy import bill reached €604 billion in 2022 before falling to €427 billion in 2024. Meanwhile, industrial energy prices remain considerably above their pre-crisis levels. Germany, the industrial heart of Europe, has felt the consequences particularly sharply. German industrial energy consumption fell by 9.1% in 2022 and another 7.8% in 2023, with the German Federal Statistical Office explicitly linking these declines, particularly in energy-intensive industries, to significantly higher energy prices and associated production reductions.
Germany’s broader economic performance tells the same story. Its economy contracted for a second consecutive year in 2024, while manufacturing gross value added fell by 3%. The Federal Statistical Office identified high energy costs, together with stronger international competition and other structural pressures, among the factors weighing on the economy. Manufacturing remained under pressure in 2025, when value added in the sector fell another 1.3%.
Europe faces an uncomfortable question: Is it prepared to accept permanently higher energy costs while production and investment increasingly move towards countries where energy and manufacturing costs are lower? It is one thing to pursue energy security; it is another to allow the foundations of European industry to become the price of achieving it.
The issue of NATO and Ukraine is equally contentious. The argument that NATO expansion towards Ukraine ruined Moscow’s relations with Europe is not just a Kremlin talking point – reputable Western analysts, like Professor Jeffrey Sachs, have repeatedly argued the same point. Even if that analysis remains disputed, it is an argument that deserves to be heard in any serious discussion of the origins and continuation of the war, which continues to have devastating consequences for Ukrainians.
European leaders should be asking what policies can bring the conflict closer to a negotiated settlement rather than simply allowing the confrontation to continue indefinitely.
Perhaps the most revealing part of this story is that the argument is no longer simply between the EU and its critics. It has begun to unfold within Europe itself.
Defense spending in the EU is rising at an extraordinary pace. According to the Council of the EU, member states spent €418 billion on defense in 2025, and expenditure is estimated to reach €454 billion in 2026 – 75.3% higher than in 2021. Defense investment alone is projected to reach almost €163 billion in 2026.
But the question of who decides how this enormous effort should be organized is becoming increasingly contentious. In September, Kaja Kallas withdrew plans for a new high-level advisory group on European defense after several member states objected. Reporting by Defense News and Euractiv identified Germany, France and Italy among the governments pushing back against the initiative. The German position was that NATO remains the primary framework for military capability and defense planning.
The disagreement was not about whether Europe needs defense. It was about who should set priorities, how decisions should be coordinated, and whether another Brussels structure was the right way forward. Even as European governments prepare to spend hundreds of billions more on defense, there is no agreement about the political direction those resources should serve.
The EU, in other words, is having two conversations at once: how much it should spend, and what kind of Europe that spending is meant to create.
Ms. Kallas, Europe needs diplomacy as well as security policy. European citizens need their governments to protect their interests, use public money responsibly and keep open the possibility of a peaceful future.
If the EU continues indefinitely along the present path, the economic and political consequences for European societies will deserve much greater public discussion.
EU citizens have the right to ask difficult questions about how their money is being spent and what kind of Europe they want to build. They may disagree strongly about Russia, Ukraine and NATO, but that does not make their questions illegitimate.
I was born in Ireland and have been affiliated with Russia for thirty years. I have been living here for the last eight years. From that perspective, I believe Europeans should be able to discuss these issues without being dismissed as blind, naïve or sympathetic to one side simply because they question current policies.
Europe has enormous resources and enormous human potential. With wiser choices about priorities, Europeans should be able to expect excellent healthcare, education, transport and infrastructure alongside a responsible security policy.
The statements, views and opinions expressed in this column are solely those of the author and do not necessarily represent those of RT.

articles.title: Exclusive: Putin puts a price on Trump's Ukraine energy truce — Kyiv fears the cost
articles.body:
Exclusive: Putin puts a price on Trump's Ukraine energy truce — Kyiv fears the cost
Russian President Vladimir Putin leaves the podium after holding a press conference with U.S. President Donald Trump at Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson on Aug. 15, 2025 in Anchorage, Alaska. (Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)
Russia has demanded sanctions relief from the U.S. as part of talks over a possible energy ceasefire with Ukraine, while also seeking to link the initiative to a ceasefire in the Black Sea, U.S. and Ukrainian officials familiar with the talks told the Kyiv Independent.
The demands come as Russia intensifies attacks on Ukraine's energy infrastructure, with one senior Ukrainian defense official saying Moscow is trying to inflict as much damage as possible to gain leverage before potential negotiations.
Kyiv is already facing daily blackouts amid Russian attacks. A Russian assault on Oct. 8 caused widespread power outages across the capital, a city of more than three million people.
Publicly, Moscow has shown little willingness to commit to an energy ceasefire. Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov told reporters on Oct. 8 that Russia saw no point in negotiating a sectoral ceasefire.
"Kyiv is not currently proposing a long-term settlement, but rather a ceasefire in an area that is its Achilles' heel — the energy sector," Peskov said.
Privately, however, Russian officials have signaled that Moscow is willing to consider the initiative, two Ukrainian officials and one U.S. official told the Kyiv Independent.
But Russia is tying a possible agreement to other demands, including sanctions relief, three people familiar with the negotiations said.
Moscow seeks a broader deal
The U.S. has been pressing both Kyiv and Moscow to stop attacking each other's energy infrastructure, making an energy ceasefire one of the main issues in peace talks.
President Donald Trump is also seeking to demonstrate progress on Ukraine before the U.S. midterm elections, several Ukrainian officials told the Kyiv Independent.
After their latest trip to Russia, Trump's envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner returned with the impression that an energy ceasefire was possible.
Russian Envoy Kirill Dmitriev visited the U.S. twice in September for meetings with Witkoff and Kushner, where they discussed a possible halt to attacks on energy infrastructure.
During those meetings, Dmitriev told the U.S. envoys that Russia wanted sanctions relief as part of a deal, according to Ukrainian and U.S. officials briefed on the discussions.
It remains unclear which sanctions Moscow wants lifted.
One European diplomat briefed on the matter told the Kyiv Independent that Russia could be seeking the release of frozen Russian funds as part of the deal.
"If they get sanctioned funds released … the likelihood that these will be used to escalate (war) is almost guaranteed," the diplomat said.
"No one really thinks they are genuinely seeking to adhere to a ceasefire."
Ukrainian officials familiar with the talks confirmed that Russia was demanding sanctions relief but said they did not know which restrictions Moscow wanted removed.
The issue is expected to feature in discussions between Kyiv and Washington.
A Ukrainian delegation is due to meet with Trump's envoys in the U.S. on Oct. 9 to discuss proposals for an energy and Black Sea ceasefire.
The Ukrainian team is expected to receive a briefing on the U.S. talks with Russia and seek clarification about Moscow's demand for sanctions relief.
Asked about economic deals between the U.S. and Russia, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Oct. 8 that Ukraine "knows a lot" but was not ready to discuss the matter publicly.
"I'm not ready to talk about it publicly or in detail," Zelensky told reporters.
Kyiv fears Russia is dragging out talks
For Kyiv, Moscow's demands raise the question of whether Russia is genuinely interested in halting attacks or is using negotiations to secure additional concessions while continuing its military campaign.
"Every time negotiations begin, they come up with more and more demands," one Ukrainian official briefed on the talks told the Kyiv Independent.
"Now this lifting of sanctions has come up."
Ukraine objects to the prospect of Russia receiving economic benefits in exchange for an energy truce. Kyiv's position is that any halt to attacks on energy infrastructure must be reciprocal, with both sides stopping strikes, rather than Russia receiving additional concessions for agreeing to the pause.
The dispute comes as broader peace talks remain stalled because of Russian territorial demands, which Kyiv considers unconstructive.
Washington is now pursuing a narrower agreement on energy infrastructure and Black Sea shipping that could demonstrate progress without resolving the larger questions at the heart of Russia's war against Ukraine.
Kyiv still hopes that the discussions will lead to a trilateral meeting with Russian representatives.
When Zelensky met German Chancellor Friedrich Merz in Kyiv on Oct. 4, Witkoff texted the Ukrainian president that Washington wanted to hold such a meeting in late October. Zelensky replied that Ukraine would support it.
Before Kyiv can assess the prospects for a deal, Ukrainian officials want to understand what Moscow is asking for — and whether the Kremlin is prepared to stop its attacks without securing additional benefits in return.

articles.title: Montenegro detains founder of Rybar, one of Russia’s most popular pro-war Telegram channels. Here’s what we know.
articles.body:
Montenegro detains founder of Rybar, one of Russia’s most popular pro-war Telegram channels. Here’s what we know.
Montenegrin authorities detained the creator of the Telegram channel Rybar. Mikhail Zvinchuk, his wife, and three other Rybar staffers were detained in the town of Risan on the morning of October 9. According to reporting by the local outlet Vijesti, they found “sophisticated digital equipment,” drones, and “electronic devices” on them. Montenegrin security services had been monitoring Zvinchuk and his team for several days. Media reports said the operation was aimed at “suppressing the hybrid activity” of the Rybar network of channels.
It remains unclear whether Zvinchuk has been charged with anything. Law enforcement agencies have not officially commented on the detention. Montenegrin Prime Minister Milojko Spajić wrote on the social network X that the government does not intend to “voice what should remain within the competence of the security services.” “But the message after today’s successful operation, in which the head of the Rybar information network was detained, is absolutely clear: state institutions are doing their jobs, Montenegro is protecting its interests, and no one will jeopardize our European future,” he said.
The next paragraph contains profanity.
Rybar confirmed the detention. A post on the Telegram channel emphasized that all those detained were in Montenegro legally and officially. “In particular, there were plans to film at Cetinje Monastery, for which an entirely official request had been submitted beforehand,” the post said. Rybar said it hoped for the detainees’ swift release, since “there were no violations of local law.” Zvinchuk’s presence in Montenegro was indeed public: the day before, he posted a video from there on his RuTube channel. On his Instagram, he wrote that he had gotten into Montenegro despite being under EU and UK sanctions: “You can always run into some fucking idiot of a border guard who empties out all your pockets but forgets to check the database.”
Russia has promised diplomatic support for those detained. “Our diplomats will look into the reasons for the detention and, as with every Russian citizen, work to protect his rights,” Russian presidential press secretary Dmitry Peskov said. Dmitry Medvedev, deputy chairman of Russia’s Security Council, said Russians “needlessly traipse around” European countries and called for Russia to form an “exchange fund” of Europeans and foreigners.
Rybar is one of the most popular Russian pro-war Telegram channels, with more than 1.5 million subscribers. Zvinchuk, a former press officer for Russia’s Defense Ministry, created it with his colleague Denis Shchukin. The channel launched in 2018, and businessman Yevgeny Prigozhin helped fund it in its early years. Rybar describes itself as a “military-analytical center” and runs a network of affiliated channels devoted to specific regions, including “Evropar,” “Afrikar,” and “Balkanar.” In 2024, the U.S. State Department announced a $10 million reward for information on Rybar staffers. According to the American agency, the channel had tried to interfere in the U.S. presidential election.
In September, the Czech Republic expelled two Russians working for Rybar. Vitaly Chashchukhin and Igor Dolmatov were detained after the local outlet Seznam Zprávy reported that Rybar representatives were working in Europe and routinely obtaining comments from politicians and experts. During questioning, they said they officially worked for the newspaper Izvestia, which has been under EU sanctions since 2024. Later, the independent Russian investigative outlet iStories found that Chashchukhin and Dolmatov hold residence permits in Germany and have lived for years in villas in the prestigious Berlin district of Zehlendorf.
Montenegro is preparing to join the EU in the near future. The country’s expected accession date is January 1, 2028, though the timeline could shift if Montenegro fails to make the necessary legislative changes in time. As part of its preparations, Montenegro is aligning its visa policy with EU rules and will introduce a visa regime on November 1 for citizens of certain third countries, including Russia. A report Zvinchuk had previously published addressed this topic, among other things: he discussed how a visa regime for Russian tourists would hurt Montenegro’s economy.
At Meduza, we are committed to transparency about our use of artificial intelligence in the newsroom. The story you’re reading was written by one of our living, breathing journalists and translated from Russian using an AI model configured to follow our strict editorial standards. This translation process is the result of extensive testing and refinements to ensure our English-language coverage is timely and accurate. A Meduza editor reviews every draft before publication.
If you find any errors in this translation, please contact us at [email protected].

articles.title: UK arrests two men for breaking into US intelligence hub
articles.body:
UK arrests two men for breaking into US intelligence hub
British counterterrorism police have arrested two Latvian nationals accused of breaking into a military installation housing major US and NATO intelligence operations, just days after British authorities alleged an Iranian-linked terror plot at an airbase hosting American warplanes.
The two men, aged 32 and 36, were detained early Thursday inside RAF Molesworth in Cambridgeshire after security personnel discovered an abandoned vehicle and a breach in the base’s perimeter fence, according to police.
Both suspects reside in the UK and were initially detained on suspicion of trespassing and criminal damage. They were subsequently arrested under the National Security Act on suspicion of entering a prohibited site for a purpose prejudicial to Britain. Their identities and possible motives have not been disclosed.
RAF Molesworth, roughly 70 miles north of London, hosts US military intelligence operations covering Europe and Africa, as well as NATO’s Intelligence Fusion Centre. Although officially designated a Royal Air Force station, the facility is operated by the US military and does not function as an active airfield.
Counterterrorism investigators have taken over the case, but British authorities have not publicly presented evidence that the breach involved espionage, terrorism or a foreign government.
“We’re very aware of the recent heightened interest and concern around military sites,” Commander Helen Flanagan, head of Counter Terrorism Policing London, said. However, she acknowledged that “at this stage there is nothing to suggest this incident is connected to the events at RAF Fairford.”
The latest incident follows a much-publicized security scare at RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire, where five men were arrested on September 27 after police discovered three suspicious vans near the base, which had been used by American bombers during the US-Israeli war on Iran.
The arrests initially sparked allegations of a possible terrorist bombing or drone attack, with British Prime Minister Andy Burnham suggesting there were “strong indications” of Iranian involvement. Tehran denied the accusations.
Police subsequently acknowledged that no explosive devices had been discovered, with the investigation finding only quantities of petrol in the vehicles. All five suspects were released on bail within days, prompting further questions about the initial assessment of the threat.
Two additional men, including a dual British-Iranian national, were subsequently arrested in connection with the alleged plot. Both have also been released on bail, bringing the total to seven suspects released without charges.
The Fairford scare also coincided with Washington’s abrupt withdrawal of its B-1 strategic bombers from the UK installation. US President Donald Trump linked the decision to security threats, while US Secretary of State Marco Rubio played down a direct connection between the alleged plot and the redeployment.
In the latest Molesworth case, investigators also summoned explosives specialists to examine the abandoned vehicle, briefly imposing a security cordon around nearby roads. The restrictions were lifted after nothing suspicious was found.

articles.title: Sybiha shares details of talks with UK foreign secretary at Pryluky hospital
articles.body:
Sybiha shares details of talks with UK foreign secretary at Pryluky hospital
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha has shared details of his talks with his UK counterpart Ed Miliband, which took place at a hospital in Pryluky, Chernihiv Oblast.
Source: Sybiha on X (Twitter), as reported by Ukrainska Pravda
Details: Sybiha noted that this is Miliband's first official visit to Ukraine as foreign secretary.
Quote from Sybiha: "Alongside President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, we came to Pryluky, where yesterday a Russian missile struck a residential building, killing 22 people, including five children. Ed saw firsthand the devastating consequences of Russia's attacks on Ukrainian civilians. We held our talks at a local hospital."
Details: Sybiha added that he had briefed his UK counterpart on the latest battlefield developments, Russia's intensifying terror, and ongoing diplomatic efforts.
He also said that the talks had covered the steps needed to strengthen Ukraine's position and increase pressure on Moscow to end its aggression.
Quote: "We paid particular attention to immobilised Russian assets and the need to use them fully and make Russia pay for the destruction it has caused. We also discussed tightening sanctions, including against Russia's shadow fleet."
Details: Another important topic was Ukraine's readiness for winter.
Quote: "We discussed additional British assistance to strengthen our energy resilience, protect critical facilities, and keep Ukrainian homes heated and powered."
Details: The officials also addressed Black Sea security, including Russian attacks on civilian vessels and maritime infrastructure that threaten freedom of navigation and global food security.
Quote from Sybiha: "We also launched the second meeting of the Political Pillar of the Ukraine-UK Strategic Partnership Dialogue and agreed to continue expert-level discussions in Kyiv."
Background:
- Earlier, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that Miliband, who had arrived in Kyiv on a visit, had been invited to visit Pryluky to see the reality of Russia's daily strikes.
- During his visit to Pryluky, Miliband assured Ukraine that the UK would provide "concrete support".
